verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: Omidyar Network India announced an end to new investments and a full India exit by end-2024 on 2023-12-11, and three possible causes were present at that time. Timing checks out. The stated reason is in TechCrunch 2023-12-11: the decision was "heavily informed by the significant change in context and the growth in the economic landscape that the India-based team has experienced since first making investments there in 2010." The CBI matter came before the exit: "The move comes a year after Omidyar Network and nine other NGOs came under the radar of India's Central Bureau of Investigation ... over alleged violation of the nation's Foreign Contribution Regulation Act", which puts it around 2022. Neither source gives an exact date or an FIR number. The portfolio losses were in 2023, before or at the same time as the announcement: "2023 has been a rough year ... Doubtnut ... sold for $10 million this month. And ZestMoney ... also announced that it was shutting down." Inc42 adds an earlier item the claim leaves out: ONI was "placed on a watch list by the home ministry" in 2021. No part of the claim fails on dates.
verdicts.identityTest: Both sources name the same entity: "Omidyar Network India", backed by eBay founder Pierre Omidyar, with the same portfolio (1mg, Bounce, Vedantu, DealShare, Doubtnut, Indifi, Pratilipi) and the same $673m AUM. There is one caveat. Inc42 says ONI "has invested through three separate entities" and names an SPV, "ON Mauritius". We still do not know which legal entity (an Indian Section 8 company, the Mauritius SPV, or the US parent) was the one the CBI named, and no CIN or FCRA registration number was found. That gap matters for c012 (the enforce edge). It does not break c013, which is a claim about the group-level decision to exit.
verdicts.baseRate: Two base rates count here. (1) Foreign VC and impact investors cutting back in India during the 2022–23 funding downturn was common. Inc42 names Lightbox, Orios VP and Together Fund changes "in recent weeks" and the Tiger Global retreat. TechCrunch says "many venture investors have struggled to make money in India." So portfolio stress is shared by most comparable firms and does not single out Omidyar. (2) Foreign-funded bodies facing FCRA action were also common: TechCrunch says "Thousands of civil society groups in India have had similar licenses canceled in the past nine years." Very few of the affected foreign donors left India altogether, but we have no denominator counting foreign impact investors under CBI/FCRA scrutiny that exited compared with those that stayed. The claim therefore cannot discriminate between causes, which is exactly what it says. The symmetry control in the SPEC (domestic philanthropy: Azim Premji, Tata, Reliance, Adani) does not apply to a foreign exit. A like-for-like control would be foreign VCs that restructured in 2023 without any enforcement context (Sequoia India became Peak XV, Tiger Global pulled back). On those, the same lens produces the same "ordinary strategy" reading.
verdicts.denialFound: No specific denial found. ONI's only public explanation is market maturity: "Today, there is more Indian led philanthropic and venture capital than ever before ..." (TechCrunch, https://techcrunch.com/2023/12/11/omidyar-network-to-pull-out-of-india-market/). In the founders' call it called the exit "a decision taken by the global leadership which would see the focus shift to other geographies" (Inc42 portfolio founder, https://inc42.com/features/omidyar-network-sudden-expected-exit-india/). Neither source says ONI was asked specifically whether the CBI/FCRA matter played a part: TechCrunch sent only a general request for comment. Record as "none found — whether asked about CBI/FCRA not recorded". The primary statement page, omidyargroup.com, is 404, as already logged as a void. WebSearch budget was exhausted for this session, so later interviews (for example with Omidyar Network CEO Mike Kubzansky) could not be checked.
verdicts.innocentReading: A foreign impact investor funded by one founder's own money winds down a 13-year country programme once domestic VC and philanthropic capital has grown, its early-stage grassroots thesis looks out of date, the 2022–23 downturn has hurt several portfolio companies, and global leadership is shifting focus to other geographies. That fits the firm's statement and Inc42's founder sourcing. Inc42 itself undercuts one part of the current innocentReading: it calls ONI's exit record "healthy for a firm of its vintage" (WhiteHat Jr at 17X, the 1mg sale to Tata) and says the firm "is likely to have faced little to no pressure from its limited partners."
verdicts.reason: The claim survives as analytic. Every one of its facts appears in the cited sources: the stated market-maturity reason, the CBI/FCRA scrutiny about a year before the exit, the Doubtnut and ZestMoney losses, and insiders doubting the "several months of deliberation" line. Its conclusion, that the record cannot rank the causes, is modest and matches Inc42's own framing ("multiple factors at play here, including the firm's problems with Indian law enforcement"). It is not a hidden conjunction implying causation. It explicitly declines to infer causation, and nothing located, whether a board memo, a named executive or a firm statement, attributes the exit to enforcement. There are three weaknesses, all fixable: (a) the list of candidate causes is incomplete compared with Inc42; (b) the innocentReading includes an unsourced statement about other exits and an overstatement about returns; (c) the Inc42 anonymous VC quote ("Omidyar's troubles with CBI were well-known. Most VCs are only surprised by how quickly the firm has announced its exit") is the strongest pro-enforcement evidence in the record and should be quoted, not left implied. None of these moves the tier: analytic is the right tier for an inference based on co-occurrence.
verdicts.corrections: 1. d: change "Three candidate causes" to at least six, all from Inc42: (i) stated market maturity; (ii) enforcement and state pressure, namely the 2021 MHA watch-list restriction on foreign donations, being named as an accused in the CBI FCRA-registration conspiracy case (~2022), and ruling-party criticism in 2023; (iii) 2023 portfolio losses (Doubtnut >75% loss per a portfolio founder, ZestMoney shut, stress at Bounce/DealShare); (iv) the angel-tax change that removed Mauritius from the exempt geographies, which hit ONI's SPV ON Mauritius; (v) the leadership gap after former managing partner Roopa Kudva left (SEBI 2021 insider-trading order); (vi) an outdated impact thesis and a global-leadership decision to shift geographies. Note that (iv) is also a state-policy factor and is separate from enforcement. 2. d: quote the anonymous Bengaluru VC partner as the only sourced statement leaning toward enforcement, and label it anonymous and single-outlet. 3. d: replace "wider post-2020 FCRA tightening" with TechCrunch's wording ("Thousands of civil society groups ... licenses canceled in the past nine years"), or add a source for the post-2020 amendment. 4. innocentReading: delete "Omidyar Network has exited other geographies without any enforcement context", which is unsourced in this record, or add a source for it. Change "its own returns disappointed" to "several 2023 portfolio companies failed (Doubtnut, ZestMoney), though Inc42 calls its overall exit record healthy and reports little LP pressure." 5. d: change "write-downs" to "distress sale / shutdown", because no mark-downs by ONI itself are documented. 6. Add a contra-style note: "ONI's public statement cites market maturity only; not recorded whether ONI was asked about CBI/FCRA." 7. killIf: keep it, and add "or a named ONI or Omidyar Network executive on record denying any FCRA/CBI role, with dated deliberation documents." 8. Sources: add Business Today (https://www.businesstoday.in/entrepreneurship/start-up/story/impact-fund-omidyar-network-to-exit-india-409191-2023-12-12) only after it is actually opened; the fetch returned no text this session.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as a sentence: USAID obligated US$97m under seven G2G projects with GoI in FY2023-24 (Apr 2023 to Mar 2024), as disclosed in the Finance Ministry's annual report 2023-24 and reported by PTI/Business Standard on 2025-02-23. The article is dated after the fiscal year it describes, and USAID was operating in India throughout FY24, before the 2025 dismantling, so the dates fit. The edge's from/to of 2023-04 to 2024-03 matches 'For the financial year 2023-24' in a GoI report. Caveat: USAID obligates money on the US fiscal year (Oct to Sep). That the report means India's FY is an inference until the report is opened.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor, USAID, is named in the source. The counterparty is wrong. The source says the projects are 'implemented by USAID in partnership with Government of India' and that the Department of Economic Affairs is 'the nodal department for bilateral funding arrangements'. It never says the Ministry of Finance received the money. USAID obligations fund implementing partners under agreements with GoI, and the DEA only coordinates. So t=min:ministry-of-finance, a grant edge carrying a=825 (money flowing s→t), and benefit.who=MoF with 'Grant finance to Union ministries' programmes' all say more than the source does.
verdicts.baseRate: Not an accusatory claim, so the discrimination test barely applies. Bilateral G2G development aid coordinated through the DEA is routine: JICA, KfW, FCDO and ADB grants all pass through the same nodal channel. US$97m in a year is small next to JICA's ODA loans to India. The controls in the NGO SPEC concern FCRA cancellations and associations, not bilateral G2G aid, so no symmetry issue arises. Recording JICA/KfW G2G flows the same way would be the symmetric treatment.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed or found, because the disclosure comes from GoI itself (the Finance Ministry annual report). The only contest is over the separate US$21m 'voter turnout' claim by DOGE and Trump. The same article reports the Finance Ministry report's statement that 'no funding was made for enhancing voter turnout' in the year, EAM Jaishankar calling the US claims 'concerning', and Congress (Jairam Ramesh) saying the US$21m was for Bangladesh. Source: https://www.business-standard.com/external-affairs-defence-security/news/usaid-funded-7-projects-in-india-in-fy24-not-related-to-voter-turnout-govt-125022300390_1.html
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a routine, publicly disclosed bilateral development programme: agriculture and food security, WASH, renewable energy, disaster management, health, forests and climate adaptation, and energy efficiency. It is coordinated by the DEA as nodal department and reported in the government's own annual report. Nothing in the claim implies wrongdoing.
verdicts.reason: The Business Standard (PTI) article, which I opened (HTTP 200), supports the core figures word for word: "Currently, seven projects worth a total budget of USD 750 million (approx.) are being implemented by USAID in partnership with Government of India," as per the Finance Ministry annual report for 2023-24. For the financial year 2023-24, an obligation of a total of USD 97 million (about Rs 825 crore) has been made by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) under the seven projects. 'reported' is the right tier: one wire story quoting a primary document the record admits was not opened. I tried to open the DEA report: curl to dea.gov.in failed TLS verification (exit 60, incomplete certificate chain), WebFetch got 503, and the proxy rejected finmin.nic.in. So no upgrade is possible now. PTI syndication elsewhere is the same wire, not an independent second outlet. The claim is not refuted, but it has three field errors, listed under corrections: the counterparty, the unsupported attribution of the rupee conversion, and the sector list.
verdicts.corrections: 1) t: change min:ministry-of-finance to a Government of India node (e.g. gov:india), or keep DEA only as the nodal counterparty with a note that it coordinates rather than receives the money. Rewrite benefit.who and benefit.how to say that USAID obligations fund implementing partners under G2G agreements, not transfers to the Ministry of Finance. 2) d: remove 'the Finance Ministry annual report's own conversion'. The article gives '(about Rs 825 crore)' in PTI's paraphrase, not in a quote from the report, and the report was not opened, so attribute it as 'about ₹825 crore per PTI'. The derived ₹6,375 crore figure for the US$750m is our own conversion and should be labelled that way. 3) d sectors: 'rural development' is not in the source. Replace the list with the source's: agriculture & food security, WASH, renewable energy, disaster management, health, Sustainable Forests and Climate Adaptation, and Energy Efficiency Technology Commercialization and Innovation. 4) State explicitly that a is an obligation, not a disbursement. 5) benefit.confidence: 'reported' rather than 'estimated'. 6) Add an innocentReading (routine DEA-coordinated bilateral aid) and a killIf (the DEA annual report 2023-24 gives different figures). Keep the upgradeIf, but note that dea.gov.in failed TLS verification (exit 60) and returned 503 on 2026-09-26, and the proxy rejected finmin.nic.in.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: DOGE (US executive) said on 2025-02-16 that USAID was giving CEPPS US$21m for "voter turnout in India", and cancelled it; Trump repeated it on 2025-02-19/20. The dates match the sources. Tribune (2025-02-17): "$486 million in grants to the Consortium for Elections and Political Process Strengthening" included "$21 million for 'voter turnout in India'", cancelled on Sunday 16 Feb. Business Standard (2025-02-21, 11:37 IST) gives the same date. The underlying award, however, is the 2022-07 CEPPS award for Bangladesh (Amar Vote Amar/Nagorik, July 2022 to October 2024). BS: "USAID's official records confirm that no projects funded by the Consortium for Elections and Political Process Strengthening (CEPPS) have been implemented in India since 2008." So there is no India-designated award in any window for the from=2025-02-16 edge to attach to. The ₹85/US$ conversion is also out of date. It comes from the FY2023-24 Finance Ministry report. The RBI reference rate in mid-February 2025 was about ₹86.6-87.0, which gives about ₹182 crore; Bhaskar's headline uses "₹182 cr".
verdicts.identityTest: The assertion is attributed correctly: the DOGE X post, and Trump quoted in BS as "Why do we need to spend $21 million for voter turnout in India? Wow, $21 million! I guess they were trying to get somebody else elected." The nodes are wrong as a money edge. ngo:usaid to ngo:cepps for US$21m exists only as the Bangladesh award, and c017 already records that award at the same ₹178.5 crore. c015 therefore gives the same money twice and puts the second copy in India. BS names the implementers as IFES, IRI and NDI, for Bangladesh. The venue is uncertain. BS says "speaking in Miami", but my recollection is that the "somebody else elected" line was said on 2025-02-20 at the Republican Governors Association in Washington, and the Miami FII speech on 02-19 used different wording. I could not verify this, so I am flagging it rather than asserting it. Trump's own version then changed: "$18 million going to my friend Prime Minister Modi" (Indian Express, 2025-02-24).
verdicts.baseRate: Several items in DOGE's February 2025 cancellation lists were later shown to be mislabelled or misattributed. The Washington Post (2025-02-22) ran "How a false DOGE claim ignited a political firestorm in India". A country label that is wrong in a DOGE list does not tell you much about any particular country. Symmetry: both sides used the same claim as a weapon. BJP (Amit Malviya, quoted in Tribune): "external interference in India's electoral process". Congress later used Trump's "my friend Modi" version against the BJP (Scroll, 2025-02-23). Under the same lens neither party is supported, because no money reached India. The Bangladesh control has a documented award; India has none.
verdicts.denialFound: A response exists, so c016's text is wrong. On 2025-08-21 MEA told Parliament, citing US Embassy data, that USAID gave no US$21m for voter turnout in India. My recollection is that this was a written Rajya Sabha answer by MoS Kirti Vardhan Singh, which said the Embassy's 2014-2024 USAID data showed no US$21m received and no voter-turnout activity implemented. I confirmed the event only from Google News RSS listings dated 2025-08-21/22. These headlines include the Indian Express ("Citing US embassy, Govt confirms: No $21-million USAID poll grant in India"), The Hindu ("USAID didn't receive funding of $21 million for voter turnout in India: Embassy to MEA"), NDTV ("US Embassy Contradicts Trump's 'USAID Fund For Voter Turnout In India' Claim"), The Wire ("MEA Says US Embassy Denies Trump's Claim of $21m USAID Funds to Modi, All USAID Pacts with India Ended August 15"), Scroll, TOI and BOOM. I could not open the article bodies (The Wire renders with JS; Google News links are encoded), so the MoS name and the 2014-2024 window are unconfirmed. Earlier, ThePrint (2025-03-17) reported that MEA had asked the US Embassy for details. The Washington Post (2025-02-22) called it "a false DOGE claim". I found no statement from CEPPS, IFES, IRI or NDI themselves; whether they were asked is unknown.
verdicts.innocentReading: DOGE staff labelled a line from the CEPPS award portfolio as "India" when the US$21m voter-participation award was for Bangladesh. Trump repeated the label, and the figure then drifted to "$18 million … to my friend Modi". The boring explanation is a clerical mislabel amplified by political speech, not a hidden India grant. It fits every piece of evidence: the Bangladesh award records, "no CEPPS projects in India since 2008", and the US Embassy's own data given to MEA.
verdicts.reason: Kill it as an edge; keep it as a narrative. The assertion is accurately sourced: both URLs say DOGE listed and cancelled "$21 million for 'voter turnout in India'", and BS quotes Trump. But the edge claims that USAID sent ₹178.5 crore to CEPPS for India. Its own killIf is met ("USAID award records show the only US$21m CEPPS voter-participation grant was for Bangladesh"). BS/Indian Express report it, and the asserting party's own government then withdrew it: the US Embassy told MEA, and MEA reported this to Parliament in August 2025. The claim's line "contra c016 = no CEPPS/USAID response recorded" is false, because the US government, which now administers what was USAID, did respond. Keeping the edge would also count c017's Bangladesh money twice and place it inside the India graph.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Remove the c015 money edge (s=ngo:usaid, t=ngo:cepps, pred=grant, a=178.5, benefit.amountCr=178.5). Keep c015 as a narrative or claim node labelled "DOGE/Trump assertion (2025-02-16/20), withdrawn by US Embassy data (2025-08)", with a=null, and set supersededBy to c017. 2) Rewrite c016 to record the US Embassy data given to MEA and reported to Parliament on 2025-08-21 (Rajya Sabha written answer). Denier node: US Embassy New Delhi or US government. Use the MEA Rajya Sabha Q&A page as the source, fetched from mea.gov.in or sansad.in, and use the Indian Express, The Hindu or The Wire articles of 2025-08-21/22 as secondary sources. Remove the "No response recorded — asked/not asked unknown" wording. Once the primary text is fetched, that contra is documented-tier. Also add the Washington Post 2025-02-22 item. 3) Fix the FX rate: use the RBI reference rate for 2025-02-17 (about ₹86.9/US$, roughly ₹182 crore), not the FY2023-24 FinMin rate of ₹85. Or drop the rupee figure altogether, since no money flowed. 4) Mark the "in Miami" venue as unverified: the "somebody else elected" line may be from the 2025-02-20 RGA speech in Washington. Add Trump's later "$18 million … my friend Modi" variant (Indian Express, 2025-02-24) to show the assertion was unstable. 5) Fill in innocentReading with the mislabelled-line-item explanation.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: USAID (Bangladesh mission) awarded CEPPS a US$21m cooperative agreement, signed July 2022 and funded until the cancellation announced 2025-02-16. The USAspending primary record FAIN 72038822LA00001 matches. It was signed 2022-07-27, with period of performance 2022-08-01 to 2025-07-31. The original description was "USAID'S AMAR VOTE AMAR (AVA) ACTIVITY". Mod P002 on 2022-11-21 renamed it "USAID'S NAGORIK (CITIZEN) ACTIVITY". Obligations were 7.0m (2022-07-27), 6.3m (2023-09-14), 1.656m (2024-03-28) and 6.044m (2024-10-10), totalling 21.0m. BS says "Between July 2022 and October 2024, this $21 million was distributed". That matches the first and last obligation dates. The claim's from=2022-07 passes. to=2025-02-16 is the DOGE cancellation date, not the scheduled end, which was 2025-07-31. Both dates are defensible if labelled.
verdicts.identityTest: Recipient on USAspending: "CONSORTIUM FOR ELECTIONS & POLITICAL PROCESS STRENGTHENING", UEI E3U6WMW4XSK7, Washington DC. Awarding office: USAID/BANGLADESH. Place of performance: BGD, "ALL OR MOSTLY IN BANGLADESH". So s=ngo:usaid and t=ngo:cepps are the right entities. BS names the implementers as IFES, IRI and NDI (the CEPPS members). I checked every CEPPS-recipient award on USAspending from FY2008 to FY2026 (3 pages, about 230 awards). None has India as the place of performance. A few 2007-08 legacy records have a null country. This supports "no CEPPS project in India since 2008". Identity problem with "the only": USAspending also shows a second US$21,000,000 CEPPS award. That is 72027823LA00001, Jordan, "USAID CIVIC AND POLITICAL STRENGTHENING ACTIVITY (CAPS)", signed 2023-06-19. Its objectives include "Women and youth's political engagement strengthened", so it is also a civic/political-participation grant. The Bangladesh award is therefore not the only US$21m CEPPS participation grant. It is the only one that fits DOGE's description (2022 start, voter/youth turnout, South Asia, cancelled in Feb 2025).
verdicts.baseRate: CEPPS runs country-specific associate awards in about 100 countries. Awards of US$15-30m are common, and at least two are exactly US$21m (Bangladesh, Jordan). South Asian CEPPS awards on record: Bangladesh 2013 and 2022, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Pakistan, Bhutan. India is the one South Asian country with none since FY2008. A US$21m CEPPS grant is therefore not distinctive in itself. What discriminates is the country field, and on that the record is clear.
verdicts.denialFound: This claim is itself the rebuttal of c015. On 2025-08-21/22 MEA told Parliament, citing US Embassy data, that USAID had given no US$21m for voter turnout in India. Coverage: Indian Express, "Citing US embassy, Govt confirms: No $21-million USAID poll grant in India"; The Hindu, "USAID didn't receive funding of $21 million for voter turnout in India: Embassy to MEA"; also TOI, NDTV, Scroll and The Wire, all 2025-08-21/22. I found these through Google News RSS listings and did not open the Parliament answer PDF. The Washington Post (2025-02-22) ran "How a false DOGE claim ignited a political firestorm in India". I found no retraction by DOGE or the White House, and no statement by CEPPS, IFES, IRI or NDI. Whether they were asked is unknown.
verdicts.innocentReading: The obvious reading holds and is dull: DOGE's list attached the wrong country label to the South Asian CEPPS youth-voter award (Bangladesh, Amar Vote Amar/Nagorik). No hidden India channel is needed to explain the US$21m figure. The claim makes no accusation against any Indian actor. It frames no family, religion or ethnicity as the actor, and the SPEC's FCRA controls do not apply.
verdicts.reason: The claim is not refuted, and the primary record now exists. BS confirms the reported content word for word: "The $21 million grant was allocated to Bangladesh, where it supported a programme called Amar Vote Amar (My Vote is Mine). The programme was later renamed the Nagorik (Citizen) Programme." It also says "By the time the cancellation was announced, $13.4 million had already been utilised" and "USAID's official records confirm that no projects funded by the Consortium for Elections and Political Process Strengthening (CEPPS) have been implemented in India since 2008." USAspending award 72038822LA00001 independently documents the US$21m, the signing date, the renaming, the recipient's UEI and the Bangladesh place of performance. It also shows no India-sited CEPPS award since FY2008. That meets the claim's own upgradeIf ("USAspending.gov award record for the CEPPS Bangladesh agreement opened"), so the tier should rise to documented. One overstatement needs fixing: "the only US$21m USAID–CEPPS voter-participation grant" is false as written, because the Jordan CAPS award (72027823LA00001) is also a US$21m CEPPS civic/political-participation grant. The US$13.4m figure is IE/BS's number for money spent at cancellation. USAspending now shows lifetime outlays of US$17,263,909.88, which includes spending after February 2025.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Tier: reported -> documented. Add src ["USAspending.gov award 72038822LA00001 (CEPPS, USAID/Bangladesh)", "https://www.usaspending.gov/award/ASST_NON_72038822LA00001_072"]. Set upgradeIf to null or mark it met. 2) text/lab: replace "The only US$21m USAID–CEPPS voter-participation grant" with "The US$21m USAID–CEPPS award matching DOGE's 'voter turnout' line". Add: "(another US$21m CEPPS award exists, Jordan CAPS 72027823LA00001, 2023)". 3) d: "sanctioned 2022-07" -> "signed 2022-07-27 (FAIN 72038822LA00001), period of performance 2022-08-01 to 2025-07-31; renamed Nagorik by mod P002 on 2022-11-21; obligated in four tranches 7.0m/6.3m/1.656m/6.044m, the last on 2024-10-10". 4) Amount: keep "US$13.4m utilised by cancellation (IE/BS)". BS says "utilised", not "disbursed". Add "USAspending lifetime outlays US$17.26m (as of 2026-09)". 5) Rupee conversion: ₹178.5 cr applies a 2025 ₹85/US$ rate to obligations made in 2022-24. Report USD as primary, or convert each tranche at its own rate (about ₹79.8/US$ in July 2022). Set benefit.confidence to "estimated (FX)". 6) "No CEPPS project in India since 2008": add a src for the USAspending CEPPS recipient search (no IND place of performance, FY2008 to FY2026). Add the Aug 2025 MEA Parliament answer citing US Embassy data as corroboration once the PDF is opened. 7) "to": state that 2025-02-16 is the DOGE cancellation date and the scheduled end was 2025-07-31. 8) innocentReading: fill it with "DOGE list mislabelled the South Asian CEPPS youth-voter award" rather than leaving it null.

verdicts.dateTest: Passes. Restated: USAID obligated US$97m (about ₹825 cr) in FY2023-24 (Apr 2023–Mar 2024) under seven bilateral projects, as disclosed in the Finance Ministry's 2023-24 annual report and reported by PTI/Business Standard on 2025-02-23. The DOGE claim (2025-02-16) and the Bangladesh CEPPS grant (2022-07 to 2025-02, c017) fall inside the window being compared. "from": "2025-02" is the disclosure date, not the date of the money. The `d` field should say the figure covers FY2023-24.
verdicts.identityTest: Fails on the target node. The source does not say the money went to the Government of India or the Ministry of Finance. Its words are: "Currently, seven projects worth a total budget of USD 750 million (approx.) are being implemented by USAID in partnership with Government of India", and "an obligation of a total of USD 97 million (about Rs 825 crore) has been made by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) under the seven projects". The source says DEA "is the nodal department for bilateral funding arrangements". That makes DEA the counterparty and signatory, not the recipient of funds. USAID in India does not give budget support. Obligated funds go to implementing partners (contractors and NGOs, including Indian associations), not into the Consolidated Fund. The edge ngo:usaid -> min:ministry-of-finance, read under the contract's s->t money-flow convention, therefore states a flow the source does not describe. The claim's wording "USAID money to GoI" is wrong for the same reason.
verdicts.baseRate: The comparison does not discriminate. Any positive figure "dwarfs" zero, so the claim's word "dwarfs" carries no information. Among bilateral donors to India (JICA, FCDO, GIZ/KfW, USAID), close to 100% have DEA-registered bilateral portfolios that nobody treats as interference. The only discriminating fact is on the other side of the comparison: the "zero documented USAID election money" in India. That rests on c017: the Indian Express investigation, carried by Business Standard on 2025-02-21, found the US$21m CEPPS grant was for Bangladesh and that USAID records show no CEPPS project in India since 2008. That is reported tier, not documented. SPEC control: this claim is itself the symmetry check. The same lens applied to the Congress-era USAID portfolio (UPA) gives the same reading, so the claim holds up on symmetry.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable as a denial, since the claim accuses no one. Party statements on record: DEA/FinMin annual report, via PTI (BS 2025-02-23): "During the year, no funding was made for enhancing voter turnout but to projects related to agriculture & food security programme; WASH; Renewable Energy; disaster management and health." Jaishankar (BS 2025-02-23) said USAID "was allowed in India 'in good faith, to do good faith activities'" and that the government was "looking into it". The `d` field's assertion that "nobody in the controversy called [the bilateral portfolio] interference" has no source. The government's own publication of the portfolio was its answer to the controversy, and Jaishankar's "bad faith" remark was about USAID's activities in general. That sentence is an unsourced negative and should be removed or sourced.
verdicts.innocentReading: The ₹825 cr is an obligation (a commitment, not a disbursement) under agreements where DEA is the nodal counterparty. The money is spent through USAID-contracted implementers on agriculture, WASH, renewable energy, disaster and health work. Its size says nothing about influence by either side. It is also not "audited G2G money" in GoI's accounts: USAID audits it under US rules, not the CAG. The "zero election money" side is an absence of evidence, reported by one investigation, not a documented negative.
verdicts.reason: The figure is confirmed exactly: Business Standard/PTI 2025-02-23, quoting the FinMin 2023-24 annual report, says "an obligation of a total of USD 97 million (about Rs 825 crore) has been made by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) under the seven projects". The claim still misstates what the figure is. The source describes an obligation for projects "implemented by USAID in partnership with Government of India", with DEA as nodal department, not "USAID money to GoI". The edge target min:ministry-of-finance therefore asserts a money flow to the ministry that the source does not support. Part of the obligated money plausibly reaches Indian associations as implementing partners, which undermines the claim's contrast between GoI and associations. The claim's other load-bearing parts also fall short. "Dwarfs zero" is non-discriminating. "Nobody called it interference" is unsourced. "G2G is audited" (from innocentReading) overstates the record. The underlying analytic point survives: the government documents only non-election USAID programming in FY24, and no document shows USAID election money in India. So the claim can stay at analytic tier once the flow framing is corrected.
verdicts.corrections: 1) text/lab: replace "USAID money to GoI (₹825 cr FY24)" with "US$97m (≈₹825 cr) obligated by USAID in FY2023-24 under seven projects implemented in partnership with GoI (DEA nodal); FinMin annual report states none was for voter turnout". Drop "dwarfs"; say instead that the government-disclosed portfolio contains no election programming and no document shows USAID election funding in India (c017, reported). 2) t: change min:ministry-of-finance to the DEA node (or keep the MoF node) but mark it as agreement counterparty, not payee. Put a note in `d` that the edge is not an s->t money flow. 3) d: delete "which nobody in the controversy called interference", or source it. Add Jaishankar's "good faith"/"looking into it" remark (BS 2025-02-23) as the government's stated position. 4) innocentReading: replace "audited G2G assistance" with "bilateral project assistance under DEA agreements, spent through USAID implementers; an obligation, not a disbursement; audited under US, not CAG, rules". 5) killIf: add "USAID/DEA records show any FY2023-24 obligation to election or civic-participation programming in India". 6) State the tier basis for the "zero" leg as reported (Indian Express via BS, c017), not documented. verdicts.dateTest: Claim: the Intelligence Bureau named Greenpeace India in a report dated 2014-06-03. The News Minute (Dhanya Rajendran, 13 June 2014, republished 25 Feb 2015) says: "The Intelligence Bureau report dated June 3, 2014 on 'The concerted effort by select foreign funded NGOs to take down Indian developmental projects'..." and "The report was commissioned by the previous government and has been submitted to the new government." The date is consistent with the government changing on 26 May 2014, so a report commissioned under UPA and delivered to the NDA fits. The BHRRC timeline also lists an item "IB Report, Concerted efforts by select foreign funded NGOs to 'take down' Indian development projects — Date: 3 Jun 2014". The date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: The IB is named as the author. Greenpeace is named, but only as "Greenpeace", with no FCRA registration number. At that time there were two FCRA-registered entities, Greenpeace India Society and Greenpeace Foundation, and the record does not say which one is meant; mapping it to ngo:greenpeace-india is reasonable, but the node should note the ambiguity. Coal India Ltd, Hindalco, Aditya Birla group and Essar are named exactly as in the source. Hindalco is itself an Aditya Birla group company, so the list double-counts. Greenpeace's actual coal campaign (Mahan, Madhya Pradesh, which TNM also mentions) was against the Mahan Coal block, an Essar–Hindalco joint venture, not against Coal India.
verdicts.baseRate: Being named in this report does not single Greenpeace out. The report names seven movements and many NGOs and activists: NAPM, PUCL, PMANE, Greenpeace, the anti-GM groups, the Posco, Vedanta and Narmada movements, and Dutch NGOs in the North East. BHRRC headlines refer to "22 NGOs in IB report". Every prominent NGO opposing a large project got the same treatment. Symmetry control from the SPEC: the report was commissioned under UPA, and the same IB lens was used by UPA in the 2012 Kudankulam-linked FCRA cancellations (PMANE-linked groups). So the framing is not unique to the NDA, and the claim's d text correctly says "Commissioned under UPA, delivered to the NDA government".
verdicts.denialFound: Greenpeace India rejected the report on 11 June 2014 (IANS via Deccan Herald, https://www.deccanherald.com/india/greenpeace-rejects-ib-report-swears-2210733; only the headline and dateline were extractable, the body text was not). This is recorded as contra c021. In the sources I opened, the IB and MHA neither disowned nor authenticated the leaked text. I could not search for a government statement because the web-search budget was used up. Other contrary reporting: the BHRRC timeline lists "IB report based on unfounded allegations, claim anti-nuclear activists" (14 Jun 2014), "PUCL Condemns IB Report" and "IB's NGO-scare report to Modi plagiarises from old Modi speech" (13 Jun 2014).
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a routine intelligence threat assessment of foreign-funded advocacy, commissioned by the outgoing government. It lists the companies whose projects the campaigns targeted as description, not advocacy on their behalf. Naming Coal India, Hindalco and Essar records what Greenpeace campaigned against. It does not show that the IB acted for those companies, or that they asked for or received anything.
verdicts.reason: The substance holds. TNM, working from the leaked report, confirms every factual element word for word: the date of June 3, 2014; the 21 pages; the "anti-developmental activities" framing; "Greenpeace is mainly against Coal India Ltd, Hindalco, Aditya Birla group and Essar"; the 2-3% of GDP estimate; and "it does not mention how it arrived at the percentage". Greenpeace's rejection exists as c021. "Reported" is the right tier: the report was leaked (first excerpted by the Indian Express) and never tabled or officially published, so upgradeIf is set correctly. The weak points are in the edge fields, not the facts. (1) The BHRRC URL is a list of headlines. It supports the report's date and the fact that it was leaked, but none of the Greenpeace, Coal India or GDP content. (2) The benefit to co:coal-india is our own inference ("confidence: unknown"), not something the source says. Coal India was not the real target of the Mahan campaign, and benefit.how mentions POSCO and Vedanta, which have nothing to do with this Greenpeace edge. (3) Calling it "enforce" is a stretch. An intelligence assessment is not a cancellation, freeze or sanction; the actual enforcement against Greenpeace came later from the MHA (fund block from June 2014, FCRA suspension in April 2015, cancellation in September 2015).
verdicts.corrections: (a) Leave the tier at reported and keep the TNM quote as the primary source. Label the BHRRC URL "timeline — date and leak corroboration only", or replace it with the original Indian Express report of 7/12 June 2014. (b) Set innocentReading, which is currently null, to the text above. (c) benefit: either delete it, or label it analytic and change who from co:coal-india to the Mahan Coal Ltd sponsors (Essar Power / Hindalco), since TNM ties Greenpeace's coal campaign to Mahan. Remove POSCO and Vedanta from benefit.how on this Greenpeace edge. Keep confidence: unknown. (d) The predicate "enforce" should carry a d note: "intelligence assessment (not itself an enforcement action)". The alternative is to re-point enforcement to the MHA edges (the June 2014 foreign-fund block and the 2015 FCRA suspension and cancellation), with this report as their stated antecedent. (e) Claim text: "Aditya Birla" should read "Aditya Birla group", as in the source. Note that Hindalco is an Aditya Birla group company. (f) Add a node note that "Greenpeace" in the source is not specified as Greenpeace India Society or Greenpeace Foundation. (g) killIf is fine as written. Also add "absence of an IB/MHA authentication or denial: not asked, none recorded".

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, restated: the IB report dated 2014-06-03 put the negative effect of "anti-developmental" activity at 2–3% and gave no method for the figure. The News Minute (Dhanya Rajendran, 13 June 2014; the page's CMS republication stamp reads 25 Feb 2015) supports this: "The Intelligence Bureau report dated June 3, 2014 ... names seven protest movements." It also says: "The report was commissioned by the previous government and has been submitted to the new government." The record's from=2014-06 is therefore correct, with no date conflict. It does leave out that the report was commissioned under UPA and delivered to NDA, which matters for symmetry.
verdicts.identityTest: The document is correctly identified: the IB report of 3 June 2014, "The concerted effort by select foreign funded NGOs to 'take down' Indian developmental projects", 21 pages, never officially published. No person or company identifier (CIN, DIN, FCRA number) applies. The target node ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate fits loosely, since the source says only that "some" of the report's financial data are FCRA figures. It does not say that all the funding the report cites is FCRA-registered.
verdicts.baseRate: This test does not discriminate much. Leaked intelligence assessments almost never show their method, so "no traceable method" is true of most IB and agency assessments and is weak evidence of bad faith on its own. The claim makes only a methodological point and implies no wrongdoing, which is right for an analytic claim. On symmetry with the SPEC control (UPA vs NDA): the source says UPA commissioned the report, and in 2012 the UPA government made its own unsourced claims that foreign-funded NGOs were behind the Kudankulam protests. Applied to either government, this lens gives the same reading, so the claim is not partisan. It should say so.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. Neither IB nor MHA has published or defended the method behind the 2–3% figure, and the News Minute piece does not say IB or MHA were asked about it. My web-search budget was used up, so I could not look further for a later government response or an economist's reconstruction of the figure. The absence of a response is recorded, not confirmed. Greenpeace's rejection of the report as a whole (IANS/Deccan Herald, 2014-06-11) is already in the file as a separate claim, and it does not address the GDP figure.
verdicts.innocentReading: Intelligence assessments are not economic papers. The figure could be a rhetorical order of magnitude, or borrowed from industry or ministry estimates of stalled-project costs (POSCO, Vedanta, Kudankulam, coal blocks), and those delays did cost real money. The report was an internal brief never meant for publication, so its missing citations are normal practice, not proof that the number was made up.
verdicts.reason: The core holds. The News Minute says directly: "The report begins prominently by saying that negative effects of such anti-developmental activities on GDP growth is estimated to be at 2-3%. ... when it quantifies the negative impact on the GDP, it does not mention how it arrived at the percentage. For some of the financial data, the IB quotes FCRA figures - but there is no mention of any money that has come through illegal means." The tier is right: "no method" is reported by the outlet, while "lawful", "not reproducible" and "rhetorical" are our own inferences, and the record carries an innocentReading. The source check is only partial, because the claim goes further than the source in three places. (1) It says "2–3% of GDP", but the source says 2–3% effect on GDP *growth*, which is a different quantity. (2) It says "the financial data it cites are lawful FCRA receipts", but the source says only "some of the financial data" are FCRA figures, and being FCRA-reported is not the same as being lawful. The source only notes that the report mentions no illegal money. (3) The 'd' field's comparison to "India's entire annual public health budget share" is loose: government health spending was about 1.1–1.3% of GDP in 2014–15, so 2–3% of GDP would be roughly double, and the comparison fails altogether under the "of GDP growth" reading. "Not reproducible from any published estimate" is a universal negative that has not been checked.
verdicts.corrections: 1) text/lab: change "2–3% of GDP figure" to "2–3% negative effect on GDP growth figure", which is the source's wording. 2) text/d: change "the financial data it cites are lawful FCRA receipts" to "some of the financial data it cites are FCRA-reported receipts; the report mentions no money received through illegal means (TNM)". Drop "(i.e., lawful)". 3) d: delete the comparison to the public health budget share, or restate it accurately (government health spending was about 1.1–1.3% of GDP in 2014–15, and the comparison only works under the misread "of GDP" framing). 4) d: soften "not reproducible from any published estimate" to "no published estimate reproducing it was located", since it has not been checked. 5) Add a symmetry note: TNM says the report "was commissioned by the previous government [UPA] and has been submitted to the new government". The unsourced claim that NGOs cost the economy money spans both governments (compare UPA's 2012 Kudankulam foreign-funding claims). 6) Add a response field: "IB/MHA not asked; no public defence of the method found". 7) upgradeIf/killIf are fine as written.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as stated: Sabrang/SACW (asserting party) say IDRF (Maryland 501(c)(3), active since the late 1980s) disbursed funds mainly to Sangh affiliates, 1994–2000. The source says: "In the years from 1994 to 2000 for which the data is available, roughly 75% of the IDRF's total disbursements (over $ 3.2 million) went to the IDRF–designated organizations." That matches the edge's from=1994 and to=2000. Footnote 36/37 cites "Annual Reports of IDRF" for 1994–2001, a minor mismatch. The report is dated 2002, and Outlook republished it on 20 November 2002. IDRF was operating across the whole window, so the date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The cited source is the full text of §4 of "The Foreign Exchange of Hate: IDRF and the American Funding of Hindutva", © 2002 Sabrang Communications & Publishing Pvt Ltd and The South Asia Citizens Web, republished by Outlook. It names IDRF throughout, the same Maryland charity as node ngo:idrf. The recipients it names are "Parivar organizations, especially those affiliated with or controlled by the RSS, the VHP and the Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram (VKA)", with Sewa Bharati and Ekal Vidyalaya named in §4.4.3. The target node "rss" is defined in the file as "RSS and its affiliates (Sangh Parivar)", so the collective target is defensible, though VKA would be more precise. The edge frames an organisational family, not a religion or ethnicity, so it passes the framing test. No EIN has been verified for IDRF, and the file's gap already records that the guessed EINs failed.
verdicts.baseRate: It is normal, not unusual, for a US diaspora religious charity to fund service networks of its own faith. Christian charities do the same through church partners (the Compassion and World Vision controls), and so do Muslim and Sikh diaspora charities. The share going to Hindu or Sangh bodies is therefore not discriminating by itself. The only discriminating evidence is inside the report: IDRF-designated funds went more than 80% to the Sangh, but "only 10% of the donor-designated funds were earmarked for Sangh charities." That contrast rests on the report's own coding of recipients (Appendix H), which the HVK rebuttal disputes. The symmetry test gives the same result: the lens that reads Sangh-affiliated service work as political funding also reads church-affiliated service work as conversion funding (narrative 5). The file's symmetryCheck and narrative already record this, and in both cases the conclusion rests on inferences from who the grantees are, not on any adjudicated finding.
verdicts.denialFound: HVK / Ashok Chowgule rebuttal, opened at https://hvk.org/specialreports/hate/1.html. Its §1.1 summarises the report as saying "because IDRF provides donations to some of the social service projects started by the Hindutva organisations, IDRF is funding the violence". It attacks the authors' agenda ("conclude first and then get the data"), "guilt by association" and "perverting the data" (§1.5). It does not dispute that money flows to Sangh-run service projects. What it disputes is the characterisation and the method. IDRF's own November 2002 "pure concoction" statement and the 2003 six-academic rebuttal (letindiadevelop.org returns 403) were not opened. WebSearch was exhausted this session, and idrf.org's current site shows nothing about the report. No evidence shows whether IDRF was asked before publication.
verdicts.innocentReading: IDRF's founders and officers had Sangh links, and in rural and tribal India the largest Hindu-oriented networks that run schools and tribal welfare (VKA, Sewa Bharati, Ekal) are Sangh affiliates. A diaspora charity picking its own grantees would send money to networks it knows and trusts. On the report's own figures, about 70% of IDRF funds went to education and about 15% to relief. Both ends of the flow were lawful and declared, and no tribunal has found that IDRF money paid for violence. The "Sangh-affiliated" coding is the critics' own classification.
verdicts.reason: The cited source was opened and it supports the core edge as an allegation by a named party: "A vast majority (in excess of 80%) of the IDRF designated funds were sent to Parivar organizations, especially those affiliated with or controlled by the RSS, the VHP and the Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram (VKA)." Alleged is the right tier. The only primary is the critics' report, the rebuttal disputes its coding, and IDRF's schedules have not been opened. A contra (c024) exists, as the tier requires. The HVK rebuttal concedes that the flow exists and contests the characterisation. The edge is not refuted, but the claim text contains a false caveat. It says the "83%" figure is "from secondary summaries, not verified in the primary text". The primary text at the cited URL states it: "None of the organizations funded can be identified with any minority community, though 8% (in addition to the 83% that are Sangh affiliated) are clearly identifiable as Hindu or Jain religious organizations." The d field's "Amount not stated in the section opened" is also wrong, because the section states "over $ 3.2 million". The claim also overstates scope. The 80–83% applies to IDRF-designated funds, about 75% of disbursements. Donor-designated funds were 10% Sangh. Combining the two gives roughly 65% of total disbursements. That still counts as "predominantly", but as the claim's own inference, not the source's sentence.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Claim text and d: delete "the '83%' figure is from secondary summaries, not verified in the primary text". Replace it with a note that §4.1 of the primary text republished by Outlook gives ">80% of IDRF-designated funds to Parivar organisations (RSS, VHP, VKA)" and "83% … Sangh affiliated". Flag that it is unclear whether the 83% is a share of organisations or of funds; Figure 2 is titled "Percentage Distribution of IDRF Funds By Ideology". 2. d: replace "Amount not stated" with: "IDRF-designated disbursements 1994–2000: 'roughly 75% of the IDRF's total disbursements (over $3.2 million)'". Note that the parenthetical could refer to either the 75% slice or the total. 3. Scope: change "IDRF disbursements went predominantly" to "IDRF-designated disbursements (~75% of total) went >80% to Sangh affiliates; donor-designated only 10% (report's coding, Appendix H)". Also record IDRF's 10% allocation to VKA on donor-designated gifts of $1,000 or more. 4. Recipient list in d: VKA, RSS and VHP affiliates in §4.1; Sewa Bharati, Ekal Vidyalaya and Bharat Kalyan Pratisthan (~$86,000) in §4.2–4.4. 5. Fill innocentReading with the lawful same-network service-funding reading above. 6. c024 contra: add the HVK summary sentence showing the rebuttal concedes the flow and disputes the "funds violence" characterisation; the contra URL can point to https://hvk.org/specialreports/hate/1.html. 7. File-level: update the gap at ~line 2173–2174 ("Narrative 6's numerators (83% …) are recorded from secondary readings only"), narrative 6's strongestCounter ("The 83% figure is unverified here") and the gaps list line ~2439. The 83% is now read in the primary text via Outlook; only its scope (organisations vs funds) is unresolved. 8. Optional: consider an ngo:vka target node instead of or alongside the collective "rss" node. benefit.amountCr stays null unless a dated USD→INR conversion is recorded.

verdicts.dateTest: Sewa International Inc (EIN 20-0638718, Sugar Land TX, IRS ruling 2004-08) existed across the whole period, so its tenure fits. The report's Sewa window is 2005–2019, not 2001–19. The 2001–19 span belongs to the seven-group total. ThePrint's article (Vandana Menon, 2022-06-14) and the report (dated 2022-05-23 on DocumentCloud) both fall inside the claim window. The date test passes, with the Sewa span needing correction to 2005–2019.
verdicts.identityTest: ThePrint, the only cited source, does not name Sewa International among the seven charities. Its one mention of Sewa is in a separate sentence about the 2021 Al Jazeera Covid-relief story: "five Right-wing groups — Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of USA, HAF, Infinity Foundation, Sewa International, and VHPA — received $833,000 of U.S. federal Covid relief funds". Sewa's membership of the seven comes only from the primary report, 'Hindu Nationalist Influence in the United States, 2014-2021' (Jasa Macher/SACW), Table 4: "Sewa International | Sevabharati Keralam | $17.1 million (2005-2019) | $12.9 million". The report's footnote 322 cites Sewa International's Form 990s, which matches the US entity (EIN 20-0638718). The node identity holds. The target node "rss" is not in either source. The only Indian recipient the report names for Sewa is Sevabharati Keralam, labelled "(Selected)", with no amount.
verdicts.baseRate: The seven were chosen for their Sangh affiliation, so 100% of them share the property by construction and the figure tells you nothing on its own. Across US faith-based diaspora charities that fund India, most send money to service networks of the same religion. The SPEC controls World Vision, Compassion and Missionaries of Charity send money through church partners, and Muslim diaspora charities send it through co-religionist bodies. On the evidence here, "a faith-based US charity funds a co-religionist service network in India" does not set Sewa apart. What would set it apart is a documented transfer to an RSS affiliate, and the report names only one selected recipient with no amount.
verdicts.denialFound: None found from Sewa International USA. ThePrint says: "ThePrint has reached out to the organizations mentioned in this article for their comments on the report." Sewa is mentioned in the article, so it was presumably asked, but no Sewa reply was published. HAF ("All the allegations [in this report] about HAF are baseless") and HSS ("a politically motivated smear campaign") replied for themselves only. Sewa's About page calls it "a Hindu faith-based, humanitarian, nonprofit service organization" that "serves humanity irrespective of race, color, religion", but it does not address the report.
verdicts.innocentReading: The report's Sewa figure comes from Form 990 Part III row 4e (2008–2019), which is total program service expenses. That covers Sewa's US work (disaster relief such as the Harvey response, refugee and Covid programmes) as well as work abroad, and it is not a record of grants to India. The report admits this: "a group did not appear to differentiate consistently between programs in the U.S. from those in India, and further investigation is needed to disaggregate the funding." ProPublica totals for Sewa's expenses in 2014–2018 come to about $9.7m, in line with the report's $12.9m for 2014–19. That suggests the $17.1m is close to all of Sewa's spending everywhere, not money sent to India. The report's own author also says "most of [these actions] are legal". The boring explanation is that this is a US Hindu faith-based relief charity with some Indian partners, and board members with HSS roles.
verdicts.reason: As written, the edge fails in three places. (1) The cited source (ThePrint) does not say Sewa is one of the seven; only the primary report does, so the source chain is only partly confirmed. (2) The record says "Amount not stated for Sewa alone", but the report gives $17.1m (2005–2019) and $12.9m (2014–19). (3) Most importantly, the edge Sewa → rss with the predicate "grant" is a conjunction that no source states. The report's figure is total program expenses, not grants. It says "much"/"some" went to India without splitting US from India spending, and the only Indian recipient it names is Sevabharati Keralam, with no amount; RSS is never named. Chaining "Sewa spent $17.1m" + "some went to India" + "recipient is Sangh-linked" into "Sewa granted money to RSS" is exactly the pattern the rubric forbids. As a narrative, "a pseudonymous SACW-facilitated report alleges Sewa is one of seven Sangh-affiliated charities that spent $158.9m", it survives at alleged, with a contra.
verdicts.corrections: t: change "rss" to a Sevabharati Keralam node (or a generic "Sangh-affiliated recipients in India, unspecified"). Do not keep an edge to rss. pred: "grant" → "program-expense (alleged, India share undisaggregated)" or similar. The record must not imply Sewa gave money to RSS. srcs: add the primary report https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/22041101/20220523_hninfluenceusa.pdf (Table 4, p.21; fn 321–322). Keep ThePrint only for the seven-group total and the author's "most of which are legal" line. d: replace "Amount not stated for Sewa alone" with "Report Table 4: Sewa International $17.1m program expenses 2005–2019 ($12.9m 2014–19); selected India recipient Sevabharati Keralam (amount not given); figure is Form 990 Part III 4e total program expenses including US programs — report concedes US/India not disaggregated." from: 2001 → 2005 for the Sewa edge. lab/text: the report says "sending much of it to India" and ThePrint says "some", so quote one and attribute it. Also note the author is pseudonymous: "Jasa Macher", facilitated by the South Asian Citizens Web. innocentReading: currently null; fill it with the program-expense/US-relief reading above. c026 d: "ThePrint states it reached out to the organisations mentioned; no Sewa International response published (HAF's 'baseless' and HSS's 'smear campaign' statements are their own)." upgradeIf: keep the Schedule F / FC-4 match. ProPublica shows the EIN is 20-0638718, so that check can be run.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: Bain & Dasra estimated private social-sector funding in India at about ₹131,000 crore for FY2024E. India Philanthropy Report 2025 was published 27 Feb 2025, so FY2024 is an estimate. There is no actor tenure to test. The dates are close but not the same: the file's FCRA comparator figures are FY2021-22 (₹22,122 cr) and FY2024-25 (₹22,963 cr / ₹22,974 cr). No FY2023-24 FC-4 aggregate is recorded, so the comparison is off by one year. The upgradeIf already names this gap.
verdicts.identityTest: Fails on the definition. The claim calls ₹1.31 lakh crore "Indian private philanthropy" and sets it against "the foreign-contribution channel". Bain's ₹131k figure is total private funding, and foreign funding is part of it. On page 11 of the Bain PDF, the chart "India's private funding growth projection by segment (INR thousand crore)" shows FY24E = 131. It splits that into Foreign (18%), Retail (30%), HNI/Affluent (21%), UHNI (5%), CSR (25%) and Corporate Trust (<1%). The chart's side note says: "Foreign private funding is salient but growing moderately at ~3%". FCRA filings and MHA Rajya Sabha disclosures are listed among its sources. So the claim compares a total against one of its own parts. The domestic private figure is about ₹107,000 crore (82%). The foreign share is about ₹23,600 crore, which roughly matches the FCRA aggregates of ₹22–23k crore.
verdicts.baseRate: Not a discrimination claim. It is the scale control the SPEC requires under "Domestic philanthropy as control on scale". Two ratios matter. Foreign funding is about 1% of total social-sector funding (~₹23.6k cr of ~₹25 lakh cr), so "rounding error against public spending" holds. It is about 18% of private funding, nearly one-fifth. That makes it bigger than UHNI giving (5%) and close to CSR (25%). "A small fraction of private giving" understates it.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is an analytic scale comparison with no accused party. None found, not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: Bain-Dasra figures are consultant estimates built from the CSR portal, FCRA filings, IT returns and Hurun lists, not audited flows. Foreign money is small next to public spending but a real share of private giving. Small foreign grants to advocacy groups can matter politically regardless of their share of the total. The existing innocentReading is fine.
verdicts.reason: The Bain source confirms the numbers: "~INR 131,000 crore ($16 billion)" in FY2024, 7% growth, family giving ~40% of private philanthropy, family-run CSR ~₹18,000 crore, and ~₹25 lakh crore total with 95% public. It contradicts the framing. The ₹131k crore is total private funding and includes foreign private funding at ~18% (Bain p.11 chart). Calling it "Indian private philanthropy" and setting it against the foreign channel counts foreign money on both sides. The d-field line "a small fraction of private giving ... the denominator every 'foreign money' narrative omits" understates an 18% share and asserts something about "every" narrative that nobody has checked. The edge's a=131000 also puts foreign money in the "domestic-grantees" node. The analytic tier survives only if the label, a and d are corrected.
verdicts.corrections: lab: "Scale control: private social-sector funding ~₹1.31 lakh crore FY2024E (Bain-Dasra), of which foreign ~18% (~₹23,600 cr) and domestic ~82% (~₹107,000 cr); public ~₹23 lakh crore". a: 107000 (domestic private, derived as 82% of 131k), or null with the figures kept in d. d: replace "Foreign contribution ... is a small fraction of private giving and a rounding error against public spending — the denominator every 'foreign money' narrative omits" with "Bain counts foreign private funding inside the ₹131k figure at ~18%, consistent with FCRA aggregates of ~₹22–23k cr. It is roughly one-fifth of private giving and ~1% of total social-sector funding." Drop "every". Add a source pointer to the PDF: https://www.bain.com/globalassets/noindex/2025/bain_report_india_philanthropy_report_2025.pdf (p.11 chart, p.8). from: "2023-04-01" (FY2023-24), with d stating "FY24E, estimate". upgradeIf: keep (FY2023-24 FC-4 aggregate from MHA/Parliament). Keep tier analytic.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out: the Intelligence Bureau (under the UPA commission, handed to the NDA) asserted, in a report dated 2014-06-03, that foreign-funded NGO-backed "anti-developmental activities" hit GDP growth by 2-3%. The News Minute (2014-06-13) says: "The Intelligence Bureau report dated June 3, 2014 ... The report was commissioned by the previous government and has been submitted to the new government. The 21 page report ..." Deccan Herald/IANS (2014-06-11) also gives the date as June 3. The NDA took office on 2014-05-26, and the Indian Express leak came about 2014-06-10/11, so "within days of the new government taking office" is loose. It was about two weeks after the government took office and about a week after the report's date. The follow-on actions (Greenpeace suspension on 2015-04-09, Ford placed on the watch list in April 2015, mass cancellations for non-filing in April 2015) do fall within a year. Ford was then taken off prior reference on 2016-03-18, according to this same file (line 1309).
verdicts.identityTest: The IB document is identified consistently by date (2014-06-03), length (21 pages) and title ("concerted effort by select foreign funded NGOs to 'take down' Indian developmental projects"; IANS gives it as "foreign-funded NGOs negatively impacting economic development in India"). Greenpeace India is correctly the party that responded (spokesperson Abhishek Pratap). No FCRA registration number is needed for a narrative record. The only party named is a class, "foreign-funded NGOs". No family, religion or ethnicity is framed as the actor.
verdicts.baseRate: This is a narrative, not a discriminating edge, so a base rate does not apply directly. On symmetry, the thesis started under UPA (the report was commissioned under UPA, and UPA ran its own 2012 Kudankulam-linked cancellations). The SPEC control is UPA cancellations against NDA cancellations, and it cuts both ways: the "foreign hand stalls development" framing is bipartisan in origin, and the NDA acted on it at greater scale. The strongestCase already mentions Kudankulam. It should say plainly that the UPA used the same framing in 2012.
verdicts.denialFound: Greenpeace India, spokesperson Abhishek Pratap, in Deccan Herald/IANS on 2014-06-11 (https://www.deccanherald.com/india/greenpeace-rejects-ib-report-swears-2210733): "We are not aware of any IB report criticising our work ... How can the IB come to that conclusion? We have never been served any notice for violating the provisions of the Foreign Contribution Act." He also confirmed that Greenpeace paid for the TISS and IIT-Bombay studies (he said IIT-Bombay, not IIT-Delhi). He denied supporting AAP candidates. The response was sought and is on record. The IB's cost method was never published and has not been defended in public.
verdicts.innocentReading: The IB report is an internal threat assessment. Its headline number is an unsourced estimate ("does not mention how it arrived at the percentage", TNM). Its financial data are lawful FCRA-declared receipts ("no mention of any money that has come through illegal means"). The project delays at Kudankulam, POSCO and Niyamgiri also have domestic causes: land acquisition, forest-rights rulings (the Supreme Court's 2013 Niyamgiri gram sabha decision), and litigation. Foreign funding is one input among many, not a demonstrated cause.
verdicts.reason:
The claim survives as a narrative correctly marked "contested". Both cited sources exist and support the core: the report is dated 2014-06-03, runs 21 pages, was commissioned by the previous government, and carries the 2-3% figure with no stated method (TNM: "The report begins prominently by saying that negative effects of such anti-developmental activities on GDP growth is estimated to be at 2-3%. ... it does not mention how it arrived at the percentage"). Greenpeace's rejection is quoted in the IANS piece. Three things fail, all in the supporting fields.
(1) The metric is misstated. The source says a 2-3% effect on GDP *growth*. The claim's "costing 2–3% of GDP a year" turns that into a loss in GDP level, per year, which the source does not say.
(2) "placed Ford and 15 other donors under prior reference" has no support in the cited sources or anywhere in the repo files. The file's own AUDIT puts total s.46 prior-reference donors at about 21 (8 under UPA, 13 under NDA), and Ford was removed on 2016-03-18.
(3) "a Delhi High Court later found the Greenpeace actions disproportionate" misquotes the sibling record, which says "arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional" (the January 2015 fund-block ruling).
The existence and content of the report rest on one leak (Indian Express), which TNM and IANS both relay. That makes them derivative rather than independent, so the tier is reported, not documented. The GDP figure itself is only an IB assertion (alleged).
verdicts.corrections:
1. Claim text: replace "costing 2–3% of GDP a year" with "cutting GDP growth by an estimated 2–3% (the IB's unsourced figure)". Quote TNM: "negative effects of such anti-developmental activities on GDP growth is estimated to be at 2-3%".
2. strongestCase: delete "placed Ford and 15 other donors under prior reference". Replace it with "placed the Ford Foundation on the prior-reference watch list (April 2015; removed 2018-03-18? no — removed 2016-03-18)". The final wording should read: "placed the Ford Foundation under prior reference (April 2015; removed 2016-03-18)". Add the BHRRC/ThePrint source, or cite fcra-actions.json for the count of prior-reference donors (about 21 in total, 8 under UPA and 13 under NDA, per AUDIT).
3. strongestCase: change "leaked within days of the new government taking office" to "leaked to the Indian Express about two weeks after the new government took office (reported 2014-06-11)".
4. strongestCounter: change "found the Greenpeace actions disproportionate" to "held the MHA fund-block on Greenpeace India 'arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional' (Delhi HC, January 2015)".
5. strongestCounter: change "never been published or tabled" to "never officially published or tabled; known only through leaked portions (Indian Express, June 2014)".
6. Add Pratap's specific rebuttal to the record ("We have never been served any notice for violating the provisions of the Foreign Contribution Act"), together with his admission that Greenpeace funded the TISS and IIT-Bombay studies. Also correct IIT-Delhi to IIT-Bombay where the file repeats the IB version.
7. Tier the report's existence and contents as reported, since TNM and IANS both derive from the same Indian Express leak. Tier the 2-3% figure as alleged (an IB assertion without method), with Greenpeace's response as the contra.
8. Symmetry: state explicitly that the report was commissioned under UPA and that UPA's 2012 Kudankulam cancellations used the same "foreign hand" thesis.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out, is "Union Government (MHA) uses FCRA to silence critics, from 2012 to 2026 under both UPA and NDA". The dated events fall inside the relevant government tenures. UPA-era actions: People's Watch/CPSC suspended in 2012–13 and INSAF suspended in April 2013 (both in HRW 2016). NDA-era actions: Lawyers Collective in May 2016, the People's Watch/INSAF/Hazards Centre refusals in October 2016, Ford listed April 2015 and delisted 18 March 2016 (Deccan Chronicle 2016-03-18: "The decision of the Home Ministry came ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to the US"), the CASA/EFI/CNI cancellations in April 2024 (FH 2025), the Amendment Rules of 22 June 2026 (Amnesty 2026) and the PIB factsheet dated 22 July 2026. The dates hold, but one link does not. The narrative says HRW 2016 covers "the UPA's 2012 Kudankulam cancellations", and that HRW release never mentions Kudankulam. The Kudankulam item comes from the sibling file fcra-actions.json, not from HRW.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the MHA (the FCRA authority), and every source names it, so the identity is correct. The problem is which groups are named. The strongestCase says "HRW (2016) on 25 groups including Greenpeace, Sabrang, Navsarjan, INSAF". HRW 2016 actually says "While the government has not published the list of affected groups, it appears to include several human rights organizations." The only groups it names are People's Watch (CPSC), INSAF and Hazards Centre (Sanchal Foundation). It discusses Lawyers Collective as a separate May 2016 suspension. Greenpeace appears only as the Priya Pillai court case. Sabrang, Navsarjan and Greenpeace as FCRA targets come from HRW 2022 ("These include the Indian Social Action Forum, Lawyers Collective, Sabrang Trust, Navsarjan Trust, Anhad, Oxfam India, Greenpeace, and Amnesty International India"). There is also an independence problem. The 2016 statement is a joint Amnesty India and HRW release, and Amnesty India was itself an FCRA target (it halted work in 2020). So "monitors across a decade" is partly the targets speaking in their own case.
verdicts.baseRate: Critics are a very small share of FCRA actions. FH 2025 cites 6,677 cancellations in 2017–21, and HRW 2016 records 11,319 cancellations for failing to renew plus 1,736 applications closed for missing documents in a single batch. Most of these were for non-compliance, not politics. Among prominent foreign-funded rights and advocacy groups, though, the share hit by some FCRA action is high: Greenpeace, Amnesty, Lawyers Collective, Sabrang, Navsarjan, INSAF, CPSC, Oxfam, CPR. That pattern discriminates only if comparable non-critical large recipients are spared, and they are not reliably spared. CASA, EFI, CNI, VHAI and IGSSS (April 2024), Compassion (2017) and Missionaries of Charity (2021) were all hit, mainly church-linked service bodies. Symmetry holds on the party axis: the UPA did the same to CPSC and INSAF in 2012–13 and to the Kudankulam-area groups in 2012, and the claim is party-neutral ("government critics"). The claim does not frame a family, religion or ethnicity as the actor.
verdicts.denialFound: The Government was asked (via public statements) and it answered, but the narrative's counter leaves out the most direct denial. PIB/MHA, 29 September 2020, "Human Rights cannot be an excuse for defying the law of the land" (https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1660095&reg=48&lang=2), called Amnesty's statements "unfortunate, exaggerated and far from the truth". It said Amnesty "is free to continue humanitarian work" but that India does not allow foreign-funded "interference in domestic political debates", a law that "applies equally to all". It alleged that Amnesty UK routed money to four Indian entities as FDI to get around FCRA, and that Amnesty had been refused FCRA approval "by successive governments" since 2000. The narrative instead cites the 2026 PIB factsheet, which says the law restricts "a narrow, defined set of foreign-funded activities" and that "Tens of thousands of associations remain validly registered". In the Ford case, Setalvad denied misusing the funds (Deccan Chronicle).
verdicts.innocentReading: FCRA is a broad compliance regime, and most cancellations are for missed filings or renewals. Large foreign-funded advocacy groups are the heaviest users of foreign money and the most likely to route it to onward grantees or through FDI or consultancy structures. They are therefore the most exposed to "improper use" findings whatever they say, and church-linked service bodies with no critical profile were cancelled on the same grounds. Courts quashing unreasoned suspensions (INSAF 2013, CPSC 2014) shows due-process failure, not proof of political motive. No court or official record has adjudicated that any cancellation was made because of speech.
verdicts.reason: The headline thesis ("used to silence critics", status "well-supported") is a claim about intent. It rests on assertions by HRW, Amnesty, CIVICUS and the UN High Commissioner, one of which (Amnesty) is itself a target. It has no adjudicated finding behind it and faces an explicit Government denial. Under CONTRACT that is `alleged` with a contra, not a settled pattern. The narrative also misstates its own sources in three places, and each change strengthens the claim. (1) It strips Freedom House's hedge. FH says "Authorities have been accused of using this power selectively against perceived political opponents"; the narrative presents this as FH "noting the power is 'used selectively…'". (2) It credits HRW 2016 with naming Greenpeace, Sabrang and Navsarjan among the 25, but HRW says the list was never published and names only People's Watch, INSAF and Hazards Centre. (3) It credits HRW 2016 with the Kudankulam 2012 cancellations, which that release does not mention. Its UPA examples are CPSC 2012–13 and INSAF 2013. The core facts hold: critics were acted against under both governments, the courts quashed several suspensions, and the Ford listing and delisting happened as described. The "well-supported" framing and the quotations do not survive.
verdicts.corrections: Change status from "well-supported" to "contested — monitors allege, Government denies; no adjudicated finding of political motive". Freedom House: quote the full sentence, "Authorities have been accused of using this power selectively against perceived political opponents." HRW 2016: replace "on 25 groups including Greenpeace, Sabrang, Navsarjan, INSAF" with "on 25 unnamed refusals (list unpublished), naming People's Watch/CPSC, INSAF and Hazards Centre, plus the May 2016 Lawyers Collective suspension", and move Sabrang, Navsarjan and Greenpeace to HRW 2022. Replace "HRW's 2016 finding … the UPA's 2012 Kudankulam cancellations included" with "HRW/Amnesty 2016: 'Successive governments have used the FCRA as a political tool…', citing UPA suspensions of People's Watch (2012–13) and INSAF (2013)", and source Kudankulam 2012 to fcra-actions.json. Note that the 2016 statement is joint with Amnesty India, an FCRA target. Ford: say it was listed on the stated ground of alleged misuse of funds given to Setalvad's NGOs, which Setalvad denied, rather than "for funding a critic's NGOs". Keep "ahead of the PM's US visit" as timing only. Add the direct denial to strongestCounter and srcs: PIB 2020-09-29, https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1660095&reg=48&lang=2. Add the 2016 base rate from HRW's own release (11,319 non-renewal cancellations and 1,736 closures for deficient documents) to show that critics are a small share. The top-level srcs cite only three URLs; include the HRW 2022, CIVICUS, Amnesty 2026 and Deccan Chronicle URLs, since the narrative relies on them.

verdicts.dateTest: Pass. Each part checked: (1) Soros spoke at Munich on 2023-02-16. The georgesoros.com page opened (HTTP 200) and says, verbatim: "India is an interesting case. It's a democracy, but its leader Narendra Modi is no democrat." It also says: "This will significantly weaken Modi's stranglehold on India's federal government and open the door to push for much needed institutional reforms. I may be naïve, but I expect a democratic revival in India." Soros founded OSF and has been its principal throughout, so actor and date line up. (2) MHA put OSF in the prior-reference category in 2016. The Tribune (2025-03-19, HTTP 200) says: "Preliminary investigation by the ED had revealed that Soros' OSF was put under the 'prior reference category' by the Home Ministry in 2016." OSF itself said in September 2023 (quoted by Al Jazeera, 2024-12-26): "Since mid-2016, our grant making in India has been constrained by government restrictions on our funding for local NGOs." (3) ED searches: The Tribune says ED "on Tuesday conducted searches at eight premises in Bengaluru", which is 2025-03-18. It carries the ED-sources quote: "In order to bypass the restriction, the OSF had subsidiaries in India and brought in funds in the form of FDI and consultancy fee." (4) Smriti Irani's press conference at BJP headquarters on 2023-02-17 is confirmed by ThePrint/ANI and bjp.org. (5) "≈US$757m in 2024" matches ProPublica's FY Dec-2024 990-PF expenses: FPOS $460,769,902 plus OSI $295,896,735 = $756.7m. I found no adjudication, show-cause order or court order up to Sept 2026, so "unadjudicated" still holds.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass, with two notes. The Tribune miscalls OSF "Open Source Foundation" and names "Economic Development Fund (EDF)". The entity is Soros Economic Development Fund (SEDF), with Aspada Investments Pvt Ltd as its Indian investment adviser and fund manager, which ThePrint describes as a wholly-owned subsidiary of a Mauritius entity. The ED allegation is about SEDF/Aspada FDI and consultancy flows, not OSF grants as such. The narrative merges these under "OSF", so it should name SEDF/Aspada separately. The two ProPublica EINs match: 26-3753801 is the Foundation to Promote Open Society and 13-7029285 is the Open Society Institute. No FCRA registration number for OSF was opened; the 2016 MHA order itself was not seen.
verdicts.baseRate: Wishing for political change in several countries is not specific to India. In the same Munich speech Soros said of Turkey "The best way to address these issues is to hold elections", welcomed Lula's election in Brazil and attacked Trump. Being watch-listed or put under prior reference is also common among large Western donors that fund rights and advocacy work in India: Ford (2015), OSF (2016) and Compassion (2017) all were. The SPEC control group is treated differently. Domestic philanthropies (Tata, Azim Premji, Reliance, Adani) face no prior-permission gate. The Sangh-linked foreign channels (Sewa International USA, IDRF), described by critics as remitting to ideologically aligned grantees, have no recorded MHA action.
