Pointing to a donor's democracy/rights grant-making therefore does not set OSF apart. What is specific to OSF is the ED allegation that money was routed through FDI and consultancy fees, and that allegation is unadjudicated.
verdicts.denialFound: Partial response exists; it is not a denial. OSF's September 2023 statement, quoted by Al Jazeera (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/12/26/how-george-soros-became-enemy-number-1-for-indias-modi), says: "Since mid-2016, our grant making in India has been constrained by government restrictions on our funding for local NGOs." Al Jazeera asked OSF about the BJP's allegations in December 2024 and "has not yet received a reply". On the March 2025 ED searches: The Tribune and newsonair.gov.in carry no OSF response. ThePrint and Maktoob reported that OSF and SEDF had been asked and a response was "awaited". I found no later OSF or SEDF statement on the FEMA matter. Status: asked, no reply found.
verdicts.innocentReading: Soros, a well-known Modi critic, publicly predicted that the Adani affair would weaken Modi, much as he commented on Erdogan, Lula and Trump in the same speech. That is political speech, not a funding programme, and the speech never mentions OSF spending in India. OSF's India grant-making has been restricted by MHA prior reference since mid-2016, which OSF itself acknowledges. SEDF's impact-investment arm (Aspada) made FDI investments that ED now says were a FEMA workaround. That is a regulatory dispute about how money came in, not evidence that it paid for electoral activity. No adjudicated finding under FCRA, FEMA or the Representation of the People Act links OSF money to parties, campaigns or elections.
verdicts.reason: Refutation fails. Every factual component of the narrative checks out against a source that opens and says it: the Munich quotes are verbatim; the Tribune supports the 2016 prior-reference listing and the eight-premise ED search, with the ED allegation attributed to "sources"; the ProPublica FY2024 expense sum is ≈$756.7m; and Irani's 2023-02-17 press conference is confirmed. The central proposition, "Soros/OSF fund regime change in India", is correctly labelled speculative. It is asserted by named parties (BJP ministers, and ED by implication), and no source in hand shows OSF money going to electoral or political activity. For the underlying proposition the right tier is "alleged", carrying a contra, and the record's status "speculative" is right. The narrative names a person and an organisation, not an ethnicity, but it must never be emitted as a graph edge (Soros → funds → regime change); it stays a narrative only. Defects needing correction: the strongest case omits the quantified ED allegation (≈Rs 300 crore since 2016, ≈Rs 25 crore to NGOs, per ThePrint/ED sources); the record omits OSF's own September 2023 statement confirming the 2016 restriction; Irani's press conference has no source attached; the "ethnicity" assertion has no source; and SEDF/Aspada is not distinguished from OSF.
verdicts.corrections: 1) srcs: add a source for the Irani 2023-02-17 claim (https://theprint.in/economy/soros-has-attacked-indian-parliament-bjps-smriti-irani-slams-billionaire-investor-george-soros-2/1378343/ or the bjp.org press release). Also add Al Jazeera 2024-12-26 for the OSF September 2023 statement and the "asked, no reply" record. 2) strongestCase: say the ED allegation concerns Soros Economic Development Fund / Aspada Investments Pvt Ltd FDI and consultancy flows, not OSF grants directly. Add the quantified ED-sources figure (≈Rs 300 crore via the FDI route since 2016, ≈Rs 25 crore to NGOs and employees, per ThePrint 2025-03-18, https://theprint.in/india/ed-raids-fund-manager-others-linked-to-george-soros-backed-osf-in-fema-probe/2552604/), labelled as unadjudicated. Optionally add the December 2024 BJP allegations (FDL-AP/OCCRP) as the political form of the narrative, attributed to the BJP. 3) strongestCounter: add OSF's own statement "Since mid-2016, our grant making in India has been constrained by government restrictions on our funding for local NGOs". Note that the same Munich speech made the same kind of wish for Turkey ("hold elections"), Brazil and the US. Remove "and, in its common form, an ethnicity" unless a source is attached, or source it explicitly. 4) Note that FPOS+OSI 2024 expenses ($460.8m + $295.9m) may double-count some intra-network transfers (OSI reported $37.8m in contributions received), and that this is global spend, not India spend. 5) In claim c008, the 2016 listing can cite OSF's own admission (Al Jazeera quote) alongside the Tribune. In claim c010, change "asked/not asked unknown" to "asked (ThePrint 2025-03, Al Jazeera 2024-12); no reply found". 6) Keep this as a narrative only; never emit it as a Soros/OSF → regime-change edge.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: DOGE (the actor) listed "$21M for voter turnout in India" on 2025-02-16 as part of US$486m in cancelled CEPPS funding. Business Standard (2025-02-21) says the grant was "sanctioned in 2022" and ran "Between July 2022 and October 2024" for Bangladesh ahead of its January 2024 poll, with "$13.4 million had already been utilised". The Wire's piece is dated about 72 hours after Trump's remarks (c. 2025-02-21/22). Its "MEA declined to engage" was accurate then, but it was overtaken on 2025-08-22. That day MoS External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh gave a written Rajya Sabha answer to John Brittas (CPI-M). He said MEA had asked the US Embassy for ten years of USAID project data. The Embassy replied on 2025-07-02, and USAID "did not receive or provide $21 million in funding for voter turnout in India" and ran no voter-turnout projects in India in 2014–24. So "MEA never produced findings" and the record's "has announced no result" are stale as of 2025-08-22.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities check out. The US$21m award is the USAID–CEPPS (IFES/IRI/NDI) "Amar Vote Amar"/Nagorik programme in Bangladesh, per Business Standard quoting USAID records via the Indian Express. The seven projects are the USAID–GoI Partnership Agreements named in the Finance Ministry (DEA) annual report for 2023-24: "seven projects worth a total budget of USD 750 million... For the financial year 2023-24, an obligation of a total of USD 97 million". The MEA spokesperson was Randhir Jaiswal, and the minister answering in the Rajya Sabha was MoS Kirti Vardhan Singh. Nothing is conflated.
verdicts.baseRate: Mostly not applicable, since this is a fact check of one specific claim rather than an attribute of an entity. On symmetry: the Congress used the Bangladesh finding against the BJP (Jairam Ramesh, quoted in BS 2025-02-23). The debunking rests on USAID records, a Finance Ministry report and a Government of India Parliament answer, so it does not depend on which side is speaking. The FCRA control in the SPEC is not relevant here.
verdicts.denialFound: The Government of India's own statement settles it. Business Standard, 2025-08-22 (https://www.business-standard.com/external-affairs-defence-security/news/usaid-funding-voter-turnout-india-govt-response-rajya-sabha-125082200606_1.html): "Kirti Vardhan Singh informed the Rajya Sabha on Friday that the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) did not receive or provide $21 million in funding for voter turnout in India... the US Embassy confirmed it had not implemented any voter turnout-related projects in India between 2014 and 2024." The Wire (Feb 2025) records the earlier MEA line: "very deeply troubling", "relevant departments and agencies are looking into this matter", and the spokesperson "declined to engage" with the Bangladesh finding. The DOGE and White House side never issued a document naming India.
verdicts.innocentReading: DOGE's X post mislabelled a CEPPS line item (the Bangladesh voter-participation award) as India's. Trump repeated the label, and the MEA's February remarks were holding language while it asked Washington for data. When the data came back it showed no India voter-turnout funding, and the Government said so in the Rajya Sabha.
verdicts.reason: The main verdict holds: the "debunked" status is correct, and each figure matches its source word for word (Bangladesh grant sanctioned 2022, US$13.4m spent, no CEPPS project in India since 2008, seven GoI projects with US$750m budget and US$97m obligated in FY24). The claim still fails as worded because "MEA never produced findings" is false. On 2025-08-22 the Government told the Rajya Sabha in a written answer (MoS Kirti Vardhan Singh, replying to John Brittas) that, per the US Embassy's 2025-07-02 data, USAID neither received nor provided US$21m for voter turnout in India and ran no such projects in 2014–24. That Parliament answer is a primary record under CONTRACT, so the debunk can move up to documented. But the narrative's strongestCounter ("has announced no result", "Neither Washington nor Delhi produced a document naming India") and whatWouldChangeThis ("An MEA statement of findings would settle the Indian side") have to be rewritten.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Claim text: replace "MEA never produced findings" with "GoI told Rajya Sabha on 2025-08-22 (MoS Kirti Vardhan Singh, written answer to John Brittas) that, per US Embassy data shared 2025-07-02, USAID did not provide US$21m for voter turnout in India and ran no voter-turnout projects there in 2014–24." (2) strongestCounter: drop "the MEA declined to engage with the Bangladesh finding and has announced no result". Keep "declined to engage" only with a Feb 2025 date, and add the Aug 2025 Parliament answer. (3) whatWouldChangeThis: remove "An MEA statement of findings would settle the Indian side", because it now exists and confirms the debunk. Keep the USAID award-document falsifier. (4) Add a source: Business Standard 2025-08-22, https://www.business-standard.com/external-affairs-defence-security/news/usaid-funding-voter-turnout-india-govt-response-rajya-sabha-125082200606_1.html. Better still, add the Rajya Sabha unstarred question PDF itself (sansad.in, 2025-08-22) as the primary source. (5) Optionally note that the US Embassy terminated all seven Partnership Agreements with DEA effective 2025-08-15, and that USAID operations ended 2025-07-01. (6) Date The Wire source c. 2025-02-21 so readers can see its "declined to engage" is a point-in-time statement.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: "The MHA cancelled church-linked FCRA registrations (CNI-SBSS, CASA, EFI) in 2024 on grounds of 'improper use', not conversion." The dates line up with other reporting. Freedom House 2025 says "In April 2024". Business Standard (3 Apr 2024, citing ET) says the MHA acted "on Tuesday", which is 2 Apr 2024. ICC says "In March". Christianity Today (2024-04-02) dates EFI's cancellation to 2023, a gap already flagged in fcra-actions.json that this narrative does not mention. The Compassion action was a 2016 prior-permission order followed by exit on 2017-03-15. The narrative says "2017", which is only partly right. The "2026 Rules" were notified on 22 Jun 2026 (PIB factsheet, posted 22 Jul 2026). So the chronology holds. What fails is the stated grounds.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor in the claim is a religious category ("Missionary NGOs"), not an entity. Under CONTRACT rule 1 that belongs only in narratives, and it is correctly kept there. The named associations are the ones the sources name: the Freedom House list matches Business Standard, NewsBharati and ICC. None of the three srcs supports the Compassion sentence. The file's own receipts records use Christianity Today 2016 and the Oakley testimony for it. Cross-reference error: narrative:4 says "mirror image of narrative 6", but ids are 0-indexed, so the RSS narrative is narrative:5. narrative:5 in turn calls this one "narrative 5", but this one is narrative:4. The text counts from 1 and the ids count from 0.
verdicts.baseRate: No comparable cancellation-rate data is in hand for religious-purpose versus other registrations. The narrative itself admits this: its whatWouldChangeThis asks for exactly that data. Christian bodies being among the largest FC recipients is expected given the size of the church welfare sector, so on its own it does not discriminate. The symmetry control holds. Run on Sangh-affiliated US 501(c)(3)s such as Sewa International and IDRF feeding Ekal and Sewa Bharati (narrative:5), the same lens gives the same shape: faith-affiliated foreign money flowing into faith-affiliated service networks. The asymmetry sits in enforcement. No MHA action is recorded against the Sangh-side recipients, while church-linked bodies were cancelled.
verdicts.denialFound: EFI general secretary Vijayesh Lal expressed surprise and pointed to the organisation's interfaith and charity work. He suggested the cancellation was retaliation for its advocacy on religious freedom and its court challenges to anti-conversion laws (Christianity Today, 2024-04-02, https://www.christianitytoday.com/2024/04/india-fcra-ngo-world-vision-foreign-funding-close/). CASA's Bishop Subodh C. Mondal called the impact "crushing" and said about 350 staff were let go (same source). Compassion said it exists "to release children from poverty, not convert them" and that 96% of its funds went to food, medicine and school fees, with 4% to "moral and spiritual values education" (Christianity Today, 9 Dec 2016, https://christianitytoday.com/news/2016/december/compassion-international-child-sponsorship-india-christmas.html). The narrative records none of these responses.
verdicts.innocentReading: Church-run welfare bodies such as CASA, CNI-SBSS and Christian Aid's 27 partners in 16 states work on caste, governance, livelihoods, health and relief. They receive large, declared foreign contributions because transnational church giving is an old and large channel. Cancellations happen across all kinds of NGOs for compliance reasons like onward transfer, non-designated accounts or unfiled returns. The government has said conversion is a concern, but no court has adjudicated conversion-by-inducement funded by foreign contributions for any named body.
verdicts.reason:
The status "contested" and the decision to keep this as a narrative are both sound. The load-bearing line in the counter is wrong, though. The narrative says "the documented 2024 cancellations cite 'improper use of foreign funding', not conversion", and that is contradicted on four points, one of them from the narrative's own source.
(1) Business Standard, 3 Apr 2024, citing ET and officials: "Allegations against these NGOs included involvement in religious conversion and violations of foreign grant regulations."
(2) Christianity Today, 2024-04-02: EFI's stated ground was that it would "prejudicially" affect "harmony between religious, racial, social, linguistic, regional groups, castes or communities". That is a religious-harmony clause, not "improper use". The project's own fcra-actions.json records this.
(3) The MHA's consolidated list of refusal and cancellation grounds (notified 8 Nov 2024, per Deccan Herald, Millennium Post and ICC) names "induced or forceful religious conversion or proselytisation".
(4) The PIB factsheet the narrative cites (22 Jul 2026) says the notified FCRA Amendment Rules 2026 "excludes proselytisation from permitted religious activity".
Freedom House's "citing improper use of foreign funding contributions" is one outlet's summary, not the orders, which are not public. So the government has explicitly linked FCRA to conversion. What is missing is an adjudicated finding, not a government claim. The strongestCase also overstates on Compassion. Christianity Today gives the official reason as "not conducive to national interest", with conversion accusations coming from security agencies and described as unsubstantiated, and none of the narrative's srcs covers Compassion. The narrative stays, but its counter has to be rewritten.
verdicts.corrections:
strongestCounter: replace "The documented 2024 cancellations cite 'improper use of foreign funding', not conversion" with: "The cancellation orders are not public. Freedom House summarises the April 2024 grounds as 'improper use of foreign funding'. Officials quoted by ET/Business Standard (3 Apr 2024) cited 'involvement in religious conversion and violations of foreign grant regulations'. EFI's stated ground was the religious-harmony clause (Christianity Today, 2024-04-02). No court has adjudicated conversion by inducement funded by FC for any named body." Add a src for this: Business Standard https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/here-is-why-modi-govt-cancelled-the-fcra-licences-of-five-prominent-ngos-124040300154_1.html and Christianity Today https://www.christianitytoday.com/2024/04/india-fcra-ngo-world-vision-foreign-funding-close/.
strongestCase: replace the vague "the Government's 2026 Rules add 'activity limitations'" with the PIB wording: "the notified FCRA Amendment Rules 2026 (22 Jun 2026) 'exclude proselytisation from permitted religious activity' (PIB factsheet, 22 Jul 2026)". Add: "the MHA's 8 Nov 2024 consolidated grounds list names induced or forceful conversion/proselytisation" (Deccan Herald https://www.deccanherald.com/amp/story/india%2Fno-fcra-permits-for-ngos-linked-to-anti-national-anti-development-protests-forced-religious-conversions-mha-3271755).
Compassion: change "the MHA has cited religious grounds in actions against Compassion International (2017)" to "the MHA placed Compassion under prior permission in 2016, officially as 'not conducive to national interest'. Security agencies' conversion accusations were reported but unsubstantiated. Compassion denied them, and exited 2017-03-15." Add the Christianity Today 2016 src.
Add the EFI date discrepancy (2023 vs April 2024) and the recorded responses (Vijayesh Lal/EFI, Bishop Mondal/CASA, Compassion).
Fix the cross-references: "narrative 6" should read "narrative:5", and narrative:5's "narrative 5" should read "narrative:4".
Keep status "contested", keep it only as a narrative, and never create an edge whose actor is a religion.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a sentence, the claim is: US charities IDRF (Maryland, operating since the late 1980s) and Sewa International USA (EIN 20-0638718, IRS ruling 2004) sent money to Sangh-affiliated Indian bodies, IDRF in 1994–2000 and the seven-group tally in 2001–19. Both donors existed across their windows, so the flow's dates overlap. Sources: the 2002 report (Outlook, published 20 Nov 2002), ThePrint (14 Jun 2022, on a report dated 23 May 2022), and the HVK rebuttal (2002–03). Three date problems. (1) Sewa's own span in the 2022 report is 2005–2019, not 2001–19. (2) The US$833,000 is 2020–21 US federal Covid relief (PPP-type money) paid to US organisations for US operations. It is not a flow to India in any window and should not appear in strongestCase. (3) "No MHA action recorded" is an absence that was never tested: fcraonline.nic.in was blocked, so the cancellation and show-cause lists that would test it were never searched.
verdicts.identityTest: Partly fails. (a) "Their US chapters": IDRF is an independent Maryland 501(c)(3), not a chapter of the RSS or of any affiliate. The 2002 report itself only argues "organizational and personnel links of the IDRF with the Sangh". "Chapter" is the critics' framing, stated as if it were a fact. Sewa International USA also presents itself as independent, and the file's own collisionRisk note separates it from the UK and Delhi Sewa entities. (b) ThePrint does not name Sewa International as one of the seven charities. Its only mention of Sewa is the Al Jazeera Covid-relief sentence. Sewa's membership of the seven comes from the primary report's Table 4, which is not in srcs. That figure is $17.1m of Form 990 program expenses for 2005–19, covering US and India work together. The report says US and India spending were not separated, and it names one "selected" Indian recipient (Sevabharati Keralam) with no amount. (c) strongestCase says "The affiliates' Indian recipients (Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of India, Sewa Bharati, VKA) hold FCRA registrations and file FC-4s (fcra-receipts.json)". The cited file says the opposite. The ngo:ekal-vidyalaya-foundation-of-india record reads "[void] No published FC-4 return or Parliament figure for Ekal's FC receipts was located in this pass; FCRA status unverified", with fcra: null. Sewa Bharati and VKA do not appear in fcra-receipts.json at all. So "declared on both ends" is unsupported on the Indian end. (d) The narrative's mirror reference "(narrative 5)" is ambiguous. Under the id scheme (0-indexed) narrative:5 is this claim, while the missionary narrative is index 4. (e) The claim frames an organisational network (RSS/Sangh affiliates), not a religion, so it passes the framing test as a narrative.
verdicts.baseRate: Non-discriminating. Almost every US diaspora faith charity that funds India sends the money to service networks of its own faith. The SPEC controls World Vision, Compassion and Missionaries of Charity do this through church partners, and Muslim and Sikh diaspora charities do the same. The seven 2022 groups were selected for Sangh affiliation, so 100% share the property by construction. The only discriminating figure is inside the 2002 report, on its own coding of recipients. IDRF-designated funds went more than 80% to Sangh bodies ("A vast majority (in excess of 80%) of the IDRF designated funds were sent to Parivar organizations"), against 10% of donor-designated funds, and HVK disputes that coding. On the symmetry control, the state acted against Ford (2015), OSF (2016) and Compassion (2016–17), and no action is recorded against IDRF or Sewa USA. That asymmetry is real, but it rests on an absence that was never searched.
verdicts.denialFound: IDRF, November 2002: it dismissed the allegations as "pure concoction, untruthful and self contradicting" (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Development_and_Relief_Fund). In March 2003 six Indian-American academics published "A Factual Response to the Hate Attack on the India Development and Relief Fund". Neither is in srcs or opened in primary form. The HVK/Chowgule rebuttal (https://hvk.org/specialreports/hate/1.html) disputes the method ("guilt by association", "conclude first and then get the data"). It does not dispute that money went to Sangh-run service projects. In ThePrint 2022, HAF said "All the allegations [in this report] about HAF are baseless" and HSS called the report "a politically motivated smear campaign". ThePrint says it "reached out to the organizations mentioned in this article", so Sewa International was presumably asked, but no Sewa response was published. None found from Sewa International USA.
verdicts.innocentReading: A US Hindu diaspora charity picks grantees it knows and trusts. In tribal and rural India the largest Hindu-oriented school, welfare and relief networks (VKA, Sewa Bharati, Ekal) happen to be Sangh affiliates. On the 2002 report's own figures, about 70% of IDRF money went to education and about 15% to relief. Sewa USA's headline figure is total program spending, much of it on US relief (Harvey, refugees, Covid), not grants to India. Both ends are lawful, and the 2022 report's author concedes the actions are "most of which are legal". No tribunal has found that any of the money financed violence.
verdicts.reason: The narrative's core survives: IDRF lawfully funded Sangh-affiliated service organisations, and even the defending rebuttal (HVK) concedes the flow. But the claim as stated overreaches in ways that decide the verdict. (1) "Declared on both ends" rests on a cross-reference to fcra-receipts.json, and that file records the opposite: no FC-4 located and FCRA status unverified for Ekal, with Sewa Bharati and VKA absent. (2) The Sewa leg is not supported by the cited source. ThePrint does not list Sewa among the seven, and the primary report's Sewa figure is program expenses not split between US and India. (3) The US$833,000 Covid-relief figure is US domestic money to US organisations, so citing it as evidence of a foreign flow to India is a conjunction error. (4) "Their US chapters" states the critics' framing as fact. (5) The 2002 and 2022 reports both come from the Sabrang/SACW network, so they are not two independent confirmations. "Well-supported" should be narrowed to the IDRF flow, at reported, conceded by the rebuttal. The Sewa leg stays alleged with a contra, and the "funds hate" characterisation stays alleged and contested.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Status: change "well-supported" to "well-supported for IDRF→Sangh-affiliated service organisations (reported; the flow is conceded by the HVK rebuttal); alleged for Sewa International USA (India share not disaggregated); contested for 'funds hate'".
2. Claim text: replace "through their US chapters" with "through US diaspora charities with Sangh-linked leadership (IDRF; Sewa International USA)".
3. strongestCase: delete "hold FCRA registrations and file FC-4s (fcra-receipts.json)". Replace it with "FCRA status and FC-4 receipts of Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of India, Sewa Bharati and VKA unverified — void in fcra-receipts.json".
4. strongestCase: remove the US$833,000 Covid-relief sentence as evidence of the flow, or recast it as "US federal relief to US organisations, not an India flow".
5. strongestCase: attribute the Sewa figure to the primary report (https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/22041101/20220523_hninfluenceusa.pdf, Table 4: $17.1m program expenses 2005–2019, US and India not disaggregated, selected recipient Sevabharati Keralam) and add that URL to srcs. ThePrint does not name Sewa among the seven.
6. strongestCounter: the "83% figure is unverified here" line is stale. The Outlook §4 text says "8% (in addition to the 83% that are Sangh affiliated)" and "in excess of 80%" of IDRF-designated funds, which were about 75% of disbursements. Note that the 2002 and 2022 reports share the Sabrang/SACW network, so they are not independent.
7. strongestCounter: add the IDRF "pure concoction, untruthful and self contradicting" statement and the 2003 six-academic "Factual Response" with URLs; neither is currently sourced. Point the HVK src at https://hvk.org/specialreports/hate/1.html, since index.html is only a table of contents.
8. Fix the mirror reference "(narrative 5)" so it points to the missionary narrative, which is index 4, narrative:4.
9. "No MHA action recorded" should read "No MHA action found; fcraonline cancellation lists not searchable (blocked)".
10. whatWouldChangeThis: keep the Schedule F × FC-4 match. Sewa USA's EIN 20-0638718 is known, so the check can be run.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MHA (FCRA wing, Foreigners Division) cancelled 4,141 FCRA registrations in 2012–13. The actor held the job for the whole window. UPA-II was in office from May 2009 to May 2014, so the cancellations did fall under UPA. The window in the claim is wrong, though. The primary record is Rajya Sabha Unstarred Q.320 of 20 July 2016, answered by MoS Kiren Rijiju. It gives cancellations by calendar year: "2012 4138 / 2013 4 / 2014 59 / 2015 10020 / 2016 (till date) 1". The bulk action was in calendar 2012, not "2012–13". Factly (29 Apr 2015, citing the MHA FCRA Wing) also says "In 2012, a total 4138 NGOs had their FCRA license cancelled", though one line of the same piece says "2011-12". The cited source's own dates don't agree: the page is dated 16 Aug 2013 but the dateline reads 30 Aug 2013, and it only says "in a recent move".
verdicts.identityTest: The actor, MHA/FCRA wing, is correct. The target is the whole population of FCRA-registered associations, not a named entity, so no registration number applies. The target id does not match: the task text has t="ngo:fcra-registered-associations" but the file has t="ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate". Pick one. The denominator of 39,236 registered associations appears only in the News Bharati/HPI piece. It is not in the RS answer, and I did not verify it against the MHA Annual Report 2012-13.
verdicts.baseRate: 4,138 out of about 39k registered is roughly 10.5% of the population, cancelled in one year. The ground was administrative: non-submission of annual returns ("violation of FCRA act & rules (failure to submit annual reports)", Factly citing the MHA FCRA Wing). This was a bulk compliance sweep with the same ground for every association, so it says nothing about targeting. Symmetry control (UPA vs NDA): the NDA's April 2015 order cancelled 8,975 on the same ground (Section 18, non-filing of returns), and the RS answer shows 10,020 for 2015. The same lens gives the same reading under both governments. Both were mass compliance purges, not targeted political action. The Kudankulam-linked actions in 2012 were a separate, small set of four NGOs.
verdicts.denialFound: No response from the affected associations was found, and none was sought. This is a bulk administrative action with no single respondent. The MHA's own position is on record in RS Q.320 (20 Jul 2016): action follows "due process as prescribed in the FCRA, 2010 and FCRR, 2011", with a show-cause notice and opportunity to reply, and orders are "subject to judicial scrutiny". https://www.mha.gov.in/MHA1/Par2017/pdfs/par2016-pdfs/rs-200716/320%20E.pdf
verdicts.innocentReading: This was a routine compliance clean-out. Associations that had not filed mandatory annual returns for several years lost their registrations in one batch. That is the same mechanism the NDA used in April 2015. Tamil Nadu (794), Andhra Pradesh (670) and Kerala (450) top the list because they have among the most registered associations, and they are also the top recipient states. The count does not show a Kudankulam-driven crackdown. That framing is an inference by News Bharati, an RSS-aligned outlet, relayed by HPI. The HPI piece also frames the cancellations around Christian NGOs, and the claim must not carry that religious framing.
verdicts.reason: The claim as written fails on specifics. The figure 4,141 appears only in a partisan secondary aggregator: HPI relaying News Bharati, with inconsistent dates and a Kudankulam framing that is the aggregator's own inference and not in the record. The primary Parliament answer gives 4,138, in calendar 2012 (plus 4 in 2013), not "2012–13". Factly independently gives 4,138 and a ground of non-filing of annual returns. The difference of 3 is not material, and the underlying fact survives: a UPA-era mass cancellation of about 4,138 in 2012. So the claim's upgradeIf condition is met, but only once it is re-sourced and re-dated. With the current source and wording it should not publish.
verdicts.corrections: Change lab to "UPA-era FCRA cancellations, calendar 2012: 4,138 (non-filing of annual returns); 4 in 2013". Set from="2012" and to="2012". Change tier from reported to documented. Replace srcs with two entries: [RS Unstarred Q.320, 20 Jul 2016, MoS Kiren Rijiju, year-wise cancellations 2012=4138, https://www.mha.gov.in/MHA1/Par2017/pdfs/par2016-pdfs/rs-200716/320%20E.pdf] and [Factly, 29 Apr 2015, citing MHA FCRA Wing: 4,138 in 2012, ground non-submission of annual returns, TN 794 / AP 670 / Kerala 450 / Delhi 299, https://factly.in/massive-fcra-cancellation-is-not-a-new-thing-4138-ngos-lost-their-fcra-licenses-in-2012/]. You can keep HPI/News Bharati as a context-only source, labelled partisan, and do not use it for the figure. Drop the "39,236 registered" denominator unless it is verified in the MHA Annual Report 2012-13 or the FCRA portal. Drop "20 accounts frozen, 60 barred" unless you find a primary source. Add ground="non-filing of annual returns (s.18 FCRA 2010)". Add innocentReading stating that it was a bulk compliance action on the same ground as the NDA's April 2015 order (8,975). Do not carry the Kudankulam or Christian-NGO framing in d. Remove upgradeIf, since it is satisfied. Reconcile the target id: ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate in the file vs ngo:fcra-registered-associations in the task.

verdicts.dateTest: Actor and timing: Parliament passed the Amendment on 2020-09-21 (LS) and 2020-09-23 (RS), and it took effect on 2020-09-29, which matches the claim's from=2020-09-29. The trouble is the conduct the claim uses as evidence. CARE India's ground (c066/c067) is a Rs 28.3 crore receipt into a non-designated account in FY2012-13. That falls under the 2010 Act's designated-account rule, not the 2020 Amendment. Oxfam's 2013-16 account allegation (c049) is also pre-2020. World Vision's window runs 2012-13 to 2020-21 and is almost entirely pre-amendment. These cases cannot show who lost under the 2020 text. Only Oxfam's "continued sub-grants after the 2020 ban" and CPR's transfer ground engage s.7 itself. Separate note: an FCRA Amendment Bill 2026 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 2026-03-25 (newsonair). Because the claim is open-ended (to=null), it should be checked against that bill.
verdicts.identityTest: The subject is aggregate ("sc" to ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate; the task payload says ngo:fcra-registered-associations, and the two should be reconciled). No DIN, CIN or registration number is at issue. The case list in field d names the wrong kind of ground for several of its entities. World Vision: c071 in the same file says "specifics not published", so the case cannot be counted as an onward-transfer or account ground. Environics: the recorded ground (c091) is Rs 1,250 paid to each of 711 "protestors for JSW agitation at Dhinkia", which is an activity or protest ground, not sub-granting. CARE India: a non-designated account in 2012-13, not sub-granting. CPR (c064): the grounds are mixed. Transfer and non-designated accounts sit alongside use for "undesirable purposes" affecting economic interests and publication "equated with current-affairs programming" under s.3, which are content grounds.
verdicts.baseRate: The file itself shows that transfer/account grounds are not the modal post-2020 ground. Post-2020 cases in the file with any stated ground: Amnesty (FDI routing, c041), CHRI (projects abroad and consultancy fees, c044), Oxfam (transfer plus "pressurise" via foreign governments, c049), MoC ("adverse inputs", c053), RGF/RGCT (a 2005-07 Chinese-embassy receipt and a 2011 IRF donation, c057/c059), CPR (mixed transfer and content, c064), CARE (a 2012-13 account, c067), World Vision (unspecified, c071), CASA and four others (conversion-related, c074), EFI ("harmony", c076), Environics (protest payments, c091), Bal Raksha Bharat (unspecified misuse, c094). About 3 of 12 are clearly transfer/account grounds (Oxfam, CPR in part, CARE). About 4 carry content or activity grounds (CPR, EFI, CASA cluster, Environics). "Modal" is therefore false on the record in hand. The mass effect of the Amendment era (5,933 cessations on 2022-01-01, c007) came mostly from 5,789 associations not applying for renewal, not from s.7. Also, c012 in the same file says the 20% administrative cap under s.8 falls on "advocacy, research and legal-aid associations whose output is salaries". That is a second operative loser class, and it correlates with orientation.
verdicts.denialFound: This is an analytic claim, so no party is accused and no denial is needed. The government's position lines up with the claim's first half. MoS Home Nityanand Rai, Lok Sabha, 2020-09-21: the Bill is "not against NGOs or an attack against a religion or community" (ThePrint, https://theprint.in/india/fcra-bill-not-against-ngos-meant-to-stop-misuse-of-foreign-funds-says-minister-nityanand-rai/507656/). Contrary position: critics call the law a "tool to silence" civil society (Al Jazeera 2020-11-13, https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2020/11/13/restrictions-on-funding-of-indian-civil-society). CPR (c065) objects to its publications being treated as current-affairs programming.
verdicts.innocentReading: The file's own reading holds for the statutory text. Parliament adopted a bright-line anti-layering rule in s.7, and Noel Harper upheld it as a remedy for "endless chain of transfers ... creating layered trail of money". Under that rule, intermediaries losing out is the design. That reading supports a claim about the text of s.7. It does not support a claim about enforcement outcomes, or about the absence of any orientation effect.
verdicts.reason: The claim joins a supported statement to an unsupported negative one. First half (supported): s.7 made the sub-granting intermediary model illegal. PRS: "The Bill amends this to prohibit the transfer of foreign contribution to any other person." Noel Harper: "a certificate of registration is not granted for acting as an intermediary ... The amended provision, therefore, completely rules out such transfer". Second half (unsupported): "not any political orientation". Neither cited source addresses orientation. The file's own symmetryCheck says the government-aligned control named in the SPEC (VIF, India Foundation, Ekal/Vidya Bharati) "were not examined in this file", so the control needed for the negative claim was never run. The supporting sentence in d ("modal ground is onward transfer / non-designated account") is contradicted by the file's own records. World Vision's grounds are unspecified (c071). Environics' ground is protest payments (c091). CARE's is pre-2020 account conduct (c067). CPR's includes content grounds (c064). EFI's is "harmony" (c076). And c012 names advocacy and research groups as the losers of the s.8 cap. As worded, the claim fails. A narrower version limited to the text of s.7 would stand as analytic.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Rewrite lab as: "The 2020 Amendment's s.7 made the sub-granting intermediary model per se unlawful; its textual target is a funding structure, not a viewpoint." 2. Drop "not any political orientation" until the SPEC control (enforcement against VIF, India Foundation, Ekal/Vidya Bharati affiliates) is run. 3. Replace d with the tally the file actually supports. Of about 12 post-2020 actions with any stated ground, about 3 are transfer/account grounds (Oxfam, CPR in part, CARE, the last for 2012-13 conduct under the 2010 Act) and about 4 carry content or activity grounds (CPR s.3/"undesirable purposes", EFI "harmony", CASA cluster conversion, Environics protest payments). Remove World Vision (grounds unspecified, c071) and Environics (protest-payment ground, c091) from the transfer list. 4. Add s.8 (20% admin cap, c012) as a second operative loser class: advocacy, research and legal aid. 5. Keep srcs at PRS and Noel Harper for the rewritten statutory claim, and drop the case sources from this edge. 6. Reconcile the target id: the file has ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate, the payload has ngo:fcra-registered-associations. 7. Keep upgradeIf and killIf. Add a note that the 2026 FCRA Amendment Bill (introduced in the Lok Sabha 2026-03-25) should be checked before the edge is left open-ended.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MHA (FCRA wing) blocked foreign remittances to Greenpeace India Society from 2014-06 until the Delhi HC order of 2015-01. The Delhi HC judgment of 20.01.2015 (WP(C) 5749/2014) records the prayer to credit "Euros 235000 transferred on 23.06.2014 from St. Greenpeace Council". It also records that Greenpeace wrote to IDBI on 04.07.2014 and to MHA on 17.07.2014, that MHA replied on 28.07.2014 (sent 03.09.2014), that a s.23 inspection notice was issued 08.09.2014 with inspection 24-27.09.2014, and that an interim FD order was made 03.09.2014. The court allowed the petition on 20.01.2015 and ordered IDBI Chennai to permit access to the account. Rajnath Singh was Home Minister from 2014-05-26, so the timing overlaps. The from/to dates 2014-06 to 2015-01 hold for this specific donor-remittance block. Account freezes did not end in 2015-01. The broader freeze of all accounts came with the 180-day suspension in 2015-04 and falls after this edge's window.
verdicts.identityTest: The target is correct. The judgment names the petitioner as "Greenpeace India Society", FCRA-registered since September 2005, with FCRA Account No. 005103000000888 at IDBI Bank, Chennai. The actor is correct at ministry level. The judgment names the "Director, FCRA Division, in the Ministry of Home Affairs". Mongabay says "Modi government" and "Indian Home Ministry". Mapping this to ngo:mha-foreigners-division is acceptable because the FCRA wing sat within the Foreigners Division. One correction: the block targeted remittances from particular donors (Greenpeace International and ClimateWorks Foundation, which MHA said were on its "watch-list"). verdicts.baseRate: Holding up foreign remittances by putting donors on a watch-list or "prior reference" category was a standing MHA tool under both governments. Under UPA, the Kudankulam-linked NGOs in 2012 and CPSC's repeated suspensions in 2012-14 were similar. So the mechanism tells us nothing about which government used it, and this edge claims no pattern. It is a single dated enforcement event that is confirmed. Symmetry holds: the same "enforce" edge would be written for UPA-era holds, and c099 already records that courts found MHA procedurally arbitrary under both governments (INSAF 2013, CPSC 2014, Greenpeace 2015).
verdicts.denialFound: MHA's position is in the court record rather than a press denial. Per the 20.01.2015 judgment, MHA counsel Jasmeet Singh said the government had "no difficulty in the petitioner accessing funds or receiving donations, generally", that the donor GPICWF was on MHA's "watch-list", and that the petitioner's activities were "detrimental to the national interest". The court found "no material whatsoever, on record" to support this. In the Priya Pillai case (Delhi HC 12.03.2015, https://indiankanoon.org/doc/64486862/), MHA said "Greenpeace India's funding was curtailed by Ministry of Home Affairs in 2014, based on specific intelligence inputs". This comes from https://indiankanoon.org/doc/90106439/. Greenpeace's response was the writ petition itself, plus Vinuta Gopal's statement quoted in Mongabay.
verdicts.innocentReading: MHA put the donors (Greenpeace International and ClimateWorks) on a watch-list after intelligence inputs, including the leaked June 2014 IB report on "take-down" of coal projects. It then told banks to seek prior clearance before crediting those donors' remittances, which is an ordinary administrative hold pending a Section 23 inspection. The court did not accept this reading: it found no material supporting the watch-listing and held that civil consequences required natural justice. Even so, that reading is the government's stated rationale and fits the sequence of events.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute it. Mongabay (2015-09-22) supports the edge directly: "Since June 2014, Modi government has blocked several Greenpeace India bank accounts and frozen their funding" and "In January of this year, for example, the Delhi High Court directed the government to unblock Greenpeace India's frozen funds." The primary record, Delhi HC WP(C) 5749/2014 decided 20.01.2015 by Rajiv Shakdher J, independently confirms the actor (the MHA FCRA Division), the target (Greenpeace India Society, IDBI Chennai FCRA account), the start date (a EUR 235,000 remittance of 23.06.2014 held back) and the end (the petition was allowed and the account unblocked). A court order is a primary record, so the tier can rise to documented. The only faults are in the wording: "account freezes" overstates what was a donor-specific remittance hold, and the Mongabay line compresses it.

Interim and procedural wins by NGOs against MHA FCRA actions are common: INSAF 2013 and CPSC 2014 under the UPA government, Greenpeace 2015 under the NDA government (the repo's c099 records this). The symmetry control (UPA-era Delhi HC rulings on INSAF and CPSC) gives the same reading: courts found MHA procedurally deficient under both governments.
verdicts.denialFound: MHA's position is on the record in the judgment itself (paras 8-8.2 and 9.2). Its counsel said the problem lay with the donor, GPICWF, which was on MHA's 'watch-list'. He also said Greenpeace's activities were 'detrimental to the national interest', and that MHA had not exercised its Section 9 powers. The court rejected these arguments. I found no separate public MHA statement about the ruling. Mongabay does not give one and does not say whether it asked for one.
verdicts.innocentReading: The court decided a narrow procedural point, not the merits. Para 9: 'there is no material whatsoever, on record, which would, presently justify' blocking access. Para 9.2: natural justice applies even if the power comes from Section 9. Para 10.1: 'the respondents will be free to proceed against the petitioners, if it is otherwise found to be in violation of any of the provisions of the FCRA.' Read plainly, MHA froze the funds without notice or evidence, and the court required proper process. The court made no finding that the action was unconstitutional.
verdicts.reason: The quoted phrase does not appear in the judgment. The label attributes 'arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional' to the Delhi High Court. Mongabay does write: 'The court also declared that the Indian Home Ministry's actions were "arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional".' But the full text of the 20 January 2015 judgment contains none of the strings 'arbitr', 'unconstitutional' or 'illegal'. That wording is Greenpeace's own description of the ruling, which Mongabay repeated as if the court had said it. What the court actually held (paras 9-10) is narrower and quotable: there was no material on record to justify the block; 'The petitioner's disagreement with the policies of the Government of India, could not, per se be construed as actions which are detrimental to national interest'; natural justice applied; and IDBI was ordered to release the funds. The underlying edge (Delhi HC ruled against MHA's Greenpeace fund block on 2015-01-20) survives and can go up to documented, because the primary court order is now open. The label as written does not survive and must be rewritten.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MHA Foreigners Division (FCRA Wing) cancelled Greenpeace India Society's FCRA registration on 2015-09-02, and the Madras HC stayed that order in mid-September 2015. Mongabay (2015-09-22) says: "On September 2, 2015, the Indian government ordered yet another clampdown on Greenpeace India. India's Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) issued an order cancelling the organization's FCRA ... registration". The Madras HC judgment of 2023-04-25 (Greenpeace India Society v Union of India, indiankanoon doc 193033308) describes the impugned order as "dated 02.09.2015 passed by the Ministry of Home Affairs Foreigners Division (FCRA Wing)". Both dates fall within MHA's continuing statutory role, so there is no tenure problem. On the stay date there is a small imprecision. Mongabay only says "The Madras High Court heard the NGOs petition on September 15, and has now granted a temporary stay on the order for eight weeks". LiveLaw published its report of the stay on 16 Sept 2015 at 6:27 PM IST. So the hearing date is 2015-09-15, and the stay order date is 15 or 16 Sept; the sources do not pin down which.
verdicts.identityTest: The target is Greenpeace India Society, the entity named in the MHA order that Mongabay quotes ("Greenpeace India Society has under-reported...") and the petitioner in the Madras HC writ. The actor is MHA Foreigners Division (FCRA Wing), named exactly that way in the 2023 Madras HC judgment. The FCRA registration number is not given in any source I opened. Identity passes, with the registration number still a gap.
verdicts.baseRate: MHA cancelled FCRA registrations in large numbers in 2015–16 (thousands, mostly bulk cancellations for not filing annual returns), so "an NGO lost its FCRA registration" does not by itself set Greenpeace apart. What is unusual here is a single order specific to one NGO, citing nine alleged violations including under-reporting under s.33. Under the SPEC control the same reading holds for the UPA government: in 2012 it cancelled the registrations of Tamil Nadu NGOs linked to the Kudankulam protests on similar grounds of misreporting or diversion. The edge makes no claim about motive, so the symmetry check does not weaken it. It is a plain enforcement fact.
verdicts.denialFound: Greenpeace India responded and denied the grounds. Mongabay reports that it "has maintained that the allegations are untrue", and quotes co-Executive Director Vinuta Gopal: "We are confident that we have a strong legal case to demonstrate that the MHA is acting without any justification" (https://news.mongabay.com/2015/09/indian-court-protects-greenpeace-against-government-crackdown-again/). LiveLaw quotes her as saying "The MHA has interpreted the FCRA law arbitrarily to build an imaginary case against us" (https://www.livelaw.in/madras-hc-orders-interim-stay-on-cancellation-of-greenpeaces-fcra-registration). No one disputes that the cancellation order was issued. What is disputed is whether its grounds are true.
verdicts.innocentReading: This could be routine s.14 enforcement following an inspection that found discrepancies in foreign-contribution reporting. The order says the Society "under-reported and repeatedly mentioned incorrect amount of foreign contribution received in violation of Section 33". The edge only says the order was issued, which is true under either reading. The grounds are MHA's allegations and have never been adjudicated on the merits: the 2023 Madras HC disposal did not rule on them and left MHA to consider any fresh application.
verdicts.reason: The cancellation fact holds. Mongabay confirms the date, the actor and the quoted ground. LiveLaw independently confirms the interim stay and the eight-week duration. The Madras HC's own 2023 judgment, a primary court record, confirms an order "dated 02.09.2015 passed by the Ministry of Home Affairs Foreigners Division (FCRA Wing)" cancelling the registration. That meets the upgradeIf condition (a second independent outlet or a primary record), so the tier should be documented rather than reported. The killIf condition (order date or ground differs in the order text) is not triggered: the court record gives the same date. The only weakness is that "stay 2015-09-15" should be read as the hearing date, since the stay was reported on 15/16 Sept.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MHA (Foreigners Division, FCRA wing) alleged under-reporting of foreign contribution and account violations against Greenpeace India Society in its cancellation order of 2015-09-02. Mongabay confirms the date: "On September 2, 2015, the Indian government ordered yet another clampdown on Greenpeace India. India's Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) issued an order cancelling the organization's FCRA ... registration." Deccan Herald (DHNS, 2015-09-04) reports the order two days later, which fits. The actor is an MHA office, so there is no personal-tenure gap. The Home Minister at the time was Rajnath Singh (2014-05-26 to 2019-05-30, c003), and the date falls inside that tenure. The date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: Both sources name the target as "Greenpeace India Society", and so does the order as Mongabay quotes it. That matches ngo:greenpeace-india. The FCRA registration number is not in any opened source, so the ID match is by name only, which is acceptable for a single well-known society. The actor is named as "India's Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)". Sources do not name the Foreigners Division as such, but FCRA cancellation orders are issued by that division, so the mapping is standard. The identity test passes, with the gap that the registration number is missing.
verdicts.baseRate: Irregular accounts are one of the most common FCRA cancellation grounds: under-reporting, wrong amounts, money moved to non-designated or non-utilisation accounts, and use for non-declared purposes. Only non-filing of returns is more common. Most cancellation orders under both UPA and NDA cite at least one of these grounds. So the stated ground does not tell us whether Greenpeace was singled out. That question sits with the context edges (c019, c020, c099: the IB report, the Delhi HC's 2015-01 finding that MHA acted "arbitrarily", the Pillai travel ban), not with this edge. Symmetry control from the SPEC: UPA-era actions such as INSAF (2013) and CPSC (2012–14) also rested on transfer and use-of-funds grounds, and courts found MHA procedurally arbitrary in both periods. The same lens gives the same reading, so the edge is not asymmetric as written.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes. Mongabay 2015-09-22 (https://news.mongabay.com/2015/09/indian-court-protects-greenpeace-against-government-crackdown-again/) says "Greenpeace India, however, has maintained that the allegations are untrue." It also quotes Co-Executive Director Vinuta Gopal: "We are confident that we have a strong legal case to demonstrate that the MHA is acting without any justification." Deccan Herald 2015-09-04 (https://www.deccanherald.com/india/govt-cites-9-reasons-action-2148825) says Greenpeace "had submitted a detailed reply on May 7, rebutting all charges and accusing the government of making a 'cynical attempt' to shut it down", and that it said it had "already answered the queries on different fora". Greenpeace was asked: MHA issued a show-cause notice and put further queries to it on 2015-08-19. The denial is already stored as c023.
verdicts.innocentReading: The boring explanation: an FCRA regulator audited Greenpeace's annual returns and bank trail and found discrepancies. These were the reported FC figures, the Rs 3.88 crore received in May 2012 and moved to non-designated accounts, FC spent on bail and writ petitions, and undeclared salary details for Greenpeace International's Greg Muttitt. Those are standard FCRA Section 17/18/19/33 compliance findings, the kind cited against many non-political NGOs. The competing reading, that these were pretexts for targeting a critic, rests on other evidence (the IB report, the earlier Delhi HC rulings) and is not part of this edge. Presented as an allegation that has not been decided on its merits, the edge is neutral.
verdicts.reason: The core allegation holds. The cited source quotes the order directly: "Greenpeace India Society has under-reported and repeatedly mentioned incorrect amount of foreign contribution received in violation of Section 33 of FCRA, 2010." The date is correct, the actor fits, and the tier 'alleged' fits a ground that no court has decided on its merits; I found no source reporting a final Madras HC judgment on merits. However, the second limb, "mixing of funds", does not appear anywhere in the cited Mongabay article. The nearest documented ground (Deccan Herald 2015-09-04, summarising the order's nine reasons) is "transfer of foreign funds to non-designated accounts", including "Rs 3.88 crore collected from abroad in May 2012 to unauthorised bank accounts". That is a different allegation from mixing foreign and domestic funds. So the source check is only partial, and the wording must be corrected rather than the edge killed.

Rs 3.88 crore received May 2012) to non-designated bank accounts; FC used for legal costs (bail/writ petitions)". Optionally add Greenpeace's 2015-05-07 detailed rebuttal of the show-cause notice to c023. 5) The upgradeIf and killIf fields are fine as they stand. Add "registration number not captured" to gaps.

verdicts.identityTest: The court is correct: the source names the "Madras High Court" and the "Indian Home Ministry", and the target min:ministry-of-home-affairs matches. The "energy:" prefix is a mis-namespacing, because a High Court is not an energy-sector entity. The Delhi HC node has the same problem (`energy:delhi-high-court`).
verdicts.baseRate: Interim stays by High Courts on FCRA cancellation or suspension orders are routine in Indian writ practice: INSAF 2013, CPSC 2014, CPR 2023 and Environics notice 2024 appear in this same file. So a stay does not in itself single anything out. The claim does not assert discrimination, though. It is a single dated court event, so the base rate does not weaken it; it only means the edge should not be read as proof of merit.
verdicts.denialFound: none found — not asked. The edge should not be read as the court rejecting MHA's under-reporting ground, which remains alleged in c022 and was never decided on the merits in any opened source. The d field already says "Interim stay; MHA directed to respond. Final outcome not in an opened source," which is the correct restraint.

I opened the Mongabay source (2015-09-22, byline Shreya Dasgupta) and it states the operative facts: "Greenpeace India filed a plea in Madras High Court, and the court has now ordered a temporary eight-week stay on the government order", and "The Madras High Court heard the NGOs petition on September 15, and has now granted a temporary stay on the order for eight weeks. The court has also directed Greenpeace India's advocate to serve a notice to the Indian Home Ministry." The court, the eight-week duration, the date and the target order all match. verdicts.dateTest: Read as a sentence, the claim says MHA (Foreigners Division) put Ford Foundation on the FCRA prior-permission list in 2015 and removed it by a letter to RBI on 2016-03-16. That falls inside Rajnath Singh's term as Home Minister (2014-05-26 to 2019-05-30, record c003), so the dates line up. The source is IBTimes, 18 March 2016, by Harish Revanna. It says: "The Hindu, citing a government official, reported that the ministry sent a letter to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) March 16 to remove the foundation from the watch list." For the start date it only says "Last year, the home ministry put the foundation under the FCRA list". The record's from=2015-04 is not in the cited source. Deccan Chronicle (18 March 2016) does give April 2015, and so does wider reporting of Kiren Rijiju's Lok Sabha answer. The FEMA registration came first: "in December 2015, Ford Foundation registered the agency under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999". December 2015 is before 16 March 2016, so "after" is correct as a matter of timing.
verdicts.identityTest: The source names "U.S.-based international donor agency Ford Foundation", the one Nehru invited in 1952. This matches ngo:ford-foundation. The actor is given as "the home ministry" / "the ministry", which matches MHA. One conflict: the Business Standard/PTI account of the same Hindu story says the Finance Ministry wrote to RBI, while IBTimes and Deccan Chronicle say the Home Ministry. The decision is MHA's either way, but who sent the letter to RBI is not settled. No FCRA registration number applies because Ford was a foreign donor with no FCRA registration.
verdicts.baseRate: This finding does separate Ford from its peers. The Hindu, via IBTimes, says "there are 15 other organisations put under watch list category", which is about 16 donors out of thousands of foreign contributors. That is far below the 80% level at which a trait stops telling you anything. The mechanism was used on others too: Hewlett Foundation (Tribune) and Compassion International (2016). On the SPEC control, the UPA government used freezes and prior-permission against NGOs linked to the Kudankulam protests in 2012. So the tool is not unique to the NDA. What is specific here is the stated ground: a complaint from the Gujarat government about grants to Teesta Setalvad.
verdicts.denialFound: No direct denial found; Ford was not asked in the cited source. Deccan Chronicle quotes Ford as having "submitted an application for registration under applicable Indian law on the direction of the government." The article does not report Ford rebutting the "anti-India" ground. Ford did make 2015 statements about respecting Indian law, but I did not open them here. https://www.deccanchronicle.com/nation/current-affairs/180316/mha-removes-ford-foundation-from-watch-list.html
verdicts.innocentReading: Ford had run in India since 1952 with no registration under any Indian law. On this reading the listing was a regulatory step: MHA held back approvals until Ford registered a branch office under FEMA, and lifted the list once it had. The US Ambassador lobbying and Modi's upcoming US visit, both mentioned in the source, also fit a diplomatic motive for the timing. On this reading, the finding says nothing about whether the "anti-India" allegation was true.
verdicts.reason: The IBTimes page opened (HTTP 200) and supports each part of the claim: placed on the list in 2015, a letter to RBI dated 16 March removing it, and FEMA registration in December 2015. Deccan Chronicle confirms the same event on its own. The claim is an enforcement action, not a finding of wrongdoing, and it names an institution, not a family, religion or ethnic group. "reported" is correct because IBTimes is a secondary aggregator citing The Hindu and TOI. The claim could go up to documented if a second outlet or the Lok Sabha answer is cited. Two soft spots remain. First, "after FEMA registration" can be read as saying registration caused the removal; the source puts the two side by side ("Meanwhile", "Now that it has registered") but never states cause. Second, the April 2015 start date is not in the cited source.

Source the from=2015-04 date: add the Deccan Chronicle article of 2016-03-18 (https://www.deccanchronicle.com/nation/current-affairs/180316/mha-removes-ford-foundation-from-watch-list.html) or Rijiju's Lok Sabha answer, since IBTimes only says "last year". 3. verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MHA (Foreigners Division) lifted Ford Foundation's prior-permission ("prior reference category") requirement on 2016-03-16. The cited source, IBTimes India (Harish Revanna, 18 March 2016 18:46 IST), relays The Hindu: "The Hindu, citing a government official, reported that the ministry sent a letter to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) March 16 to remove the foundation from the watch list." A second chain, PTI via Deccan Chronicle 2016-03-18 (https://www.deccanchronicle.com/nation/current-affairs/180316/mha-removes-ford-foundation-from-watch-list.html), says: "The Home Ministry has decided to remove Ford Foundation from the prior reference category with immediate effect, a Home Ministry spokesperson said on Friday" (Friday was 2016-03-18), and "The Home Ministry has asked the Reserve Bank India to inform all banks about the decision." Rajnath Singh was Home Minister (May 2014 to May 2019), so his tenure covers the action. The two dates fit together: the letter to RBI is dated 16 March and the public announcement came on 18 March. Only the Hindu/IBTimes chain gives the exact 16 March date. PTI dates only the announcement.
verdicts.identityTest: Both outlets name the US-based Ford Foundation, operating in India since 1952, and IBTimes says it registered a branch office under FEMA in December 2015. That matches the node ngo:ford-foundation. Ford is a donor, not an FCRA registrant, so it has no FCRA registration number to check. The actor is the Home Ministry, stated by the official quoted by The Hindu and by the MHA spokesperson quoted by PTI. Assigning the action to the Foreigners Division (the FCRA wing) is a reasonable internal attribution, but neither source names the division.
verdicts.baseRate: IBTimes/The Hindu say 15 other organisations were also on the prior-permission list, so Ford was 1 of about 16. Being taken off the list is not unusual in itself. The claim records an event and does not infer anything from it, so no base-rate problem arises. As a symmetry check, the claim does not frame critics against non-critics. The listing (c025) is the contested act, and this edge records that it was reversed.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed, because the claim does not accuse anyone. The government's own statement is the MHA spokesperson quoted by PTI (Deccan Chronicle, URL above). The only Ford statement on record is an earlier one, relayed by PTI: "the Foundation had said it had submitted an application for registration under applicable Indian law on the direction of the government." I found no Ford statement about the removal itself. The file does not record whether Ford was asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: Removal followed Ford's registration under FEMA 1999 in December 2015, which the ministry had demanded. PTI: "The Ministry asked the Foundation to get itself registered under the Foreign Exchange Management Act." This reads as ordinary regulatory normalisation once Ford complied. Both outlets also note the timing, just before Modi's US visit, and IBTimes mentions US diplomatic pressure from Ambassador Richard Verma. That supports a diplomatic reading too, and it does not undermine the event.
verdicts.reason: The source says exactly what the claim says: the actor (Home Ministry), the action (removal from the prior-permission list) and the date (letter to RBI on 16 March 2016). A second, independent chain confirms the event: PTI, carried by Deccan Chronicle, quoting a named-role MHA spokesperson on the record. IBTimes relays The Hindu, and PTI is independent of The Hindu, so there are two independent credible outlets. Under CONTRACT.md that meets 'documented'. Nothing I opened contradicts the claim, and no hidden conjunction is at work, since it is a single reported event.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Raise the tier from reported to documented. Add the source ["PTI via Deccan Chronicle 2016-03-18 — MHA spokesperson: Ford removed from prior reference category with immediate effect; RBI asked to inform banks", "https://www.deccanchronicle.com/nation/current-affairs/180316/mha-removes-ford-foundation-from-watch-list.html"]. This also meets c025's upgradeIf ("a second outlet"), so re-examine c025 for an upgrade as well. 2) Change 'd' to: "MHA letter to RBI dated 2016-03-16 (The Hindu via IBTimes, citing a government official); MHA spokesperson announced removal from the 'prior reference category' with immediate effect on 2016-03-18 (PTI). Follows Ford's registration of a branch office under FEMA 1999 in 2015-12." 3) Use the official term in the label: "Ford Foundation removed from MHA prior reference (watch) list, 2016-03-16". 4) State in 'd' that IBTimes is a relay of The Hindu, not first-hand reporting. 5) Optionally, add a supersede edge c026 -> c025, or note that this 'enforce' edge records the lifting of an earlier enforcement action, so the graph does not read it as a new punitive action.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: the MHA Foreigners Division put the Ford Foundation under FCRA prior-permission (watch list) on grounds X, from 2015-04 to 2016-03-16. The action was reported on 2015-04-23/24 (AFP via Gulf News; CNBC 2015-04-23). IBTimes (2016-03-18) says "Last year, the home ministry put the foundation under the FCRA list" and that the ministry "sent a letter to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) March 16 to remove the foundation from the watch list." Rajnath Singh was Home Minister from 2014-05-26 to 2019-05-30 (fcra-actions:c003), which covers the whole window. The dates pass.
verdicts.identityTest: Ford Foundation (New York; registered as an Indian branch office under FEMA in 2015-12) is the entity the source names, so the target passes. "Setalvad-linked associations" is loose. The source names "Citizens for Justice and Peace and Sabrang Communications and Publishing Pvt Ltd". Sabrang Communications is a private limited company, not an association. Ford's reported grants went to Sabrang Trust ($250,000 in 2009), which is a separate entity from the company. The attribution also needs splitting. The "anti-India" ground comes from the Gujarat government report. The non-FCRA and for-profit ground is, in the source's words, something "The ministry then had reportedly found", sourced to the Times of India, and is not part of the Gujarat complaint. The record's d field ("Gujarat government complaint adopted by MHA") merges the two.
verdicts.baseRate: The Hindu, as relayed by IBTimes, reports that "there are 15 other organisations put under watch list category", so prior-permission listing is not unique to Ford. Among foreign donors, though, listing is rare. Most foreign contributors are not on the list, so the listing does discriminate. The alleged grounds ("anti-national", "communal disharmony", funding unregistered bodies) are the standard FCRA ground language used against Greenpeace, Compassion and others. The claim is only that the allegation was made, so base rate does not undercut it. Control (UPA 2012 Kudankulam cancellations): the UPA also alleged that foreign funds were diverted to "anti-national" protest activity, so the same lens gives a symmetric reading and there is no asymmetric framing problem.
verdicts.denialFound: A response was found, which contradicts "no Ford response recorded". AFP, carried by Gulf News on 2015-04-24 (https://gulfnews.com/world/asia/india/india-restricts-us-charity-ford-foundations-funding-1.1498186): "The New York-based Ford Foundation said it was cooperating with a home ministry investigation into its grants but was confident it had complied with Indian laws." Search results also carry a Ford statement that it had learned "the Ministry of Home Affairs is reviewing information related to their ongoing investigation of Sabrang Communications and Publishing" and was confident it was complying with the law and transparent about its grants (CNBC 2015-04-23; that page returned 403 to direct fetch, and the text came from the search snippet).
verdicts.innocentReading: Ford made legitimate grants to Sabrang Trust (last one in 2009, for peace-building in Gujarat and Maharashtra) and to CJP. The Gujarat government, which was then pursuing Setalvad in several cases, reframed those grants as "anti-India". Ford's long-standing unregistered status in India (operating since 1952 at Nehru's invitation) made its grants administratively irregular, not subversive. It fixed this by registering under FEMA in 2015-12, and the listing was lifted without any adjudication of the substantive allegation. Ford stated that it complied with Indian law.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the core claim. The IBTimes source, opened and quoted, says the ministry listed Ford "after the Gujarat government said in a report that the U.S.-based agency funded 'anti-India' activities of Citizens for Justice and Peace and Sabrang Communications", and that "The ministry then had reportedly found that the foundation was funding certain non-FCRA registered NGOs, including Sabrang Communications, and other profit-making NGOs." AFP/Gulf News corroborates the Gujarat complaint independently. `alleged` is the right tier because a named government party made the assertion and it was never adjudicated. The claim's statement that no Ford response was recorded is false: AFP reported Ford as "confident it had complied with Indian laws." The attached contra (fcra-actions:c028) is therefore empty when it should be filled. The attribution also merges the Gujarat allegation with the MHA/TOI finding.
verdicts.corrections:
1. c027 text/lab: delete "(no Ford response recorded)". Replace "Setalvad-linked associations" with "Citizens for Justice and Peace and Sabrang Communications & Publishing Pvt Ltd (Teesta Setalvad)". Split the grounds: the "anti-India" ground is from the Gujarat government report; the non-FCRA and for-profit ground is an MHA finding reported by the Times of India via IBTimes.
2. c027 d: replace "Gujarat government complaint adopted by MHA" with "Listing followed a Gujarat government report alleging 'anti-India' activity / 'interfering in the internal affairs' and 'abetting communal disharmony' (AFP); MHA reportedly (TOI) also found grants to non-FCRA-registered and profit-making entities. Never adjudicated; lifted 2016-03-16 after FEMA branch-office registration."
3. Add a second source to c027: Gulf News/AFP, 2015-04-24, https://gulfnews.com/world/asia/india/india-restricts-us-charity-ford-foundations-funding-1.1498186.
4. c028 (contra): set d to "Ford Foundation said it was cooperating with the MHA investigation and was confident it had complied with Indian laws (AFP, 2015-04-24); it was asked." Add the Gulf News URL as the source, and the CNBC 2015-04-23 URL (https://www.cnbc.com/2015/04/23/india-targets-ford-foundation-as-national-security-risk.html) as a secondary source. Tier: reported.
5. c027 upgradeIf: keep "Gujarat government report text", and add "or the MHA prior-permission order / Parliament answer naming the grounds."

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: the MHA (FCRA wing, Foreigners Division) blocked Compassion International's funds from 2016, and Compassion left on 2017-03-15. The Compassion UK blog carries no date, never says "2016", and gives March 15 as a planned date: "If nothing changes in the next couple weeks, our last day of operation in India will be March 15. Months ago, the Indian government began blocking funds." The cited CT 2024-04-02 piece gives only the year 2017: "The first sizable organization of any faith to lose its FCRA license was Compassion International in 2017." The 2016 start date is not in either cited source. It is in CT 2017-03-01, which the CT 2024 piece links to but the claim does not cite: "since last February, when India's Ministry of Home Affairs put it on a list of organizations needing prior approval before transferring funds into the country. Then the government refused to grant such approval." That piece also says "its final day of operation will be March 15." So the dates hold: prior-permission listing in February 2016, planned exit on 2017-03-15, and CT 2024 confirms after the fact that the exit happened in 2017. The actor, the MHA's FCRA administration, was in office for the whole period.
verdicts.identityTest: The target is Compassion International, the US ministry run by CEO Santiago "Jimmy" Mellado, as the foreign donor placed on the MHA prior-approval list. CT 2017 says "put it on a list", which matches ngo:compassion-international. Its Indian recipients (the "two offices") are not named in the opened sources, so no FCRA registration number can be checked. The 2024 CT phrase "lose its FCRA license" is loose, because the mechanism was a prior-permission listing and refusal to approve transfers, not a cancelled registration. The edge label's "(prior-permission category)" is the accurate wording and CT 2017 supports it. There is no identity confusion.
verdicts.baseRate: This edge records that an enforcement step happened. It does not assert wrongdoing or motive, so a base rate does not discriminate much. Prior-permission listing of foreign donors in 2015–16 also hit Ford Foundation, Greenpeace and others, and the file's symmetryCheck puts Compassion among the non-critic Christian relief bodies (World Vision, CASA, EFI). The edge is not being used for a targeting inference.
verdicts.denialFound: Compassion, the party affected (Compassion UK blog, https://www.compassionuk.org/blogs/compassion-closes-india-operations/): "Compassion has broken no laws in India"; it denies the Indian media's conversion allegation. That response is already recorded as c031 against c030. No MHA statement disputing that funds were blocked was found. The government's stated ground (sub-granting to NGOs without FCRA registration) appears only in search summaries, per c030. No MHA response was found because I did not ask and web search was exhausted. CT 2017 reports that one Indian official told India Today the case could be reconsidered.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a routine FCRA compliance action. The MHA put a large foreign donor that sent about $45m a year straight to local churches through two offices on its prior-approval list, then declined approval, possibly over onward transfers to unregistered partners. The edge stays neutral on motive, which is correct.
verdicts.reason: No part of the claim is refuted, but its date support comes from a source the claim does not cite. Every element checks out against a source: funds blocked (Compassion UK), exit on March 15 (Compassion UK and CT 2017), exit year 2017 and US$45m a year (CT 2024: "brought about $45 million annually into India"; CT 2017: "channels about $45 million into the country every year"). The ₹300 crore conversion is correct arithmetic at the stated, flagged rate of about ₹67/US$ (45 × 67 ≈ 301.5). The 2016 start date and the prior-permission mechanism are not in the two cited sources; they come only from CT 2017-03-01. "Reported" is the right tier: the evidence is one credible outlet (CT, 2017 and 2024) plus the affected party's own statement, with no MHA order or Parliament answer opened.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Add to srcs ["Christianity Today 2017-03-01 — Compassion International leaving India", "https://www.christianitytoday.com/2017/03/compassion-international-leaving-india-child-sponsorship/"]. It is the only opened source for the February 2016 prior-approval listing and the refusal. 2) Change from "2016" to "2016-02", citing CT 2017's "since last February". 3) In d, add that the Compassion UK blog is undated and that its March 15 date was prospective; the exit is confirmed by CT 2024 ("in 2017"). 4) Do not rely on CT 2024's "lose its FCRA license" for the mechanism, because the action was a prior-permission listing, not a cancellation. Keep the label's "(prior-permission category)". 5) Optionally, quote CT 2017's "145,000 children" next to Compassion's own "147,000" figure. 6) Keep the tier at reported. upgradeIf: an MHA order or Parliament answer naming Compassion's prior-permission listing.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the Indian government (MHA FCRA wing) put Compassion International on its watch list / prior-permission list and blocked its funds from 2016, on an alleged ground of conversion inducement and/or onward transfer to non-FCRA NGOs, until Compassion exited around 2017-03-15. The window holds together. Matters India (2017-01-11) dates the watch-list listing to 2016-03-28. The Compassion blog is dated 2017-03-01 in its page metadata and says "Months ago, the Indian government began blocking funds" and "If nothing changes in the next couple weeks, our last day of operation in India will be March 15." The listing and the exit both fall within Rajnath Singh's time as Home Minister (2014-05-26 to 2019-05-30). There are two date errors. First, the source label "(2017-03-15)" is wrong: the blog was published around 2017-03-01 and 15 March was a planned end date, not the publication date. Second, "from: 2016" can be narrowed to 2016-03-28 (watch-list or prior-permission listing, per Matters India, citing unnamed officials).
verdicts.identityTest: Target: the entity is Compassion International, the Colorado-based child-sponsorship charity. The blog is signed by CEO Santiago "Jimmy" Mellado, so the entity matches. It has no FCRA number because it is a foreign donor; the Indian recipients named in press reports are Caruna Bal Vikas (Chennai) and Compassion East India. Actor: the Compassion source says only "the Indian government". It does not name the MHA or the Foreigners Division. Deccan Herald (2017-03-10) does name the MHA ("the decision of the Ministry of Home Affairs to put it in 'prior-permission category'"), but as Compassion's own claim. The node ngo:mha-foreigners-division is a fair reading, but the cited source does not name it. The claim does not frame a religion, family or ethnicity as the actor; the target is a named organisation.
verdicts.baseRate: The only cited source does not give a ground-specific base rate. Conversion-related grounds are rare among the more than 20,000 cancellations; most are for non-filing (the 2022 cessations were 97% non-application). The same is true of prior-permission listings of foreign donors: they are a small, discriminating set (Ford Foundation, Compassion and a few others in 2015–16), not something ≥80% of comparable entities share.
