Q.3253 (29.03.2023) later revised WB to 727.20 / 798.18 / 906.12.' 3) Change 'registered' to 'holding valid registration' to match the answer's wording ('FCRA registration certificate of 16383 number of Associations is valid'). Replace '(RS answer via DH)' with '(RS USQ 1662, 15.03.2023)'. 4) Optionally state the national sums from the same Q.1662 table: ₹16,306.04 cr (2019-20), ₹17,058.64 cr (2020-21), ₹22,085.10 cr (2021-22). Narrative strongestCounter at line ~3207 uses the Q.3253 sums (22,121.75 / 17,166.34 / 16,359.48) and says the DH numbers 'are' the Q.3253 WB rows (906.12 / 727.20). It should cite Q.1662 for the exact match. 5) Tier stays analytic. The 16,383 figure could separately carry documented tier on the Q.1662 source.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: Amit Shah held the office of Minister of Home Affairs from 2019-05-30 to the present, a window covering the 2022–26 cancellations and the 2026 Bill. His tenure: sworn in 30 May 2019, with portfolios allocated 31 May 2019, and he kept Home Affairs in Modi III (cabinet.json since 2024-06-10). The PMIndia portfolio page, fetched today, lists "2 Shri Amit Shah Minister of Home Affairs; and Minister of Cooperation." Tribune (19 Jan 2024) refers to a July 2023 open letter "to Home Minister Amit Shah". South First (published 2026-03-25T08:49 per page metadata) says Naidu "personally raised the matter with Union Home Minister Amit Shah". The office overlaps the whole 2022–26 span, and the 2026 Bill was referred to the JPC on 2026-08-12. Small point: the Home portfolio was formally allocated on 31 May 2019, a day after the swearing-in on 30 May. Either date works for this edge.
verdicts.identityTest: Both outlets name "Home Minister Amit Shah" / "Union Home Minister Amit Shah", and the PMIndia primary portal matches. There is only one Union Home Minister, so no one else could be meant. The entity pol:amit-shah matches cabinet.json id amit-shah (BJP, Gandhinagar LS).
verdicts.baseRate: Not a discriminating claim. A role edge records who held an office, and any holder of the office has this property by definition. It says nothing about the person's own conduct.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. Nobody disputes that Shah holds the office. No denial was sought and none is needed for an office-holding edge.
verdicts.innocentReading: Holding the office does not mean he personally decided on any FCRA cancellation. Cancellations and non-renewals are handled by the MHA's FCRA wing (Foreign Division) under delegated powers. The edge has to stay a pure 'role' edge and must not be read as making Shah the decision-maker on WVI, Oxfam, CPR or other individual cases. The 'during the 2022–26 cancellations' wording in lab/text only describes timing, and nothing in the sources links him to any individual decision.
verdicts.reason: Both cited sources say what the claim says: Tribune quotes the "open letter to Home Minister Amit Shah" of July 2023, and South First quotes "Union Home Minister Amit Shah" in March 2026. The PMIndia portfolio page (a primary official portal, which the claim's upgradeIf names) was opened today and confirms "Shri Amit Shah Minister of Home Affairs". Under CONTRACT.md, an official portal, or two independent credible outlets, meets 'documented'. The claim is under-tiered, not over-tiered. It is not a conjunction problem because the edge asserts only office-holding over time.
verdicts.corrections: tier: reported → documented. srcs: add ["PMIndia — Portfolios of the Union Council of Ministers (updated 25 Jul 2026)", "https://www.pmindia.gov.in/en/news_updates/portfolios-of-the-union-council-of-ministers-2/"]. d: replace "PMIndia source not re-opened" with "PMIndia portfolio page opened 2026-09-26 confirms current office". Optionally note that the portfolio was allocated 2019-05-31 (sworn 2019-05-30). upgradeIf: satisfied, so set to "—". Add an innocentReading/caveat to the edge: "office-holding only; FCRA case decisions are taken by the MHA FCRA wing and are not attributed to the Minister personally by these sources".

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: MHA told the JPC (Sept 2026) that 1 association received more than ₹500 cr and 14 received ₹100–500 cr "between 2022 and 2024". The band counts and period match ThePrint/PTI word for word: "Between 2022 and 2024, one NGO received over Rs 500 crore, 14 NGOs received between Rs 100 crore to Rs 500 crore, 294 got betwen Rs 10 crore to 50 crore. As many as 4508 received between Rs 5 lakh to Rs 50 lakh." The denominator fails the date test. The source gives 14,466 as the number of NGOs "currently" active at the September 2026 JPC meeting ("there are 14,466 FCRA registered active NGOs"). It is not the number active in 2022–24. The file's own series puts registrations in that window at about 16,383 (March 2023) and 16,242 active (May 2024), and some 2022–24 recipients have since been cancelled or have expired. So "of ~14,466 active in 2022–24" mixes two time windows. Also, the record's from/to (2022-04-01 to 2024-03-31) is our reading of "between 2022 and 2024". The source does not say whether it means calendar years or FY2022-23 to FY2023-24, or whether the amounts are cumulative or per year.
verdicts.identityTest: This is an aggregate node, so no individual entity is named. MHA gave only bands, with no FCRA registration numbers, and no attribution to a person or organisation is possible or attempted. The actor is MHA (Home Secretary Govind Mohan) presenting to the JPC chaired by Sanjay Jaiswal, and that matches the source.
verdicts.baseRate: Heavy-tailed concentration is normal in donor markets. Domestic philanthropy (the SPEC control: Azim Premji Foundation, Tata Trusts, Reliance) and foreign-aid markets elsewhere show the same pattern of a few large recipients. The property does not discriminate, and the claim draws no inference from it. 15 of about 14,466 is about 0.1%. With a time-consistent denominator of about 16,000–16,800 it is about 0.09%. The reported bands leave gaps (₹50 lakh–₹10 cr and ₹50–100 cr are missing), so no share of total money can be computed. The claim says this correctly.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; not asked. No NGO is named, so there is no party to respond. The source is MHA's own presentation. Every outlet found (ThePrint, Millennium Post, Daily Excelsior, ETV Bharat, Kashmir Observer, Nagaland Post, Highland Post, India CSR) repeats the same PTI copy. No contrary reporting found.
verdicts.innocentReading: Large international health, child-sponsorship and education NGOs, plus big institutional recipients, account for most foreign contribution, as in any donor market. The concentration says nothing about purpose or legality. The record already carries this reading.
verdicts.reason: The substance holds. PTI (via ThePrint, confirmed by opening the page) reports exactly 1 association above ₹500 cr and 14 at ₹100–500 cr in 2022–24. The note "bands only, top-20 share not computable" is also correct, because the bands skip ₹50–100 cr. The analytic tier fits: the concentration framing is our reading, it carries an innocentReading, and it implies no wrongdoing. The underlying band counts are reported-tier: one wire story (PTI) of MHA's JPC presentation, syndicated everywhere, so India CSR is not an independent second source. The one flaw is the denominator. 14,466 is the active count in September 2026, but the claim presents it as the population active in 2022–24. That is a conjunction of two true figures from different windows and needs fixing, but it does not defeat the claim.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Text: change "of ~14,466 active in 2022–24" to "15 associations received ≥₹100 cr in 2022–24 (1 above ₹500 cr); 14,466 are active as of Sept 2026 (active registrations in 2022–24 were ~16,200–16,800)". The lab should do the same: drop "out of ~14,500 active" or date it "(Sept 2026)". 2) The `d` field says "294 at ₹10–50 cr; 4,508 at ₹5–50 lakh". Add that the ₹50 lakh–₹10 cr and ₹50–100 cr bands were not reported. Also add that "between 2022 and 2024" is not defined in the source (calendar vs financial years; cumulative vs annual), so from/to 2022-04-01 to 2024-03-31 is an interpretation and should be flagged as one. 3) The baseRates entry (numerator 15 / denominator 14,466) uses a denominator from a different window. Relabel it "vs Sept 2026 active count", or use a 2022–24 figure (16,383 in March 2023 or 16,242 in May 2024). 4) Source note: India CSR repeats the PTI copy ("reportedly") and is not independent. Do not count it as a second source for any future upgrade of the band counts. 5) upgradeIf is fine as is ("Association-wise receipts published"). killIf "—" could become "MHA/JPC record shows different band counts or period".

verdicts.dateTest: Restated, the claim is: FCRA-registered associations in aggregate received ₹17,832 cr in FY2015-16 and ₹22,974 cr in FY2024-25, while active registrations went from 29,022 to 14,466. ThePrint/PTI (18 Sep 2026) confirms both figures: "The funds received by the FCRA registered NGOs from abroad went up to Rs 22974 crore in 2024-25 from Rs 17832 crore in 2015-16. During the same period, the number of active NGOs dipped from 29022 to 14466." There is one small date mismatch. The same article also says "There were 29022 FCRA registered active NGOs in 2015", which is calendar 2015, not FY2015-16. The 91.3% share does not belong to the 2015-25 window. It is a share of all 21,983 cancellations to date: "The government has so far cancelled FCRA registration of 21983 NGOs — 91.3 per cent for not filing annual returns, 7.9 per cent for being inactive, 0.4 per cent for legal violations." Some of those cancellations happened before 2015, for example the 2015 purge of non-filers for the 2009-12 returns. So the innocent reading applies a cumulative figure to a window it does not measure.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is the whole population of FCRA-registered associations as MHA presented it to the JPC on the FCRA Amendment Bill (Home Secretary Govind Mohan; JPC chaired by Sanjay Jaiswal). There is no single-entity identity problem, and s=t=ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate is correct. The second source, IndiaCSR (20 Sep 2026), reproduces the same MHA numbers ("an increase of Rs. 5,142 crore, or nearly 28.8%"). It is derived from the same PTI/MHA feed, so it is not independent.
verdicts.baseRate: This is an aggregate claim, so no peer-fraction test applies. The deflator test does apply, and it fails the claim on its own killIf ("Series shows receipts fell in real terms"). CPI-Combined annual averages (Economic Survey 2025-26, Statistical Appendix Table 4.3, base 2012=100) went from 125 in 2015-16 to 193 in 2024-25, a rise of 54.4%. Receipts therefore fell by about 16.6% in real terms (1.288/1.544 = 0.834). Average INR/USD went from about 65.5 in 2015-16 to about 84.6 in 2024-25 (+29%). In dollars, receipts were flat: about US$2.72 bn → US$2.72 bn. The whole 28.8% nominal rise is rupee depreciation. On the UPA control, the same dormancy pattern was already there: the file records 16,756 non-filers out of 41,844 registrants in Dec 2013. The halving of the registration count is therefore not unique to the NDA period.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The figures are MHA's own, presented to the JPC, and the claim accuses no one. On the related bill, the government denied that it targets minorities, saying the legislation "is not religion-specific and is aimed at regulating foreign contributions" (same ThePrint article). That denial is not relevant to this arithmetic.
verdicts.innocentReading: The boring explanation fits completely. Money from abroad was flat in dollars and fell in real rupee terms. The registration count halved mainly because dormant or non-compliant registrants were purged (91.3% of all cancellations to date were for non-filing, plus 7.9% for inactivity) and because registrations lapsed at renewal. The 'rise' is an artefact of measuring in nominal rupees. The existing innocentReading wording also needs care. Non-filing is a proxy for dormancy, not the same thing: MHA lists "inactive" (7.9%) as a separate ground, so not every non-filer is proven dormant. The fall in the active count (−14,556) also includes non-renewals and is offset by new registrations. It is not the same thing as the 21,983 cancellations.
verdicts.reason: The source numbers check out. But as worded ("Receipts +28.8% while active registrations halved"), the claim presents a nominal-rupee rise as growth. At its own endpoints it meets its own killIf: CPI-deflated receipts fell about 17%, and in USD they were flat (about $2.72 bn in both years). The comparison survives only if it is restated with the deflation built into the claim, not tucked into the innocent reading. The 91.3% figure is also applied to the wrong base (all cancellations to date, not the 2015-25 window). The file's narrative strongestCounter ("aggregate receipts rose to a record ₹22,974 cr") inherits the same nominal-only framing. Its own whatWouldChangeThis condition (a real-terms fall) is already met at the endpoints.
verdicts.corrections:
1. lab/text: change to "Nominal foreign contribution rose 28.8% (₹17,832 cr FY2015-16 → ₹22,974 cr FY2024-25) — flat in US$ (~$2.72 bn both years) and ~17% lower in CPI-deflated terms — while active registrations halved (29,022 in 2015 → 14,466)."
2. innocentReading: replace "91.3% of cancellations were dormant non-filers" with "Of 21,983 cancellations to date (not confined to 2015-25), 91.3% were for non-filing of returns and 7.9% for inactivity; the active-count fall also reflects renewal lapses; the rupee rise equals INR depreciation."
3. killIf: its condition is already met at the endpoints, so either rewrite the claim as in item 1 or reword killIf to "Year-wise USD series shows a sustained decline."
4. srcs: add the deflator sources, Economic Survey 2025-26 Stat. App. Table 4.3 (https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/stat/tab4.3.pdf) and the RBI reference rate. Note that IndiaCSR is a derivative of the PTI/MHA figures, not an independent source.
5. from: 29,022 is dated "in 2015" (calendar year) in the source. Say so in d, or set from to 2015-01-01 for the count.
6. Knock-on fix in the same file: in the narrative strongestCounter (line ~3149), change "aggregate receipts rose to a record ₹22,974 cr" to "nominal receipts rose to ₹22,974 cr (flat in US$, down in real terms)". The source does not say "record".

verdicts.dateTest: Written out: the Ministry of Home Affairs told the JPC on the FCRA Amendment Bill 2026, at its first meeting (reported by PTI on 18 Sep 2026), how much foreign contribution each category of association received in FY2024-25. The from/to fields (2024-04-01 to 2025-03-31) match the "2024-25" in both sources. The event date, 18 Sep 2026, falls after the Lok Sabha referred the bill to the JPC on 12 Aug 2026. No chronology problem.
verdicts.identityTest: The node is ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate, used as both s and t. It is an aggregate and names no association, so there is no FCRA registration number, CIN or DIN to check. The label is wrong, though. The sources describe a classification of ASSOCIATIONS, not of purpose. ThePrint/PTI says "Christian associations received the bulk of the funds in 2024-25 at Rs 1345 crore, Hindu NGOs followed with Rs 328 crore". IndiaCSR says "classified contributions received by different categories of associations". Neither source uses the phrase "religious-purpose FC", and neither says what test MHA used to put an association in a religious category.
verdicts.baseRate: The sources give no count of registrants by religious category, so no share of comparable entities can be computed. Scale checks: the named categories add up to ₹1,803 cr (1,345 + 328 + 60 + 51 + 19). That is about 7.8% of the ₹22,974 cr total, or 8.0% if PTI's ₹1,841 cr is used. The ₹5,150 cr "religious associations" figure would be 22.4%. Christian-run schools and hospitals have long been among the largest FCRA recipients, so a large Christian share is the expected pattern, not a discriminating one. Symmetry check against the SPEC controls: Christian-linked recipients (World Vision, Compassion partners, Missionaries of Charity) and Hindu-linked ones (Ekal and Vidya Bharati affiliates) sit in the same MHA table. The classification is MHA's own, and the lens gives the same reading for both sides.
verdicts.denialFound: None found on the figures. Christian bodies have commented on the bill itself: CBCI sought referral to a JPC and removal of Clause 16 (https://theprint.in/india/mizoram-cm-christian-bodies-urge-centre-to-refer-fcra-amendment-bill-to-jpc/3010053/), and the new National Federation of Churches in India was weighing a joint response on 18 Sep 2026 (https://www.licas.news/2026/09/21/indias-new-church-federation-weighs-joint-response-to-proposed-funding-law-changes/). Nothing I found responds to the ₹1,345 cr figure or the religion breakdown. Whether anyone was asked is not recorded.
verdicts.innocentReading: MHA sorts registrants by self-declared nature (religious, and within that by faith). Church-run hospitals, schools and relief bodies have been in the FCRA system for decades and receive money from US, UK and German church donors, so the Christian category comes out largest simply because that is how the sector is built. The ₹5,150 cr and ₹1,841 cr totals most likely come from two different MHA tables or bases, and a wire summary put them side by side. None of this implies wrongdoing by any faith group.
verdicts.reason:
The figures themselves are confirmed: ₹1,345 cr Christian, ₹328 cr Hindu, ₹60 cr non-religious, ₹51 cr Buddhist, ₹19 cr Muslim, and ₹5,150 cr for "religious associations". The claim fails on three other points.

1. It misses the denominator in the PTI lede. ThePrint/PTI opens with "Christian associations accounting for nearly three-fourth of the total Rs 1841 crore in 2024-25", and 1,345/1,841 = 73%. The basis for the named categories is therefore not unknown: the wire reports a ₹1,841 cr total, which the named categories almost exhaust (₹1,803 cr, leaving about ₹38 cr unnamed). The real inconsistency is ₹1,841 cr against ₹5,150 cr inside the same PTI copy, a gap of about ₹3,309 cr. The record's guess ("associations classified religious vs purpose-coded receipts") is not in either source.

2. It relabels the data as "religious-purpose FC", but the source classifies associations, not purposes.

3. Its central frame is a religion-against-religion comparison ("Christian ₹1,345 cr vs Hindu ₹328 cr") on an aggregate self-loop edge. That makes faith communities the actor. Under the fleet rule this is killed as an edge and kept only as a narrative. The narrative's figures should be tiered "reported", not "documented": IndiaCSR repeats the PTI wire almost word for word and is not independent, and the MHA presentation to the JPC has not been published.

The "mirror the donor-country mix" part of the innocent reading is our own inference; no source says it.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Kill c070 as a graph edge (pred analytic, s = t = ngo:fcra-associations-aggregate). Move the content to a narrative entry at tier "reported", with the source given as "MHA presentation to JPC, as reported by PTI 18 Sep 2026".
2. Replace "Religious-purpose FC" with "FC received by associations MHA classifies by religion (classification basis unpublished)".
3. Add the PTI lede figure to the lab or d field: "Christian associations nearly three-fourth of total ₹1,841 cr" (1,345/1,841 = 73%). Record that the named categories sum to ₹1,803 cr.
4. Rewrite d as: "PTI copy gives two totals — ₹1,841 cr (religion-classified breakdown, lede) and ₹5,150 cr ('religious associations', body); ₹3,309 cr gap unexplained in the source."
5. Delete the speculative line "associations classified religious vs purpose-coded receipts".
6. Drop "vs" and any Christian-against-Hindu contrast in the text. List all five categories in neutral order along with the ₹60 cr non-religious figure.
7. Mark "mirrors donor-country mix (US, UK, Germany)" in the innocentReading as our inference. The donor-country figures (USA ₹12,113 cr, UK ₹2,414 cr, Germany ₹1,782 cr) are totals for all FC, not religion-specific.
8. Note that IndiaCSR is derivative of the PTI wire, so it is not a second independent source.
9. Keep upgradeIf as "JPC/MHA table with classification basis published".
10. Add a contra line: "No response recorded — asked/not asked unknown".

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: MHA told the JPC (September 2026 presentation) that FCRA associations as a whole held ₹35,968 cr of unutilised FC at the end of FY2024-25. The actor is MHA as the reporting ministry and the holders are all associations in aggregate, so no tenure window applies. The record's from/to of 2025-03-31 matches the sources: ThePrint/PTI says "in 2024-25" and IndiaCSR says "at the end of 2024-25". The ratio divides this ₹35,968 cr stock by the ₹22,974 cr FY2024-25 receipt flow from the same presentation: 35,968 / 22,974 = 1.566, so "~1.6 years" is correct and matches IndiaCSR's "56.6% higher". There is a period mismatch in the innocent reading. It cites RS Q.3253 (29.03.2023), which covers FY2019-20 to FY2021-22 only, so it cannot show how the FY2024-25 balance behaves.
verdicts.identityTest: The node is the aggregate of all FCRA associations and no single registrant is named, so there is no FCRA number, CIN or DIN to match. The figure is attributed to "MHA representatives" presenting to the JPC on the FCRA Amendment Bill, and both sources name the same body. The amounts are all in INR crore, with no conversion. The three components add up: 21,140 + 8,394 + 6,377 = 35,911, which is ₹57 cr short of 35,968. That gap is presumably rounding or unlisted accounts in the source, and the claim does not assert the components sum exactly.
verdicts.baseRate: The property is aggregate, so it cannot single out any entity. RS Q.3253 is the only official flow table opened. My sum of its annexures shows national FC utilised exceeding FC received in all three years: ₹27,984.86 cr vs ₹16,359.48 cr (2019-20), ₹25,686.35 cr vs ₹17,166.34 cr (2020-21) and ₹25,506.87 cr vs ₹22,121.75 cr (2021-22). Utilisation exceeded receipts in 30, 30 and 26 of the 34 states/UTs, which argues against persistent hoarding. No published comparable exists for domestic trusts or the SPEC controls (Azim Premji Foundation, Tata Trusts), so I cannot say what balance-to-receipts ratio is normal for grant-making or grant-receiving bodies. Multi-year project funding and corpus fixed deposits are ordinary practice.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. No association and no sector body (for example VANI) was asked about the balance figure. MHA is the source, not an accused party. IndiaCSR's own write-up gives the benign reading: "The large accumulated balance may include funds received over multiple financial years for continuing or long-term projects." (https://indiacsr.in/fcra-registered-ngos-foreign-funding-india-22974-crore/)
verdicts.innocentReading: The ₹35,968 cr is a stock built up over several years, set against a single year's inflow. Multi-year grants, corpus and endowment money kept in fixed deposits, and interest earned on those deposits all push the stock up without any misuse. RS Q.3253 shows that in FY2019-22 associations spent more than they received each year, nationally and in most states, which is what drawing down earlier balances looks like. Part of the "utilised" figure may also be FC passed from one FCRA association to another and counted again. Money sitting in utilisation and designated accounts is the normal working capital the FCRA account structure requires.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives. ThePrint/PTI states the figure exactly: "as much as Rs 21140 crore of the total Rs 35968 crore unutilised foreign contribution in 2024-25 was lying as fixed deposits, Rs 8394 crore in the utilisation accounts of these NGOs and Rs 6377 crore in designated accounts". IndiaCSR independently carries "Rs. 35,968 crore was unspent at the end of 2024-25". The ~1.6-year ratio is correct arithmetic on the ₹22,974 cr receipts from the same presentation. The claim attributes nothing to any single actor, implies no wrongdoing and carries an innocent reading, so the analytic tier is right. The underlying figure should still be treated as reported rather than documented: the MHA presentation to the JPC has not been published, and IndiaCSR probably derives from the same PTI copy, so the two outlets are not independent. Two weaknesses remain. The innocent reading leans on a FY2019-22 table to describe a FY2024-25 balance, which joins two periods. And it understates its own evidence by saying "several states/years" when the table shows all years and most states.
verdicts.corrections: 1. innocentReading: replace "utilisation exceeding receipts in several states/years" with "national utilisation exceeded receipts in all three years FY2019-20 to FY2021-22 (₹27,985/25,686/25,507 cr vs ₹16,359/17,166/22,122 cr; 30/30/26 of 34 states), consistent with drawing down earlier balances; that table predates the FY2024-25 balance and does not describe it directly." 2. d: add "Stock-to-flow ratio (35,968 / 22,974 = 1.57), our arithmetic; the underlying figure is from an unpublished MHA presentation to the JPC, reported via PTI; IndiaCSR probably relies on the same copy, so the underlying fact is reported, not documented." 3. Add upgradeIf: "JPC report or MHA presentation published, or a Parliament answer giving unutilised FC balances." 4. Note that the listed components sum to ₹35,911 cr, ₹57 cr short of the ₹35,968 cr total. 5. The narrative strongestCase at line ~3223 of fcra-receipts.json uses the ₹35,968 cr as the pool of assets the Designated Authority could take over. That is wrong: the balance is held mainly by active associations, not the ~37,700 cancelled or expired ones. It should be qualified there.

verdicts.dateTest: Pass. The claim covers three periods, and each figure matches the source for its year. FY2011-12 donors: Deccan Herald of 20 Mar 2014 reports the MHA annual report: "Foreign donors were topped by the Compassion International of the US (Rs 183.83 crore) followed by Church of Jesus Christ of Latter day Saints of the US (Rs 130.77 crore)." FY2015-16 recipients: The News Minute of 20 Mar 2017, citing TOI, says "With Rs 826 crore in foreign contribution, Ayana Charitable Trust in Kerala topped the list" and "Param Shakthi Peeth, which had links to the RSS and VHP, came in a distant second with foreign donations of Rs 417.94 crore"; Believers (Rs 342.63 cr) and WVI (Rs 319.26 cr) were third and fourth, and RDT (Rs 208.78 cr) sixth. FY2024-25: ThePrint/PTI of 18 Sep 2026, reporting the MHA presentation to the JPC, says "Christian associations received the bulk of the funds in 2024-25 at Rs 1345 crore, Hindu NGOs followed with Rs 328 crore" and "went up to Rs 22974 crore in 2024-25". The narrative never compares FY16 recipients with FY25 totals as if they were the same year. The 2026 Rules proselytisation exclusion is confirmed by the PIB factsheet of 22 Jul 2026.
verdicts.identityTest: Mostly passes. Ayana, Believers Church India, WVI (Chennai), Param Shakthi Peeth (New Delhi) and RDT (Anantapur) are named in the source as the claim names them. Three problems. (1) RDT is described as "Christian-founded" in strongestCase ("four of the top six"). The sources only say "Vincent Ferrer was the person who started RDT" and that his stand was "India does not need an additional God". Ferrer was a former Jesuit who had left the order, and RDT presents itself as non-religious. Counting RDT as Christian repeats the IB note's framing. The supportable statement is "three of the top four". (2) TNM does not name recipient #5, so "four of the top six" rests on an unverified slot. (3) The FY2024-25 split is by association category, not by purpose code. PTI and IndiaCSR say "Christian associations" and "religious associations received Rs 5,150 crore". Yet the file's claim label (line ~3011) says "Religious-purpose FC", and strongestCounter says "religious-coded receipts" and "most FC is coded social/educational/health". No opened source says the rest of the FC is coded social, educational or health; that is our inference. The PTI lead also gives a total of "Rs 1841 crore", which differs from the ₹1,743 cr sum of named categories and from the ₹5,150 cr figure. The file flags this gap, but the narrative should state it.
verdicts.baseRate: Share of total FC: Christian associations received 1,345 of 22,974 cr in FY2024-25 (5.9%). All named religious categories came to 1,743 cr (7.6%), and on the broadest basis "religious associations" received 5,150 cr (22.4%). In FY2015-16 the three undisputed Christian recipients in the top four took 1,488 of 17,832 cr (8.3%). "Dominated" therefore fails on every basis for total FC. It holds only inside the religious-association category (about 73% of 1,841 cr per PTI). Donor side: US, UK and Germany supplied 16,309 of 22,974 cr (about 71%). Charities from majority-Christian donor countries are the expected main source, so Christian affiliation among large foreign donors does not discriminate much. Category undercount: faith-based bodies registered as social or educational (e.g. WVI, Caritas, Sewa, Ekal) fall outside the religious categories. This hides both Christian-affiliated and Hindu-affiliated money, so the 5.9% figure is a floor, not a ceiling, for both.
verdicts.denialFound: Recorded, from the parties concerned. RDT to MHA, via Deccan Chronicle of 23 Mar 2024: it "has never encouraged any religious conversions in the past 55 years" and "has even dismissed persons from its employment in case they have a tendency of converting people" (https://www.deccanchronicle.com/news/non-renewal-of-rdts-fcra-threatens-3k-jobs-medical-aid-886199). Government position, via PTI/ThePrint and IndiaCSR of Sep 2026: the Bill is "not religion-specific", while MoS Nityanand Rai called it "dangerous" for those engaged in "forced religious conversion" using foreign contributions (https://indiacsr.in/fcra-registered-ngos-foreign-funding-india-22974-crore/). Believers Church said its registrations were "under revision" (Christian Post, per the file). No response on the narrative itself was found from Ayana/GFA, WVI or Param Shakti Peeth; whether they were asked is unknown. No court or adjudicated finding that FC was used as an inducement to convert was found in any source opened.
verdicts.innocentReading: About 70% of India's FC comes from the US, UK and Germany, where the largest private international-aid charities are church-derived (Compassion, World Vision, GFA, LDS humanitarian). Their Indian partners run child sponsorship, hospitals and schools. Christian institutions are over-represented in Indian health and education delivery relative to population, as they were before 2014. So Christian-affiliated bodies leading the religious-association category is what donor geography and sector mix predict, with no conversion motive needed. The same lens applied to Hindu-affiliated bodies (Param Shakti Peeth #2 in FY16; Hindu NGOs leading receipts in Gujarat, Delhi and Tamil Nadu in FY25 per PTI; US-based Ekal/Sewa/IDRF-type donors, whose receipts the file could not find) gives the mirror allegation ("foreign money for Hindutva"). That symmetry is a finding about the lens.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the claim. All five cited sources were opened (HTTP 200) and say what the narrative says on amounts, years and actors: 1,345 vs 328 cr, 22,974 cr, 5,150 cr, Ayana 826 cr, Param Shakthi Peeth 417.94 cr at #2, and Compassion/LDS as top donors in FY2011-12. The verdict does not overreach: the "dominated" limb fails on every denominator (5.9–22% of total FC), and the "aimed at conversion" limb has no adjudicated finding. The narrative names a religion as the actor, so under CONTRACT rule 1 it must never become an edge. It stays a narrative, so the tier is analytic. It survives only with the corrections below. Three parts of strongestCase and strongestCounter are our inference or framing, not the sources': RDT as "Christian-founded", "most FC is coded social/educational/health", and "precisely because the returns did not distinguish it". Arguably the status should be "unsupported" rather than "contested", because the strong form (dominance of all FC, conversion aim) has no support. Only the weak form (Christian associations lead the religious-association category) is documented-to-reported.
verdicts.corrections: 1. strongestCase: replace "four of the top six recipients (… RDT ₹209 cr) were Christian-founded" with "three of the top four recipients (Ayana ₹826 cr, Believers ₹343 cr, WVI ₹319 cr) were Christian bodies. RDT (#6, ₹209 cr) was founded by ex-Jesuit Vicente Ferrer and describes itself as non-religious; #5 is not named in the source." 2. strongestCounter: drop "most FC is coded social/educational/health" (no source) or mark it [analytic]. Replace "religious-coded receipts" with "receipts of associations the MHA classified by religion". Drop "precisely because the returns did not distinguish it"; PIB says only that the Rules "exclude proselytisation from permitted religious activity". 3. Add the PTI lead figure: "Christian associations accounting for nearly three-fourth of the total Rs 1841 crore". Note that 1,841 / 1,743 (+60 non-religious = 1,803) / 5,150 do not reconcile. 4. Add the symmetry facts to strongestCounter: PTI says "Hindu NGOs received the bulk of the amount in Gujarat, Delhi, Tamil Nadu", and TNM says Param Shakthi Peeth "had links to the RSS and VHP". Also note that category coding undercounts faith-affiliated bodies registered as social on both sides. 5. Relabel the claim at line ~3011 from "Religious-purpose FC" to "FC by association religious category (MHA to JPC)". Its tier should be reported: one PTI wire, with IndiaCSR probably derived from it, so not two independent outlets. 6. Consider changing status from "contested" to "unsupported (strong form); weak form reported". 7. Keep as a narrative only; never emit a religion→money edge.

verdicts.dateTest: The dates hold, with one caveat about the start of the cancellation count. The pieces, each with its actor and time window: (1) MHA refused Oxfam India's renewal on 2022-01-01 and cancelled CPR on 2024-01-10 (notice date). Both fall inside NDA rule, with Amit Shah as Home Minister from 2019-05-30. (2) MHA suspended CARE India on 2023-06-14, also inside NDA rule. But the ground it gave is a FY2012-13 receipt, which is UPA-era conduct. (3) 16,756 of 41,844 registrants had not filed FY2011-12 returns as of 18.12.2013 (RS *199, MoS R.P.N. Singh, UPA). This is confirmed in the PDF: "total 16756 NGOs have not filed their annual returns for the year 2011-2012 so far" and "Total number of NGOs registered under FCRA, as on date are 41844". That gives 40.0%, so the figure is correct. (4) "The government has so far cancelled FCRA registration of 21983 NGOs" (PTI in ThePrint, 18 Sep 2026). The start date is not stated. The Tribune says 16,000 were cancelled between 2015 and 2024, so the 21,983 cumulative total may include UPA-era cancellations, such as the 2012 round. That means "91% of NDA cancellations" cannot be read from this figure. (5) RDT was cleared in March 2026 after CM Naidu (TDP, an NDA ally, in office since June 2024) raised it with Amit Shah (South First, 25 Mar 2026). This is consistent.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities are named correctly: Oxfam India, Centre for Policy Research, CARE India (CISSD), World Vision India, RDT. However, the FCRA registration numbers are null on every entity node (identity.fcra: null). This is acceptable for a narrative but not for the edges underneath it. CARE India's action is recorded as a 180-day suspension. The record itself says "Final cancellation (2024?) NOT verified in an opened source", so saying CARE "lost access" goes beyond the suspension that is on record.
verdicts.baseRate: The 91.3% non-filing share (MHA to the JPC via PTI, confirmed verbatim: "91.3 per cent for not filing annual returns, 7.9 per cent for being inactive, 0.4 per cent for legal violations") says nothing either way about the targeting thesis. The thesis is about a few dozen prominent critics, not about the roughly 20,000 dormant registrants whose registrations lapsed. The comparison that matters is the set of cancellations "for violation": 1,827 in 2018–22 per the RS March 2023 answer, which is about 8% of 21,983. That conflicts with MHA's own 0.4% figure (about 88 cases). The file flags this conflict in its gaps and in claim d, but the narrative does not. So the counter-case rests on the accused ministry's own classification, and that classification conflicts with its own Parliament answer. The SPEC's aligned-side controls (VIF, India Foundation, Ekal, Vidya Bharati) are empty for both receipts and enforcement actions. So the symmetry test compares critics with Christian service charities, not critics with government-aligned groups. The Kudankulam-linked UPA cancellations of 2012, which the SPEC names as a control, are not mentioned in this narrative.
verdicts.denialFound: Responses from the organisations are on record. CPR said the decision was "incomprehensible and disproportionate ... policy reports emanating from our research being equated with current affairs programming" (Tribune, 19 Jan 2024, https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/fcra-licences-of-16-000-ngos-cancelled-in-9-years-582883/amp). Oxfam India said the refusal "will severely hamper these collaborations" but gave no ground (https://www.oxfamindia.org/press-release/fcra-renewal-denied). CARE India said it is "committed to serve the nation" and that the suspension is temporary (recorded in fcra-actions.json). On the government side, MHA's position is that cancellations are for non-filing or violations (JPC briefing, 18 Sep 2026, PTI). MoS Nityanand Rai said the Bill is "dangerous" for those who use FC for "forced religious conversion" (IndiaCSR, https://indiacsr.in/fcra-registered-ngos-foreign-funding-india-22974-crore/). I found no government statement directly answering the "strangling critics" charge. Whether MHA was asked about it is unknown.
verdicts.innocentReading: MHA cleared out a registry that was about 40% non-compliant before 2014. Most cancellations were administrative removals of dormant registrants. The prominent cases (CARE, Oxfam, CPR, WVI) share a common legal thread: after the 2020 Amendment, onward transfer and receipts into non-designated accounts became illegal per se. fcra-actions.json itself records "the modal ground is onward transfer / non-designated account (Oxfam, CPR, CARE India, ...), not content". Aggregate receipts recovering to about ₹23,000 cr fits a smaller set of compliant, larger recipients. The competing reading also fits the same record: selective scrutiny of critics using technical grounds. The Christian charities hit hardest by money fit a different political motive, anti-conversion, so calling them "apolitical" does not rule out politically driven targeting.
verdicts.reason: The overall verdict, "contested", can be defended. The narrative text, however, makes three factual statements that its own sources and sister files do not support. (1) "Oxfam, CPR, CARE lost access with content-linked grounds." CARE India's stated ground (The CSR Universe, recorded in fcra-actions c067) was ₹28.3 cr of foreign money received in FY2012-13 into a domestic-contributions account, plus the remittance purpose codes. That is not content. The Oxfam press release gives no ground, and claim c042 says "Ground not stated in either opened source". Only CPR's ground is content-linked, and that is CPR's own description of MHA's reasons. CARE's final cancellation is also unverified. (2) "Aggregate receipts hit a record." Neither ThePrint/PTI nor IndiaCSR says "record" or "highest". The file has no national totals for FY2022-23 or FY2023-24 ("no answer opened"). The "record" is nominal only, just above ₹22,137 cr in FY2014-15 and ₹22,122 cr in FY2021-22. (3) The 91% non-filing share comes from MHA's own classification. It conflicts with MHA's RS answer of 1,827 violation cancellations in 2018–22, and the narrative presents it without that caveat. The cumulative 21,983 may also include pre-2014 cancellations. Each of the other numbers checks out against its source (40.0% non-filing in 2013; 21,983 and 91.3%; ₹22,974 cr; RDT cleared via Naidu), but together these overstatements make the counter look stronger than the evidence supports.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Replace "Oxfam, CPR, CARE lost access with content-linked grounds" with: "Oxfam (2022, renewal refused; ground not in opened source; later CBI FIR alleges post-2020 sub-grants and designated-account circumvention), CPR (2024, cancelled; CPR says policy reports were equated with current-affairs programming) and CARE India (suspended 2023-06-14 over a FY2012-13 receipt into a non-FCRA account; final cancellation unverified). Only CPR's ground is content-linked on the record." Apply the same fix to strongestCase and to symmetryCheck, which says "critic cases (Oxfam, CPR) carry stated grounds tied to content". 2) Drop "record". Write "₹22,974 cr in FY2024-25, the highest in the years we have (FY2022-23 and FY2023-24 totals not opened; nominal ₹)". 3) Qualify the 91%: "91.3% of 21,983 cumulative cancellations (period unspecified, may include pre-2014) were for non-filing per MHA's own JPC briefing. This conflicts with MHA's RS answer of 1,827 cancellations for violation in 2018–22 (~8%), not 0.4%." 4) Change "apolitical service charities" to "service charities that are not government critics (largely Christian-founded; an anti-conversion motive is a competing reading)". 5) Add to whatWouldChangeThis: the SPEC aligned-side controls (VIF, India Foundation, Ekal/Vidya Bharati) are empty for both receipts and enforcement actions, and the UPA 2012 Kudankulam-linked cancellations are absent. Both are needed before the symmetry claim can hold. 6) Keep status "contested"; for the underlying edges use analytic, with innocentReading attached.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as written: "FCRA-registered associations (in aggregate) received ₹17,832 cr in FY2015-16 and ₹22,974 cr in FY2024-25; the FY2016-19 dip was about 10% and reversed." Both endpoint figures carry the right financial years. The start year is the problem. FY2015-16 was chosen as the base, but the same file has FY2014-15 at ₹22,137 cr (c003, IndiaSpend citing LS Q.1603, 26.07.2016). That was the first full year of the NDA government and the year before the 2015–16 mass cancellations. Measured from FY2014-15, the nominal rise to FY2024-25 is only +3.8% over ten years. The "~10%" figure is also wrong. The trough was FY2016-17 at ₹15,355.17 cr (Deccan Herald: "The year 2016-17 witnessed Rs 15,355.17 crore"), which is 13.9% below ₹17,832 cr and 30.6% below ₹22,137 cr. The ~8% number only appears if you compare to FY2019-20 (₹16,359 cr) and skip the trough. The nominal series did recover, passing FY2015-16 in FY2021-22 (₹22,121.75 cr, RS Q.3253 Annexure I, verified in the PDF).
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is the right one. PTI and India CSR both describe the aggregate as FC received by FCRA-registered associations, per the MHA presentation to the JPC. Quote from ThePrint/PTI, 18 Sep 2026: "The funds received by the FCRA registered NGOs from abroad went up to Rs 22974 crore in 2024-25 from Rs 17832 crore in 2015-16." India CSR repeats the same figures: "an increase of Rs. 5,142 crore, or nearly 28.8%". It does not appear to be an independent source, since it re-reports the same MHA/JPC deck. PIB (22 Jul 2026) gives ~₹22,963 cr for FY2024-25, which corroborates the endpoint. Two comparability caveats. (a) The figures come from returns filed by a given date. The FY2019-20 figure in Deccan Herald was only ₹2,190 cr as of Mar 2021 because returns were still coming in, so snapshot dates differ between years. (b) The 2020 amendment banned sub-granting between FCRA associations. Totals before 2020 may double-count re-granted money, which makes nominal before/after comparisons structurally inconsistent.
verdicts.baseRate: This is an aggregate, so a peer fraction does not apply. The relevant base is inflation and the exchange rate. The CPI-combined annual average (2012=100) was about 124.7 in FY2015-16 and about 192.9 in FY2024-25, a factor of about 1.55. At FY2024-25 prices, ₹17,832 cr equals about ₹27,600 cr, so ₹22,974 cr is a real fall of about 17%. Measured from FY2014-15 (CPI ~119), the real fall is about 36%. In dollars (RBI average about 65.5 in FY15-16 and 84.6 in FY24-25), the total was about $2.72 bn in both years, so it is flat, and down about 25% from about $3.6 bn in FY2014-15. The real series in FY24-25 rupees reads: FY15 ~35.9k, FY16 ~27.6k, FY17 ~22.7k, FY18 ~24.4k, FY19 ~22.8k, FY20 ~21.6k, FY21 ~21.1k, FY22 ~26.0k, FY25 ~23.0k. That is a step down in 2015–17 that never recovered. These CPI and FX values are approximate and have not been opened from a source in this session. Symmetry check: FY2011-12 was ₹11,548 cr (Parliament, UPA period). The FY2014-15 doubling to ₹22,137 cr ("Foreign funding doubled in 2014-15 to Rs 22,137 crore… compared to Rs 12,000 crore in 2013-14", IndiaSpend) is itself an outlier, so the choice of baseline drives the result either way.
verdicts.denialFound: This is a quantitative narrative, not an accusation, so no party is required to respond. MHA's own framing, via PTI to the JPC, is that funds "went up", and the narrative adopts it. I found no MHA or civil-society statement on real or dollar terms. My web search budget ran out, so I did not search for contrary analyses.
verdicts.innocentReading: Two innocent readings fit the "no collapse" side. First, the FY2014-15 ₹22,137 cr may be a reporting artefact: it doubled in a year and was attributed to one LS answer that has not been opened. If so, FY2015-16 is a fair base. Second, the rupee depreciated about 23% against the dollar, which lifts nominal receipts, while the number of recipients halved because 91.3% of cancellations were for not filing returns, not for enforcement. On the "decline" side, a flat dollar value over a decade in which India's nominal GDP roughly doubled is a real and relative contraction. That is not a collapse, but it is not a rise either.
verdicts.reason: The narrative fails its own falsifier. Its whatWouldChangeThis field asks for "a real-terms series (deflated, US$-adjusted) showing a sustained fall". Simple deflation of the file's own series shows exactly that: about −17% real from FY2015-16, about −36% real and −25% in dollars from FY2014-15, flat in dollars from FY2015-16, and no recovery in real terms after 2016–17. Two supporting facts are also wrong or selective. The dip was ~14% nominal at the FY2016-17 trough, not ~10%. The FY2015-16 baseline leaves out the higher FY2014-15 figure that is in the same file. "Collapsed" is still an overstatement, but "unsupported, receipts rose" is only true in nominal rupees. The correct status is contested. The endpoint figures themselves are reported (PTI/JPC) or documented (PIB, RS Q.3253), and they are accurate.
verdicts.corrections: narratives[2].status: "unsupported" -> "contested". Claim text: change "the 2016–19 dip was ~10% and reversed" to "nominal receipts fell ~14% to ₹15,355 cr in FY2016-17 (−31% vs FY2014-15's ₹22,137 cr) and recovered in nominal terms by FY2021-22". strongestCounter: add the trough year FY2016-17 ₹15,355.17 cr (c006). State that the +28.8% rise is nominal; in real terms it is about −17% (CPI-deflated) and flat in dollars (~$2.72 bn both years). strongestCase: add FY2014-15 ₹22,137 cr (c003) → FY2024-25 ₹22,974 cr (+3.8% nominal, ~−36% real, ~−25% in dollars), and flag that c003 is an unexplained one-year doubling awaiting the LS Q.1603 PDF. whatWouldChangeThis: drop the real/USD test, which is now met, and replace it with "a verified FY2014-15 Parliament figure; comparable-snapshot returns; adjustment for pre-2020 sub-grant double counting". Add an analytic claim holding the deflated and USD series, with an innocentReading covering rupee depreciation and non-filer cancellations. Mark India CSR as derivative of PTI, not an independent second outlet.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: MoS Nityanand Rai told the Rajya Sabha that NGOs received ₹905.50 / ₹798.18 / ₹727.16 cr in FY22 / FY21 / FY20, on 15 Mar 2023. The Deccan Herald piece is "Published 15 March 2023, 21:25 IST" and says "The government on Wednesday told the Rajya Sabha". RS Q.3253 was answered on 29.03.2023, two weeks later. So DH cannot have been quoting Q.3253. The answer DH actually used is RS Unstarred Q.1662, answered 15.03.2023 (Satish Chandra Dubey, "Foreign Funds received by NGOs", MHA PDF RS15032023/1662.pdf). The narrative's "March 2023 RS answer" is right for the myth. Its source chain is wrong because it ties the numbers to Q.3253.
verdicts.identityTest: Q.1662 Annexure I, last row: "34 West Bengal 727.16 798.18 905.50". This matches DH's three figures to the paisa. DH's "total of Rs 2,430.84 crore in foreign funding in the last three years" equals 905.50 + 798.18 + 727.16, which is West Bengal's three-year sum. Q.3253's West Bengal row is 727.20 / 798.18 / 906.12 (returns as on 22.03.2023), so only one of the three numbers matches exactly. That makes "those three numbers are West Bengal's rows in the annexure to RS Q.3253" inexact. They are West Bengal's rows in Q.1662. The identity (West Bengal, not all of India) holds.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable as a discrimination test, because this is a data-provenance debunk, not an accusation. The arithmetic can be reproduced. My sums of the 34 rows of Q.3253 Annexure I are 16,359.48 / 17,166.34 / 22,121.75, which match the narrative. My sums of Q.1662 Annexure I are 16,306.04 / 17,058.64 / 22,085.10. Both are about 20–25 times the quoted "₹700–900 cr". Every national series (Q.1662, Q.3253, the MHA presentation to the JPC giving ₹22,974 cr for FY2024-25) puts receipts above ₹16,000 cr a year.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. DH's live page (fetched 26 Sep 2026) still says "Rai said an amount of Rs 905.50 crore in foreign funding was received by NGOs in 2021-22…" and "Indian NGOs received a total of Rs 2,430.84 crore", with no correction notice. DH was not asked by us. No MHA clarification found either. The ministry's own annexure is the record.
verdicts.innocentReading: The DH (DHNS) reporter read the last row of the state-wise annexure (West Bengal, row 34) as the national total, or read the question's national framing onto the final line. This was a transcription error, not deliberate minimisation. The narrative already frames it as a misreading, which is correct. It does not name a family, religion or ethnicity as an actor.
verdicts.reason: The debunk holds on the primary record. MHA's RS USQ 1662 of 15.03.2023 (the answer DH reported that day) lists exactly 727.16 / 798.18 / 905.50 as West Bengal's row. Its 34-row national sums are about ₹16,306 / ₹17,059 / ₹22,085 cr. Q.3253 (29.03.2023) gives about ₹16,359 / ₹17,166 / ₹22,122 cr. The claim that NGOs get "only ₹700–900 cr a year" is therefore false and documented as false. The narrative's source chain is defective, though. It pins the DH figures to Q.3253, which was answered two weeks after DH published and has a slightly different West Bengal row (906.12 / 727.20). The fix is to re-source the narrative, not to kill it.

verdicts.dateTest: Pass. Restated claim: the Union government (MHA, with MoS Nityanand Rai moving the Bill) introduced a Bill creating a Designated Authority to take over FC-created assets, introduced in Lok Sabha on 2026-03-25 and referred to the JPC on 2026-08-12. The Bill is still pending (PIB, 22 Jul 2026: "presently under consideration of Parliament"). The narrative correctly says the Bill "lets" this happen and does not claim any seizure has taken place. The s.15 date is right: the FCRA 2010 received assent on 26-09-2010, and PIB's factsheet lists "Vesting of Assets" among the 2010 changes. The JPC meeting was on 18 Sep 2026, per PTI.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass, with one nuance. The Bill is correctly identified as the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 (PRS bill track). "The Union" as the seizing party is fair shorthand. PRS says proceeds and unutilised FC go "to the Consolidated Fund of India" and assets may go to "ministries, departments, authorities or agencies of the central or state government". PTI calls it "an authority designated by the government". Under the existing s.15, by contrast, assets vest in "a prescribed State Government authority" (PIB). So the move from a State authority to a Union authority is part of what is new. "Church" is how critics frame the target. The Bill itself does not name any religion.
verdicts.baseRate: The provision is religion-neutral on its face. It applies to all 37,710 cancelled or expired certificates (22,498 + 15,212 per PRS, as of 15 Jul 2026) and to every active one on future cessation. That covers religious and secular, Hindu and Christian, government-critical and government-aligned associations alike, so the vesting power does not single anyone out. Any uneven impact would come through who holds FC-built assets. PTI/JPC data show religious associations received Rs 5,150 cr in 2024-25, with Christian associations the largest religious category. Applying the SPEC controls (critical NGOs such as Greenpeace, Amnesty and CPR against aligned or neutral ones such as VIF, India Foundation, Ekal, World Vision and Missionaries of Charity) gives the same legal exposure to all of them. PTI reports 91.3% of the 21,983 cancellations were for not filing returns. That points to an administrative trigger, not one based on viewpoint.
verdicts.denialFound: Government response recorded (ThePrint/PTI, 18 Sep 2026, https://theprint.in/india/fcra-registered-ngos-down-by-half-in-last-10-years-contribution-rises-from-rs-17832-cr-to-rs-22974-cr/3046874/): "The government has rejected the charges and challenged the opposition parties to identify even one provision that discriminates against minorities. The government has also maintained that the proposed legislation is not religion-specific." In the same report, Rai said the Bill is "indeed dangerous" for those engaged in "forced religious conversion" using foreign contribution. PIB factsheet, 22 Jul 2026: the Authority "cannot convert" places of worship, and "No official benefits personally." The narrative does not carry this response and should.
verdicts.innocentReading: About 35,000 registrations were cancelled or ceased over a decade, leaving FC assets "in limbo, which States said they could not take possession of, maintain or manage under the bare Section 15" (PIB). On this reading the Bill supplies a custody and disposal procedure for a vesting power that already existed. It returns assets if registration is restored, protects the religious character of places of worship, and cuts the maximum prison term from 5 years to 1. The plain explanation is administrative clean-up of a legal gray zone, not confiscation aimed at churches.
verdicts.reason: The narrative survives as a contested item because every component is in primary or near-primary sources. PRS says: "The Bill creates a Designated Authority for the vesting, supervision, management and disposal of foreign contribution and assets ... the Authority must ensure that its religious character is maintained. The Bill reduces the maximum penalty ... from imprisonment of five years to one year." PRS also confirms proceeds are "credited to the Consolidated Fund of India". PIB confirms s.15 has vested assets "since 2010". Two problems prevent a clean pass. (1) The strongestCounter uses PIB's framing, which PRS contradicts. PIB says cessation already triggers vesting, but PRS says "The Bill adds that cessation of the certificate will also lead to vesting of assets." PRS also identifies other new elements: permanent vesting and sale; an asset "created or acquired partly by foreign funds ... shall entirely vest"; no way to exit FCRA without losing assets; the Rs 10 lakh two-year utilisation rule under the 2026 Rules; and no appeal or hearing when renewal is denied. "s.15 has existed since 2010" is therefore true but understates what changes. (2) The strongestCase joins two figures that do not belong together. It cites Rs 35,968 cr of unutilised balances as the "pool" at risk, but PTI gives that figure as total unutilised FC for 2024-25 (FDs, utilisation accounts and designated accounts), which mostly sits with active filers. No source says it belongs to cancelled or ceased registrants.
verdicts.corrections: narratives[4].strongestCase: remove "(₹35,968 cr unutilised balances alone)" or rephrase it as "total unutilised FC across all registrants in 2024-25 was ₹35,968 cr (MHA to JPC); the share held by cancelled/ceased registrants is not published". Also add PRS's key issues: non-renewal now triggers vesting; partly-FC assets vest entirely; no way to leave FCRA without losing assets; the Rs 10 lakh/2-year utilisation rule can trigger loss; no appeal or hearing on renewal denial. narratives[4].strongestCounter: qualify "s.15 has vested such assets since 2010" to "s.15 has vested assets of cancelled (and, since 2020, surrendered) registrants in a State-prescribed authority since 2010; the Bill adds cessation, a central Designated Authority, permanent vesting and sale to the CFI". Also add the government response: rejects the minority-targeting charge, says the Bill is not religion-specific, and that places of worship cannot be converted (PTI 18 Sep 2026; PIB 22 Jul 2026). Add the opposition's allegation (PTI: provisions "will choke legitimate funding for Christian NGOs") as the named party making the church framing. Keep it as a narrative only. It must not become an edge that names a religion as a target or actor. Keep status "contested", with the component facts at the documented tier. For consistency with PRS, note that the PIB figure of "nearly 20,000 cancelled" differs from PRS's 22,498.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim, it reads: RGF received money from a Chinese state source in FY2005-06 (and FY2006-07 per Shah). The date holds. The Indian Express article of 24 Oct 2022 says: "The RGF annual report for 2005-06 mentions the Embassy of The People's Republic of China as one of the 'partner organisations and donors'." UPA was in office from 2004 to 2014 and Sonia Gandhi chaired RGF, so the periods overlap. The receipt falls under FCRA 1976, not the 2010 Act. The PMNRF-to-RGF allegation is dated by Nadda to "UPA years", and the donor-list images he posted cover 2005-06 and 2007-08. No source puts a PMNRF transfer and the Chinese receipt in the same transaction or year as each other.
verdicts.identityTest: This fails on the donor. Every source names the "Embassy of the People's Republic of China" (IE), or "People's Republic of China and the Chinese embassy" (Nadda, quoted in IE), or "the Chinese embassy" (Shah, Tribune 2022-12-14). None of them names the Chinese Communist Party. CPC appears only in the Congress counter-attack about BJP/RSS contacts with the CPC (HT 2020-07-08). "The same government the family led" is also wrong on identity. The UPA Prime Minister was Manmohan Singh. PMNRF is chaired by the PM, and HT itself says PMNRF "does not get any budgetary support", so "taxpayer" money is contradicted by the cited source. The claim also makes a family the actor, which the stance rules forbid for an edge.
verdicts.baseRate: Foreign-embassy funding or partnership for Indian think tanks and foundations was common before the 2010 Act, and was mostly lawful under FCRA 1976 with prior permission or registration. Embassies routinely appear on donor and partner lists of policy institutes, so being listed as a donor does not single RGF out. Symmetry: the same lens applied to the SPEC controls, such as government-aligned think tanks with foreign-government exchanges, or BJP-CPC party delegations (which Congress raised), would produce a "China money" story just as easily. We have not quantified this. What does single RGF out is the 2022 cancellation, and its grounds are unadjudicated and not published.
verdicts.denialFound: Partial. HT 2020-07-08: "In its response, the Congress said the BJP was engaging in diversionary tactics, questioned it on visits and exchanges between the BJP and the Communist Party of China (CPC) over the past decade, and alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared a 'strange bonhomie' with China even as the borders were insecure." I found no specific RGF rebuttal of the amount or the purpose in the sources I opened. The web-search budget was exhausted, so I could not look further. The file correctly records the Congress response as a contra (c011).
verdicts.innocentReading: The PRC embassy was one of many donors and partners listed in RGF's and RGICS's FY2005-06 annual report. That was routine disclosure, during a period when UPA government policy itself was exploring closer economic ties with China. An RGICS study found an India-China FTA beneficial, which IE describes as a study "suggested it to be beneficial to India". That is consistent with an ordinary policy view and does not need a paid-for quid pro quo. PSU and ministry donations to a large foundation were common, and no source shows PMNRF money paying for, or linked to, the China-funded work.
verdicts.reason: The narrative's headline sentence turns an opposition allegation into a statement of fact, and it joins three separately sourced items into an implication that no source makes. The three items are: (1) the embassy listed as a donor, which is documented; (2) Nadda's allegation that PMNRF funded RGF, which is alleged; (3) a study the BJP characterises as China-favourable, which is alleged. The phrase "Chinese Communist Party" is in no source, since all of them say embassy/PRC. The phrase "taxpayer" is contradicted by HT's own note that PMNRF gets no budgetary support. "To produce China-favourable research", meaning paid purpose, is Nadda's and Prasad's claim only. The strongestCase also misstates the ₹1.35 crore figure as coming from "the cancellation order itself". Per Tribune, it came from Amit Shah's remarks to reporters outside Parliament ("Had he got the opportunity, said Shah, he would have told Parliament..."). The order has not been published. The "contested" status and the counter paragraph are sound. Only the claim text and that citation fail.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Rewrite narrative.claim as attributed allegation: "BJP leaders (J P Nadda, Ravi Shankar Prasad, 25 Jun 2020) alleged that RGF took $300,000 from the PRC and Chinese embassy in 2005-06 to fund studies 'not in the national interest', and separately that PMNRF donated to RGF in UPA years." Drop "Chinese Communist Party", "in effect paid for by the same government", "taxpayer", and the family-as-actor framing. 2) strongestCase: replace "the government's 2022 cancellation order itself cites a ₹1.35 crore Chinese-embassy receipt" with "Home Minister Amit Shah said on 2022-12-13/14, to reporters and not on the Lok Sabha floor (Tribune), that RGF received ₹1.35 crore from the Chinese embassy in 2005-06 and 2006-07, 'not in conformity with the FCRA laws'; the order itself is not public". Note the two differing amounts: $300,000 (Nadda) versus ₹1.35 crore across two years (Shah). 3) Add the HT sentence "PMNRF ... does not get any budgetary support" to strongestCounter. 4) Sibling fcra-actions:c057: its label says "Lok Sabha", but Tribune reports the statement was made outside the House. Fix the label. 5) Keep status "contested" and tier alleged. Do not create a CPC→RGF or PMNRF→China-research edge.

verdicts.dateTest: Limb 1–2: "India Foundation had ministers as directors and undisclosed revenue sources, as of Nov 2017." The Wire (4 Nov 2017) names the directors from IF's own website at that date: "defence minister Nirmala Sitharaman and commerce and industry minister Suresh Prabhu, and two ministers of state – Jayant Sinha (civil aviation) and M.J. Akbar (external affairs)". The dates overlap with ministerial tenure in Nov 2017. But only two were cabinet rank. Sitharaman was MoS (Independent Charge) from 2014 and became Cabinet Defence Minister only in Sept 2017. Sinha and Akbar were MoS, and Akbar joined the ministry only in July 2016. So "cabinet-minister" fits 2 of 4, and c015's "four directors appointed ministers in 2014" (Wikipedia paraphrase) is wrong for Akbar and is not in The Wire text. Outlook (24 Nov 2014, cited in The Wire's 5 Nov 2017 follow-up) reported that Sitharaman had "left the foundation's board of directors after joining the ministry", so her director window is itself disputed. Limb 3: "Vivek Doval ran GNY Asia Fund (Cayman), registered 21 Nov 2016, per documents to July 2018." The Caravan published this on 16 Jan 2019, so the window is consistent. No date problem, but no date ties the fund to IF.
verdicts.identityTest: This fails on the decisive limb. The Caravan names Vivek Doval (UK citizen, Singapore resident) as director of GNY Asia Fund and links it to "businesses run by his brother Shaurya": Zeus Caps/Zeus Strategic, Torch Investment and Torcia Advisors. It does not link it to India Foundation. The only IF mentions describe who Shaurya is ("a BJP politician who heads the India Foundation") and say that "Several BJP ministers serve as India Foundation's directors". There is no sentence tying the fund, its money or its staff to India Foundation. "Doval family runs" names a family as the actor, while the source names two individuals (Vivek, with administrative overlaps to Shaurya's firms). Ajit Doval is named only as the father who "demands crackdown on tax havens", not as someone running anything. India Foundation is identified only by name. No trust registration number is on file. The Wire and its follow-up cite the FCRA certificate number, which the record should capture.
verdicts.baseRate: Opaque funding is weakly discriminating. Most Indian registered trusts and think tanks do not publish audited accounts or donor lists. The controls: VIF publishes little, RGF published annual reports with donor lists, and CPR/ORF publish annual reports. Sitting ministers serving as directors of a party-aligned think tank that takes corporate sponsorship is rare, and that part does discriminate. On symmetry: the RGF control has sitting UPA-era office-holders on its trustee board (Sonia Gandhi throughout UPA; the file should verify whether ministers such as P. Chidambaram served as trustees while in office). The same lens must be applied there before this is framed as unique to India Foundation. Relatives of senior officials running offshore-domiciled funds is common in finance (Cayman is the default domicile for Asia hedge funds). The distinguishing point in the Caravan story is the contrast with Ajit Doval's 2011 tax-haven report, not any illegality.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, three responses. (1) India Foundation statement by Shaurya Doval, 4 Nov 2017, reproduced in full at https://thewire.in/politics/shaurya-doval-response-the-wire-questions-answers-india-foundation and covered at https://www.thequint.com/news/hot-news/ajit-dovals-son-shaurya-conflict-of-interest-the-wire. It calls the article "speculative and clearly intends to insinuate wrong-doing where there is none". It says the directors were associated with IF before becoming ministers and that "No foreign funding has ever been received by the Foundation from any overseas private corporation or individual". It says "The Foundation and its Directors have not furthered the commercial or private interests of any company". It says the Foundation "is in complete compliance with all statutory requirements". The four ministers were sent questionnaires and did not reply. (2) The Caravan: Vivek Doval, Shaurya Doval and Ajit Doval were all sent questionnaires and did not respond. Vivek Doval then filed criminal defamation against The Caravan, Kaushal Shroff and Jairam Ramesh, alleging "inferences and innuendos" implying money laundering and round-tripping. (3) Indian Express, 20 Dec 2020 (https://indianexpress.com/article/india/defamation-case-jairam-ramesh-apologises-to-vivek-doval-7111783/): Ramesh apologised "for any hurt the statements may have caused", and Doval's lawyer said "proceedings against The Caravan and Shroff will continue". Final outcome not found; web search budget exhausted.
verdicts.innocentReading: India Foundation is a registered trust whose founding directors happened to become ministers and stayed on its board, which is an impropriety of appearance rather than proof of favours. It pays for events through conference sponsorship. Its leadership says that is not a "foreign contribution", and Indian trusts generally do not publish donor lists. Separately, Vivek Doval is a UK-resident fund manager who set up a small ($11.19m per a July 2018 SEC filing) Asia equities fund in the Cayman Islands, the standard domicile for such funds. It shares staff with his brother's Singapore/India asset-management firms, which is ordinary for family businesses in one sector. None of this involves India Foundation's money.
verdicts.reason: The claim as worded is a conjunction that implies something none of its sources say. The Wire (4 Nov 2017, opened and quoted) supports "opaque financials" ("it refuses to part with any information about its source of revenue") and alleged conflicts of interest from ministers serving as directors. The Caravan (16 Jan 2019, opened; body rendered) supports only a Cayman fund run by Vivek Doval that is "linked inextricably to businesses run by his brother Shaurya". Nothing in it connects that fund to India Foundation. "Undisclosed" is also unsupported: the fund was traced through SEC, Companies House and Cayman filings. The "tied to it" link to India Foundation is the load-bearing inference, and it is source-does-not-say. "Doval family runs" makes a family the actor, which the contract bars from edges and allows only as a calibrated narrative. The first two limbs survive at reported (one credible outlet with published documents, with IF's denial on record). The offshore limb survives only as "Vivek Doval runs a Cayman fund with administrative overlaps with Shaurya Doval's firms", tier reported and contested by a defamation suit still pending against The Caravan as of Dec 2020.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Split narrative:1 into separate claims. (a) "India Foundation did not disclose its revenue sources, and in Nov 2017 listed two cabinet ministers (Sitharaman, Prabhu) and two ministers of state (Sinha, Akbar) as directors": reported, The Wire. (b) "Vivek Doval directs GNY Asia Fund (Cayman, reg. 21 Nov 2016), with administrative overlaps with Shaurya Doval's firms (Zeus/Torch/Torcia)": reported, The Caravan, contested by a pending defamation suit. For the claim that the offshore fund is tied to India Foundation, set status: unsupported, with killIf/upgradeIf naming any document linking GNY/Torch money or staff to IF. 2. Remove "Doval family" as the actor and "undisclosed" from the narrative text. 3. Replace "cabinet-minister" with "two cabinet ministers and two ministers of state". 4. Fix c015 d-field: The Wire does not say the four were "appointed Union ministers in 2014". Akbar became MoS in July 2016, and Sitharaman became Cabinet Defence Minister in Sept 2017. Add the Outlook 24 Nov 2014 report (via The Wire follow-up) that Sitharaman had left the board, as contra. Drop the "could not render The Wire body" caveat: the articleBody is extractable from JSON-LD in the page source. 5. Update whatWouldChangeThis: the Caravan body was rendered (curl with browser UA). Add IF's full 4 Nov 2017 denial text and URL to strongestCounter. Note the Quint report and the Wire follow-up URL as sources. Record that ministers and the Dovals were asked and did not reply. 6. Add an RGF symmetry note checking whether sitting UPA ministers served as trustees, so the ministers-as-directors point is tested against the control.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as: Parliament (NDA majority; Finance Minister Arun Jaitley) amended FCRA's definition of "foreign source" through the Finance Act 2016, backdated to FCRA 2010. It then used the Finance Act 2018 to backdate the change to 5 Aug 1976. These amendments cleared pre-2009 Sterlite/Sesa (Vedanta) donations to BJP and INC, which the Delhi HC had found in breach on 28 Mar 2014. The order holds together. The donations run up to 2009 (the judgment says the petition covered donations "up to the year 2009"). The HC order is dated 28 Mar 2014. The amendments come in 2016 and 2018, and the 2018 one reaches back to FCRA 1976's start date. Carnegie (Vaishnav, 6 Feb 2018) quotes the Finance Bill 2018 Statement of Objects and Reasons: "It is proposed to bring the said amendment with effect from the 5th August, 1976 the date of commencement of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976". Neither of the narrative's own sources gives the 2018 date or the 1976 backdating. Wikipedia only says "on two separate occasions". Its FCRA-related Finance Acts are 2016 and 2017, and those concern electoral bonds.
verdicts.identityTest: The Indian Kanoon judgment (W.P.(C) 131/2013, Nandrajog and Jayant Nath JJ, 28 Mar 2014) names the parties only as "Respondent No.3" and "Respondent No.4". The strings "Bharatiya" and "Congress" do not appear in the fetched text. It identifies Respondent No.3 through the STC/MMTC donations admitted by "Sh.Motilal Mehra, the Treasurer of the party", which is INC. The BJP link for Respondent No.4 comes from outside the judgment. Carnegie 2018 names both parties explicitly: "found both the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its principal rival, the Indian National Congress, guilty". The donor is identified correctly: Sterlite, 55.1% held by Vedanta Resources plc (UK). The same judgment also records that "Sh.Anil Aggarwal, an Indian National and a citizen of India holds more than 50% issued share capital of Vedanta Resources plc". So the money was "foreign" only through the ownership structure, and was Indian-controlled in substance. The narrative leaves this out.
verdicts.baseRate: India routinely uses retrospective amendments passed as Finance Act money bills. Examples are the 2012 Vodafone tax amendment and the 2016 and 2017 electoral-bond changes to the RPA, Companies Act, IT Act and RBI Act. So the vehicle alone tells us little. What does discriminate is that the change was made after a court finding against the two parties that benefited, and was then extended back to 1976 specifically to cover the pre-2010 donations. The claim is symmetric: it names both BJP and INC. The fleet control (UPA 2011–14 versus NDA 2014–26) does not change the reading. No other party was a respondent, so there is no rival for comparison.
verdicts.denialFound: None found from BJP or INC. I did not locate any statement from either party, and whether anyone asked them is unknown. The government's stated rationale appears in the Finance Bill 2018 Statement of Objects and Reasons, quoted by Carnegie. The operative change says a company is not a "foreign source" if its foreign shareholding is "within the limits specified for foreign investment", which aligns FCRA with FDI/FEMA limits. That is the official innocent reading, and the narrative does not record it. The WebSearch budget was used up, so I could not check for any later SC disposition of the parties' appeals or the ADR challenge.
verdicts.innocentReading: The FCRA 1976/2010 test (more than 50% of shares held by a foreign-incorporated company) treated Indian-controlled groups as foreign. Vedanta Resources plc was itself majority-held by an Indian citizen, Anil Agarwal. Aligning the test with sectoral FDI limits is a coherent policy change that critics also accept is debatable. Carnegie itself says: "To be fair, reasonable people can disagree as to the appropriate definition of what a foreign company ought to be." Congress's non-opposition to a money bill it could not block in the Rajya Sabha could reflect agreement on the policy rather than collusion. The HC finding was "prima-facie" and remitted to MHA to "re-look and re-appraise". It was not a final adjudication of unlawfulness with penalty.
verdicts.reason: The factual core holds. The Delhi HC found BJP and INC's Sterlite/Sesa receipts "prima-facie ... clearly fall foul of the ban imposed under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976" (para 73). Finance Acts 2016 and 2018 then redefined "foreign source" retrospectively back to 5 Aug 1976, with the opposition supporting it or not resisting. What fails is the claim as framed and tiered. (1) "Cover-up" attributes intent. That is a characterization by commentators, not a documented fact: Carnegie/Vaishnav ("in their rush to cover up their tracks") and ADR co-founder Jagdeep Chhokar in the Deccan Herald ("in attempts to save the BJP and the Congress from being prosecuted"). Chhokar's organisation was the petitioner, so he is an interested party. (2) The narrative's second source is Wikipedia, which is not a credible outlet under the contract. Its "shield the BJP and the Congress" line is Chhokar's op-ed restated. That op-ed also gets the HC case wrong ("under the guise of receiving donations from electoral trusts"), and Wikipedia calls the Act the "Foreign Currency Regulation Act". (3) Neither listed source supports the 2018/1976 specifics. Only Carnegie, which is not listed, does. (4) "Unlawful" overstates a prima facie finding and omits that the donor was Indian-controlled. (5) status "well-supported" relies on reasoning from absence ("NOT contested ... itself informative") and ignores the government's stated FDI-alignment rationale. The claim is not a kill: the uncomfortable part is well sourced. But the bipartisan-cover-up framing should be recorded as analytic, attributed to named critics, with the innocent reading attached. It should not be published as a well-supported narrative.
verdicts.corrections: narratives[2].status: change "well-supported" to "contested". The factual core can be called well-supported only in a separate sentence. narratives[2].claim: reword to "The 2016 and 2018 Finance Acts retrospectively redefined 'foreign source' under FCRA back to 5 Aug 1976, removing the basis of the Delhi HC's 2014 prima facie finding that BJP and INC accepted foreign-source donations from Vedanta subsidiaries Sterlite and Sesa; critics (Carnegie's Milan Vaishnav; ADR's Jagdeep Chhokar) call this a bipartisan cover-up."
